TRANSCRIPT:
Q: Intro greeting
A: Hi, um, it's really nice to meet you. I'm Anya. I'm looking forward to the chat. I, uh, have a lot to say about language learning!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, um, I grew up in Ukraine, and I've been living in Poland for, like, the past year or so. I moved because of, you know, all the conflict back home. It's been, uh, quite a journey and a big adjustment. I'm trying to learn Polish really fast because, um, I need to work and communicate here. It’s, uh, quite a struggle sometimes. My background is in teaching, so it’s, like, really strange to be the one learning something so urgently now.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine. It's a beautiful city, full of history and life. Everything feels really vibrant and, you know, connected.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was wonderful! Kyiv is, um, such a lively place. There’s always something happening, like festivals, music, everything. I loved the summers there, spending time with friends in the parks, just, you know, enjoying life. It was normal, and safe, until, well, recent events.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: The biggest turning point was, uh, when I had to leave Ukraine. It was, um, something I never imagined doing. Packing up my life, just like that, and moving to Poland. It was, uh, so sudden and overwhelming. But, you know, I had to look for safety and a future.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because everything changed. My sense of security, um, my plans, my future, all shifted. Suddenly, I was in a new country with a new language, no familiar faces. It made me, um, rethink everything about my life. My priorities changed overnight.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I just took it day by day. It was really hard, but, um, I focused on practical things, like finding a place to stay and starting to learn Polish immediately. I had no choice but to adapt quick. I leaned heavily on, you know, the Ukrainian community here and whatever resources I could find.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Honestly, right now, it’s all about stability. I need to be able to communicate effectively, find a stable job, and, you know, create a new life here in Poland. So, learning Polish is my top priority. It’s frustrating, but crucial.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because without language, you can't really integrate. I mean, I want to be independent, not rely on, you know, translators or other people all the time. Language is the key to, um, every opportunity here, from work to just ordering a coffee.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? Hmm, it's when I manage to get through a conversation in Polish without much help, you know? Or when I feel I've learned something new that's, um, useful. Meeting new friends, maybe, or just feeling a bit more at home here.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: It's that sense of progress. Like, when I can, um, look back and see, hey, I handled that conversation with my neighbor, or I understood more in the Polish news. It’s small, but these little victories mean a lot.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I try to weigh the options, you know? I think about the benefits and risks, talk to people I trust, and then, um, sometimes just go with my gut. Like, moving to Poland, there wasn’t a perfect decision, just what felt like the only decision then.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I used to be more of a planner, but, um, everything lately has taught me to go with the flow more. Plans change, things happen unexpectedly, so I try to, uh, adapt and adjust now.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, like when I first got here, I planned to start Polish classes right away, but they were full. Instead of waiting, I just jumped into using apps and, um, learning from people around me. It wasn’t ideal, but it was necessary.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Oh, I don’t love risk, but I’ve learned, uh, to face it head-on. Sometimes, like with moving here, it’s unavoidable. I try to prepare as much as I can and then, you know, just push through. It gets easier, but, uh, it’s still nerve-wracking.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: I start with some Polish practice, either on Duolingo or, um, by talking to locals. Then I head out to look for work opportunities, maybe attend a class if I can. Afternoons are for more practical things, like shopping or, you know, appointments. I try to, um, take a bit of time to relax in the evening, but it’s often filled with more study—trying to cram in as much as I can.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the language study. It’s mentally exhausting. Polish is, um, quite different from Ukrainian. Plus, the constant need to find work, to navigate daily life in a new language—it's a lot. The uncertainty of, you know, what each day will bring, that’s tiring too.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more energy for, um, socializing. Making new friends here is hard, and I’d like to, you know, build a support network. Also, just some time for myself, to relax and, you know, not always stress about the next challenge.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Time and language, definitely. Um, everything was about adapting quickly, learning fast. But the language has been this, um, constant barrier. I feel like it holds me back from, you know, just living normally, getting jobs, making connections.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I’m doing as much as I can, like using Duolingo and other resources, attending local classes when I can. Also, um, I try to talk to people, listen more, you know, immerse myself as much as possible. It’s slow, but I keep pushing.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: Right now, it’s mostly people back in Ukraine, like family and old friends. They’re, um, my main support even from afar. Also, a few people I’ve met here in Poland, mostly through, um, community groups and language networks.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: With my family, it’s a constant line of support. We talk almost daily. My new friends here, it’s more, um, tentative but supportive. We’re all in similar situations, trying to find our way in a new country, so we help each other out.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Probably in my apartment or at, um, local cafés. Places where I can sit and study, just focus. Also, language classes occasionally, those are, um, really important right now.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Safe, in a way, but also kind of isolated. At home, it’s my personal space, but I also feel, um, cut off from the world. In public places, I’m just, you know, another face in the crowd, working hard.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The language barrier, mostly. It’s like, when I’m home, I can relax a bit, but when I step out, everything feels, um, challenging. Always trying to understand or be understood, it’s tiring.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: My family, definitely. We’re still really close, and, um, they know me best. Here in Poland, I try to reach out to my new friends and, uh, the community groups I’ve joined. It helps to talk things through with people who, you know, understand.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: It was definitely when I had an interview for a job and, um, I couldn’t understand half of what they were asking. I felt so defeated, knowing I could do the job but couldn’t communicate that. It was, um, really discouraging.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a blow to my confidence, you know? I questioned whether I’d ever get to a point where I’m fluent enough. It made me, um, doubt my progress and feel anxious about the future, where I’d fit in or how I’d sustain myself here.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I took a step back to, uh, reassess how I was learning. I added more practical conversations into my routine, like talking more with locals or language partners. It helped to see, you know, actual improvements outside of apps. Just a reminder that every little bit counts.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Music, definitely. Just, um, listening to familiar Ukrainian songs or even trying Polish music to help with the language. It kind of, you know, brings me peace and helps me reset my mind.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to be fluent in Polish, working in my field here, and have a solid group of friends. I want to feel, um, really at home and part of the community, not like an outsider just getting by. Stability is what I’m aiming for, ultimately.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d love for this constant stress about language to be gone. I want the freedom to, you know, pursue opportunities without that barrier. And more time for personal things, not just survival, you know?

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: I started with textbooks and online resources, but it was, um, really dry and didn’t help with speaking. I tried attending some group classes, but they were either too full or, um, slow-paced. I needed something more flexible and, you know, quick to access.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of immediate feedback, really. I’d spend ages on, you know, exercises, and I wasn’t sure if I was saying things right. It was hard to gauge, um, real progress and it was often easier to just not speak at all.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: During a community event here, I, um, tried to introduce myself and ended up making a simple mistake that, you know, changed the entire meaning. Everyone was polite, but I felt so embarrassed. I realized then that I needed more, like, practical, everyday Polish.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: Through a friend also learning Polish. They mentioned it as, um, an easy way to practice daily, and since it’s an app, I thought it would fit well into my routine, you know?

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I liked the idea of, you know, structured lessons that could give immediate feedback. Plus, it was free, which is, um, really helpful when you’re on a tight budget. The promise of being able to practice anytime, anywhere was really appealing too.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure, so I, um, opened the app in the morning. I usually start with a quick review of the previous lessons. Then I dive into a new lesson, maybe on, like, food vocabulary or practical phrases. I mean, I try to focus on things I’ll actually use in daily conversation. The exercises, they’re mostly matching words or translating simple sentences. I like that it's interactive, but I find myself, you know, wanting more context or examples.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The immediate feedback. When I type something wrong, it, um, corrects me right away. It’s good for, you know, picking up on spelling errors or grammatical mistakes. And the ability to repeat things as much as I need is really handy.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: It’s how slow the progression feels. I mean, I need to be conversational, like, yesterday, not just able to name fruits and animals. I get that it’s building basics, but, um, the urgency of my situation just isn’t there in the app's pacing.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: It treats learning like a game with, you know, points and streaks, which is fun but, um, not enough for real-life necessities. I need to progress faster and handle real conversations, not just earn virtual trophies.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: I was trying to order at a café, and I realized I didn’t know how to, um, string together the right words. I mean, Duolingo covered basic phrases, but real-life speaking is much more complicated. I felt really limited in that moment. It just, you know, hit me how much further I needed to go.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, definitely. I use other apps like Memrise for more vocabulary, and I, um, look up YouTube videos for listening practice. I also try to have conversations with, you know, locals or other learners to supplement what I'm not getting from Duolingo.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They offer more context and, um, real-world usage. Duolingo’s phrases sometimes feel out of touch with, you know, everyday conversation. Other resources can be a bit more comprehensive in covering more practical and modern language.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: That I never reach the level of fluency I need to, um, fully participate in Polish life. I mean, if I can’t communicate, I may face issues with finding stable work or, you know, building a life here. It’s, um, worrying to think about being stuck.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it’ll make me conversationally fluent, quickly. Every time I open it, I want it to, you know, push me closer to speaking with ease and understanding the nuances of the language. But, uh, often it doesn’t feel fast enough.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I successfully, um, use what I’ve learned in real situations. Like, if I can hold a conversation at the store or, you know, understand a newscast better than before. That’s when I feel it’s making a difference.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d add more practical conversation modules, you know? Stuff that’s immediately useful, like handling everyday situations—ordering food, making appointments. More focus on real-life interactions, less on just leveling up.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there were more free resources focused on rapid language acquisition for people with urgent needs, like refugees. It should be, you know, more about immediate integration than just traditional learning paths.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Not really, I think we covered a lot. Just, um, thanks for listening. It’s nice to share these thoughts and, you know, maybe it’ll help improve things for others in my situation.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, if it helps create better resources or solutions, then, uh, go ahead. Anything to, you know, make this process easier for others too.

TRANSCRIPT:
Q: Intro greeting
A: That’s fine with me. I’m happy to share as long as you’re actually interested in serious learners, not just people playing around.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: I’m 31, I work in tech, and most of my choices have been driven by career goals—what will open more doors, what will increase my options. I’m pretty disciplined and structured in how I spend my time; I like setting a goal, building a system, and then grinding toward it.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a mid-sized city outside the U.S., then moved here for grad school. So I’ve already done one big relocation and know how much language and culture matter for opportunities.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was competitive in a different way—more about grades and professional prestige than hobbies. The expectation was that you’d aim for something 'respectable,' so I got used to thinking about education and skills as investments.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: A big turning point was getting an offer from a company abroad and realizing that my lack of advanced language skills was going to keep me on the sidelines for certain roles. I could do the job, but I wasn’t able to handle higher-level conversations in the local language, and that bothered me.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It was the first time I felt capped by something other than technical ability. It drove home that language isn’t just a 'nice to have,' it literally affects whether I get invited into key rooms or not.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I decided I needed to treat language learning like any other serious skill: have a clear goal, long-term plan, and consistent practice. I started testing different tools and approaches, trying to find something that fit a more intensive, professional mindset.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I care most about building a career that gives me geographic and professional flexibility. Being able to move countries, work with international teams, and not be limited by language is a big part of that.

Q: Why is that important?
A: I don’t want my career trajectory to be dictated by where I was born or which language I grew up speaking. Language is leverage—if I can operate in multiple languages at a high level, I have more control over my path.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: On a really good day, I get through a deep work block, make progress on a long-term project, and fit in a solid study session where I actually push my limits. It’s less about feeling 'cozy' and more about feeling like I advanced the ball in meaningful ways.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I can point to concrete steps toward my bigger goals—completed tasks, new concepts mastered, hard conversations handled well—then it’s a good day. I like visible progress, not just checking boxes.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I look at it through the lens of long-term impact. I’ll think about whether this decision expands or narrows my future options, and I’ll usually map out best, middle, and worst-case scenarios before committing.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I’m definitely a planner. I can adapt, but I’m most comfortable when I have a structure and know how my efforts connect to bigger goals.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Recently, I started considering relocation to another country, and instead of just daydreaming, I built a plan: which language level I need for interviews, which certifications help, which networks to build. Language learning is part of that plan, not just a side hobby.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I evaluate whether the risk is calculated or reckless. If the upside is meaningful for my long-term goals and the downside is survivable, I’m willing to take the risk, but I still want a strategy behind it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: On a typical weekday, I start with some light admin, work a full day in a fairly demanding role, and then carve out time in the evening for skill-building: reading, coding, or language practice. I try to treat language study like going to the gym—it’s on the calendar, not optional.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Work takes the most time and energy, especially when I’m leading projects or meetings. After that, the 'second shift' is investing in my future self—studying, networking, or planning next moves—which is rewarding but tiring.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I’d like more uninterrupted blocks for deep study—like focused reading, conversation practice, or intensive exercises in the language. Short, scattered sessions are better than nothing, but they don’t get me to the level I’m aiming for.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Time and cognitive load have been the main constraints. I’m juggling a demanding job and serious upskilling, so I have to be very picky about tools that waste my time or slow me down.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I’ve cut out a lot of 'lightweight' activities that don’t move the needle, and I evaluate tools based on ROI. If something feels like fluff or busywork, I either change how I use it or drop it.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I’m closest to a couple of friends who are also career-focused, plus my partner. They understand that my schedule is structured and that a lot of my life is built around long-term goals.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Supportive, honest, and aligned. We respect each other’s ambitions and sometimes act as accountability partners.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly at work and at home, with a lot of time online because so much of my work and learning happens on a screen.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I’d say focused and somewhat stressed, in a purposeful way. I’m pushing myself, but it’s in service of goals I chose, so it feels more like training than random chaos.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I’ve built my environment around productivity—quiet workspace, good tools, clear plans. That helps, but it also means I get impatient with anything that feels like it’s wasting my effort.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to research—articles, books, or expert advice. If it’s something murky or emotional, I’ll talk to my partner or a close friend, but first instinct is: gather information, then decide.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: One tough moment was being in a meeting with senior people from another country and realizing I couldn’t contribute at the level I wanted because my language skills weren’t strong enough. I understood parts, but I couldn’t jump in comfortably with nuanced points.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It felt like a ceiling I kept hitting. Day to day, it pushed me to take language practice more seriously, but it also made me more critical of tools that felt too superficial or slow.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I started doubling down on more intensive methods—reading articles in the language, watching long-form content, and looking for conversation partners. I still used Duolingo, but more as a warm-up, and I got increasingly frustrated when gamified features and hearts got in the way of serious, intensive practice.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: It helps to zoom out and remember why I’m doing this—reminding myself that each hour invested gets me closer to real fluency. Then I pick one focused task, do it well, and rebuild momentum from there.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: A few years from now, I hope I’m either relocated or working in a role where language is a non-issue for me—I can operate in meetings, negotiations, and social settings without feeling like the foreigner who needs everything simplified. I want language to be a strength, not a limitation.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like my language skills to feel more integrated into my professional identity, not something I’m still 'working on.' Right now, I’m somewhere between basic comfort and real fluency, and I want to cross that gap.

Q: Before PRODUCT, how did you handle the core job?
A: Before Duolingo, I used textbooks, online courses, and some tutoring. It was more traditional—grammar explanations, structured exercises, and occasional conversation sessions.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The downside was that it could be dry and sometimes overwhelming to manage alone. It took effort to keep things engaging and to know what to study next, especially on busy days.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: It didn’t 'fail' in a dramatic way, but there were periods where I’d stall because planning the next steps felt like work on top of work. That’s what made me try more guided tools like Duolingo in the first place.

Q: How did you first hear about PRODUCT?
A: I heard about Duolingo like everyone else—online, through friends, and through the general buzz about it being a popular language app.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I liked the idea of having a structured path and something I could do in short bursts on my phone. I thought it might be a good way to keep the basics fresh between heavier study sessions.

Q: Walk through a recent PRODUCT use.
A: Recently, I opened Duolingo after work intending to do some targeted practice on a grammar point I’m working on. I did a couple of lessons, made a few mistakes, burned through hearts faster than I expected, and then found myself locked out of 'normal' practice unless I either waited, watched ads, or did specific exercises; at that point I got annoyed, because I was in the mood for serious practice and the hearts system was literally slowing me down.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The helpful part is that it gives me a quick, structured way to review vocabulary and basic sentence patterns. For that, Duolingo is okay for basics—it keeps core material circulating in my head.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: The frustrating part is the feeling of being throttled by the gamified systems when I’m trying to work seriously. When I’m ready to focus, hearts and other mechanics that limit practice feel like the app is putting training wheels back on, even though I’m asking it to let me work harder, not easier.

Q: Most frustrating part of PRODUCT overall?
A: The most frustrating part of Duolingo is that it treats error and intensity as things to be slowed down or punished rather than leaned into. For a serious learner, Duolingo is okay for basics, but the hearts and some of the gamified features actively get in the way when I want intensive practice and don’t mind making mistakes.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: One time I set aside a focused hour to drill a weak area using Duolingo. Within 15–20 minutes, I’d run out of hearts because I was pushing myself on harder content, and the app basically told me to stop or switch to something else; I remember thinking, 'I carved out this time to work and the app is telling me I can’t practice because I’m making mistakes—that’s exactly when I need more reps, not fewer.'

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: I use Duolingo mostly at lower intensity and pair it with other tools: textbooks, grammar sites, and conversation practice. If I want serious practice, I’ll switch out of Duolingo as soon as hearts or game mechanics start interfering.

Q: What do workarounds give you that PRODUCT doesn’t?
A: The other tools let me push as hard as I want without artificial limits. They’re not as 'fun,' but I can repeat exercises, dive into explanations, and make as many mistakes as necessary without being slowed down by a game system.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case is investing a lot of time in tools that make me feel productive but don’t translate into real, professional-level ability. I don’t want to be the person with a nice Duolingo streak and no capacity to handle a complex meeting or negotiation.

Q: When you open PRODUCT, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping Duolingo will give me efficient, structured practice that supports my broader learning—something I can use to reinforce basics without dumbing things down. I want it to help me build and maintain a strong foundation, not get in my way when I’m ready to go deeper.

Q: How do you know PRODUCT worked?
A: If I’ve reviewed key vocab or structures and can recall them later in a more serious context—like reading or conversation—then Duolingo 'worked' for that day. If I spend most of the time fighting hearts or clicking through light content, it feels like a waste.

Q: One thing you'd change about PRODUCT?
A: I’d add a 'serious mode' that either removes hearts or drastically relaxes them and tones down some of the gamified interruptions. I want the option to use Duolingo as a real practice tool, not just as a game.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d like language-learning tools to be more honest about the needs of advanced or career-focused learners. There’s a lot aimed at casual beginners, but not enough that bridges from 'fun basics' to 'I can operate in this language at a professional level.'

Q: Intro greeting
A: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás? Soy Carlos, mucho gusto.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: So, I'm originally from Puerto Rico, born and raised there. Moved to Florida like about, oh, fifteen years ago. You know, it’s been a journey, adapting to life here and all. I’m a dad of two nene chiquitos, and bilingual is, like, super important to our familia because, you know, I want my kids to stay close to their roots, pero también they gotta fit in here, too.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Yeah, it’s beautiful allá, with the beaches and the mountains. I miss it sometimes.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was amazing, the gente, the culture. Everything is so vibrant, you know? It's like one big familia. We had a lot of freedom growing up, playing outside all the time, always surrounded by music and good food. Sabes, it was warm in every way, not just the weather.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Hmm, I’d say moving to Florida was a big one. It was a cambio, leaving everything familiar behind. Employment was tough back home, así que I took a chance to provide a better life for mi familia. It was hard at first, adapting and all, pero I think it opened up nuevas oportunidades.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it changed everything, you know? New language, new culture. I had to learn to navigate a different world and it forced me to grow, be more open-minded, and appreciate what I left behind even more. Plus, my kids were born here, so it's like a whole new chapter.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I mean, poquito a poco, you take it step by step. At first, it was just about survival, finding work and a place to live. Pero, you gotta stay positive, keep your head up. Making friends helped, finding our little comunidad here, and of course, arroz con gandules on Sundays helps keep that connection.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Honestly, my kids, their education and making sure they don’t lose touch with their culture. Es importante que they speak Spanish, así como inglés because it keeps them close to our heritage. That's why we use Duolingo as one of the tools, so they can practice español at home.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Porque their roots are important. It's who we are. I don’t want them to forget their abuelos or the stories, the language. Spanish opens doors, it connects them to our family back in Puerto Rico. It’s identity, it’s pride, something I want them to hold onto.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day starts with a cafecito, maybe a walk with the kids. A day where I can spend time at home, cook some traditional food, like some pasteles. If we end the day with a family game night or even a movie in Spanglish, that’s perfecto.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I see the kids happy and speaking Spanish throughout the day, that’s when I know. También, when I feel like I’ve balanced work and family, and we've all had a good laugh, yo digo, sí, eso fue un buen día.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I like to weigh my options, pero most importantly, I talk them out with my esposa. We have to be on the same page, you know? Sometimes, I even call mi mamá back in Puerto Rico for her advice. I like to think things through, pero at the end of the day, it’s what feels right.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I try to be a planner, pero sometimes life just happens and you gotta roll with it, so I guess a bit of both. Un poco de estructura, pero also flexible enough to adapt, you know?

Q: Example showing that?
A: Like, when we plan a trip back to Puerto Rico, I try to organize everything, but once we’re there, we just let things happen naturally. Esas son the best adventures. We might plan to visit family, but then también make time for spontaneous trips to the beach or just walk around Old San Juan.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I’m not really a big risk-taker. It’s more about calculated risks for me. I mean, moving to the States was a risk, but I had a job lined up, so it wasn’t just jumping without a net. I think it’s about being smart and not reckless, especially because it’s not just me I have to think about.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Pues, I get up early, make some café, and help the kids get ready for school. Work starts around 9, so I juggle that from home. It’s meetings and calls, pero I try to squeeze in a lunch break with some quick Spanish practice with the kids if they’re around. Once work is done, it’s dinner and maybe Duolingo time with the kids. Then, if there's time, I like to unwind with some TV o leer un poco.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely balancing work and making sure I’m present for the kids. Working from home has its perks but también it’s a lot of distractions. Sometimes, keeping the kids interested in Spanish after a long day is hard—we’re all tired, pero it’s important to keep at it.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time to focus on personal projects, like learning more about nuestra historia, or just reading more books. Sometimes I think about trying to write down the family stories abuela used to tell, so we don’t lose them. And, of course, more time for language learning with the kids without feeling exhausted.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Last year, it was the whole COVID situation, schooling from home and trying to keep everyone on track. It was tough managing everything from home, making sure los nenes kept learning and didn’t fall behind, especialmente with Spanish, since, you know, English is everywhere for them.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: It was un reto, but we tried to keep a routine, even if it wasn’t perfect. We had to be creative with resources, leaned on digital stuff like Duolingo for Spanish practice. Also, group calls with family back in Puerto Rico helped, so the kids could practice talking with their primos.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: Definitely mi esposa and the kids, and then mi familia en Puerto Rico. I talk to my mom almost every day, and I try to keep in touch with my brothers and cousins. We’re spread out, pero close. And I have a couple of good friends here in Florida too, who are like family.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: My relationship with my wife is built on teamwork, and with the kids, it’s about guiding them, but with lots of love and fun. Family back home, it’s all about supporting each other despite the distance, and with friends here, it’s like having an extended family, helping each other out.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Eh, mostly at home these days. It’s the hub for everything, like work, school, and family time. We’ve tried to make it cozy y acogedor, so everyone feels comfortable.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I feel content mostly, especially when we’re all together. But with the house being everything right now, sometimes it feels a bit, um, confined. There are days cuando uno necesita respirar afuera, you know? Pero it’s our space, filled with laughter and good moments too.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It’s the memories, seeing my kids grow, and making it feel like a small piece of Puerto Rico in Florida. But also, the same walls every day can get a bit too familiar—nice to break the routine sometimes with a change of scenery.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Primero, my wife, of course. We talk things through. If it’s something bigger, I’ll call my mom, for that bit of advice—and because she’s been through a lot, she knows what’s up. And I’ve got a couple of friends who are great for sounding things out too.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was a time last year when my job became uncertain. It was stressful, you know, porque the bills don’t stop. And with everything else going on, like homeschooling the kids, it felt overwhelming. I was worried about how to provide if things went south.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was definitely a lot of sleepless nights, trying to figure out what to do if I lost my job. I was anxious for a while, but it made me realize how important it is to have a backup plan and reminded me of the resilience we have as a family.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Talking it out with my wife helped. We made a financial plan just in case. I tried to focus on what I could control—updating my skills online, and keeping my network alive. Also, those Zoom calls with family back in Puerto Rico; they reminded me to keep looking forward and not lose sight of what’s important.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Honestly, taking a step back and breathing. Sometimes we’ll go for a walk or listen to música tropical to chill out. And, um, silly as it sounds, sometimes just doing a lesson or two on Duolingo with the kids takes my mind off stuff. It’s simple and routine, which can be calming.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I see us being more stable, maybe with a house of our own, and the kids fluent in both English and Spanish. I’d love to travel more, take them to Puerto Rico often so they know their roots first-hand. Maybe have a job that allows me more flexibility, para estar más presente para mi familia, sabes?

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like us to feel less rushed, less stressed financially. More secure, you know? And also, I’d want a world where my kids can be unapologetically bilingual without having to justify it all the time. Just a bit more balance in life overall.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Honestly, before Duolingo, it was more like traditional textbooks and trying to sneak in games in Spanish. It was kinda hit or miss because the kids were, like, not very excited about it. We’d watch Spanish cartoons, but it wasn't formal. Without a structured way to practice, they’d forget easily.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Ay, the most annoying thing was how boring it felt. Trying to keep kids engaged with dusty books is tough. And, you know, I’m not a teacher, así que trying to come up with exercises or games that actually work, it was a challenge. Plus, it felt disconnected from real life.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: One time I tried organizing a little Spanish night, with games and stories. I spent hours setting up, but the kids got, like, bored so quickly. They were just not into it. Ended up with them just watching Netflix, so it felt like a lot of effort for a failed outcome. It was disheartening.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: Oh, I think it was from a friend who was using it to learn French. I remember asking him, and he said it’s a pretty good app, especially for kids. So I thought, ¿por qué no? Let’s give it a try for Spanish.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: Well, the fact that it was, like, a game was a big draw. Anything that feels like playing instead of studying is a win with kids, you know? Plus, I heard it was free to start, so no risk there. And, it seemed structured enough to provide consistent practice.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: So, the other night after dinner, we sat down and I opened up the Duolingo app. The kids picked a lesson on animals. We went through the vocabulary, and they started speaking into the mic to answer questions. They like the little animations and sounds that let them know they got it right. Después, we did a short story. They love that porque it's like a mini game itself. Finished up with a round of matching words. The kids get competitive, and it’s fun to watch them actually try to beat each other's scores while picking up new phrases.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Oh, definitely the immediate feedback with the little checks and sounds. It keeps the kids motivated, and they know right away if they got it wrong and why. También, the stories are great. They give context, make it feel real, not just words on a screen. It really helps in making Spanish practical for them.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes it’s the repetition, like, too much of the same thing, you know? It can feel a bit tedious for the kids and they lose interest. Y también, some of the sentences are, like, not what we’d actually say in real life. They’re learning the language, sure, but it sometimes doesn’t feel authentic enough to our culture.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Overall, I’d say it’s when we hit a plateau. Vamos bien, then it suddenly feels like they’re not learning anything new. The kids get stuck at a level and start to feel bored, and that’s when the resistance to practice kicks in. Also, there’s limited cultural context, and I wish it had more of our specific phrases or references.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was a week where we were focusing on food vocabulary. My daughter kept getting frustrated porque every day it felt like the same words and exercises. She said, 'Papá, we know this already!' She wanted to learn more complex sentences or how to order comida at a restaurant, but the lessons were stuck on basic stuff. It was hard to keep her interested that week, and I had to mix in other resources to keep her engaged.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Sí, definitivamente. When the kids get bored, I switch things up with real-life practice, like role-playing scenarios. We’ll pretend to shop at the 'market' in Spanish or have them call their abuelos to talk about what they learned. It helps mix it up and keeps the practice relevant and fun.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give us that cultural touch and real-life application. It’s one thing to know the words, but actually using them with familia makes it stick harder. Plus, these workarounds break the monotony and bring in that personal connection, which is missing in a standard app setting.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: The worst case would be the kids losing interest in Spanish altogether. Eso sí would be tough because once they disconnect, it’s really hard to bring that back. If they start seeing it as just a chore or a game, and not something relevant to their lives, it could weaken their bond with their heritage.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it makes learning feel like an adventure for the kids, you know, not a task. That it pulls them in with engaging content, teaches them something new, but also connects them to their culture. I want it to reinforce their language skills in a way that’s fun but also meaningful.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I hear them use words or sentences they learned spontaneously in conversation. Or when they confidently speak to their abuelos without switching back to English. That’s when I know it’s working, when it transfers beyond the screen into real life.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d love to see more cultural integration, like more stories and exercises that include Puerto Rican history or idioms—something that makes the experience richer and more personal for us Boricuas.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there were more resources focused on cultural context, not just language. It's not just about speaking, it's about understanding the heart of a culture. More tools that help tie language learning to identity and roots, that'd be invaluable.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Hmm, I think we covered a lot. Just maybe emphasizing how important it is for these apps to feel personal. Language is personal, sabes, and the more they reflect that, the better they’ll be.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, if it helps improve the experience, go for it. As long as it respects our privacy and cultural nuances.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?

A: My main 'hack' is strategically picking lessons that give good XP for less effort—review lessons, specific types of exercises, that kind of thing. I also sometimes screenshot the leaderboard when I’m in first as a little trophy, especially if I had to fight for it.

Q: What do workarounds give you that PRODUCT doesn’t?
A: The lesson-picking hack lets me play Duolingo more like a competitive game and less like a class when I’m in that mood. The screenshots give me a record of 'wins' that I can look back on even after the league resets and everything disappears.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case is I burn a ton of time chasing XP and rankings but don’t actually feel more confident using the language in real life. It would feel like I 'won the game but lost the point,' which is not the outcome I want long-term.

Q: When you open PRODUCT, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping Duolingo will keep language learning fun and competitive enough that I stick with it, while still actually improving my skills. On some nights, I honestly open it just to see if I can stay in the top three of my league because Duolingo is fun as long as I’m winning.

Q: How do you know PRODUCT worked?
A: If I gain a good chunk of XP, move up or hold my position on the leaderboard, and also feel like at least one new word or phrase really stuck, I consider that a win. It feels best when the competitive side and the learning side both get fed.

Q: One thing you'd change about PRODUCT?
A: I’d add a mode or signal that says, 'I’m in serious practice mode now, not league mode,' with lessons and feedback geared more toward mastery than XP. I’d also love leagues that reward doing harder content, not just spamming any lesson.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love if language-learning tools used competition in a way that lined up more closely with real-world skills—like leaderboards based on conversation practice or comprehension, not just taps and points. That way, winning would automatically mean I’m actually better at the language.

Q: Anything important we didn’t cover?
A: I really do like Duolingo—it’s one of the few learning apps I actually look forward to opening. Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Yeah, that’s fine with me. If my competitive tendencies can help you design better league systems or game modes, I’m all in.

A: So, just the other morning, I opened the app over breakfast. I did a quick practice of vocab basics—picking the right word for pictures, then translating sentences. I like the little ding sound when I get something right, you know? It gives a nice sense of accomplishment. After a few lessons, I checked my streak, which always feels rewarding, like I’m on a roll! Q: Most helpful part?
A: It’s definitely the accessibility. I can just whip out my phone and do a quick session wherever I am. Plus, having topics broken into bite-sized lessons makes it easier to digest.

A: Probably the repetitive nature of some exercises. Like, once I’ve grasped a concept, I want to move on, but sometimes it keeps repeating the same stuff. It can feel like I’m not progressing fast enough.

A: Yeah, I’d say the lack of real conversation practice. It's mostly isolated phrases, and I wish there were more contextual dialogues. The app is great for vocab and grammar basics, but I need those dialogues for actual speaking skills.

A: The worst case? Probably would be relying solely on an app like Duolingo and missing out on speaking and listening practice, which are crucial. It’d be like learning to read but never speaking.

A: I hope it engages me and that I learn something new each time. It’s that little sense of progress that keeps me coming back. And I hope it’s a smooth, glitch-free experience too!

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I find myself remembering the words and phrases outside the app, like when I'm speaking or listening in real situations. And, of course, hitting my daily streak feels like proof that I’m being consistent.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d add more interactive, contextual dialogues. Like, actual scenarios you might encounter in meetings or social settings. It would bridge the gap between learning vocab and real world usage.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Bringing more cultural context into language apps. It’s not just words and grammar; understanding culture is key to truly mastering a language. It would make learning much more complete and immersive.

A: Not really, I think we covered quite a lot! Just that, um, language learning is a journey, not a race. Patience is key.

A: As long as it helps improve language learning tools, sure, why not?

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there, how you doing? It's Emmanuel here. Ready when you are!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, I was born and raised in Haiti, and then I made my way to Boston, ya know? I grew up speaking French and Creole, and now I'm trying to add Spanish to the mix. I got into computers and tech, which brought me over here for work. I love the mix of cultures here, feels like home in a way but new and exciting too.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Port-au-Prince, right in the heart of Haiti. It's vibrant, full of life, and, oh man, the food is something else!

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Growing up there was... it was beautiful but, you know, challenging too. We had a tight-knit community, everyone looked out for each other. It taught me resilience, how to make the best of what you got. Plus, the music and the sunshine, can't beat that.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Moving to the U.S. was definitely a big turning point for me. It changed my perspective on a lot of things, opened up more opportunities career-wise. It was tough leaving home, but the change pushed me to grow in ways I hadn't imagined.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It was like stepping into a whole new world, you know? Different culture, language barriers, everything was new. But it forced me to adapt, to learn non-stop. It's the move that got me interested in learning Spanish, actually.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: At first, it was a lot of trial and error. I relied on French and Creole communities here, which helped me feel less homesick. Then, I just dove into the culture, tried to learn as much as I could, bit by bit, day by day.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's all about balancing my work and personal growth. I want to improve my Spanish, but I'm also focused on career advancement, making sure I keep developing my skills in technology. It's important to keep things balanced, so I don't feel stuck, you know?

Q: Why is that important?
A: I guess it's about staying relevant and connected. Language, well, it connects you to people, and with tech changing so fast, I don't wanna fall behind. It keeps my mind sharp and my spirit curious.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day... hmm, it starts with a strong cup of coffee, for sure! If I can get through work without too much stress, maybe learn something new on Duolingo, and then end it with some Haitian music or a chat with family, that's a good day for me.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel like I've accomplished something, no matter how small. Even if it's just a new word in Spanish or helping a friend. It's about feeling productive and connected, you know?

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: Ah, I usually take my time with big decisions, talk it out with family or friends. I weigh out pros and cons, you know, maybe make a list. And, of course, I pray on it. That gives me peace of mind.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Oh, I'm definitely more of a planner. I like to have a sense of what's coming. I mean, I can be flexible, but having a plan keeps me grounded.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Sure, when I decided to move to Boston, I spent months planning, figuring out the job market, housing, all that. It was a big move, so having a plan just made me feel more secure about taking the leap.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risks... they're tricky. I try to mitigate them as much as I can. I do my research, like a lot of research! I talk to people who've been through similar situations. But sometimes, you gotta just take the leap and hope for the best.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Weekdays start with some breakfast and coffee, then it's off to work. My job can be pretty demanding, a lot of tech stuff, coding, and meetings. I squeeze in some Duolingo practice during lunch or breaks. After work, I usually cook, maybe watch some TV or read a bit. I try to fit in some Spanish practice, but, you know, energy levels can be hit or miss by then.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Work definitely, especially when we have tight deadlines or big projects. It can be mentally exhausting. Learning Spanish is a good mental break from that, but if I'm tired, even that takes energy.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time for painting. It's something I used to do back home that really relaxed me. But with everything going on, work and learning, it's hard to fit it in.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Ah, definitely the pandemic. It was hard being away from family, not being able to travel. Work was remote, which was okay, but the isolation, man, that was tough. It made everything feel like it was in slow motion.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I kept in touch with family back in Haiti through video calls, which helped a lot. I also took up jogging to clear my mind and get outside safely. Trying to find small joys in daily life kept me grounded.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: Definitely my family. My mom and siblings back in Haiti, they're my rock, you know? And I've got a few close friends here in Boston who feel like family too.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They're rooted in trust and support. My family, we may not see each other all the time, but we're always there for one another. Friends here, they're the ones I turn to, to share a laugh or lean on when things get tough.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly at work or at home. Sometimes, I like to go out to the local cafes or parks when I need a change of scenery.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Work can be hectic, so it's like go-go-go mode. Home is where I unwind, find peace. Cafes are my little escapes, they give me this feeling of being part of the community, you know?

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: At home, it's just comforting, my little slice of Haiti in Boston. Cafes, it's the buzz, the quiet hum of conversation…it makes me feel connected.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to my sister. We talk about everything, she gives the best advice. And I've got a mentor here in Boston who helps me out with work-related stuff.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was this big project that almost got derailed because of some miscommunication. It was stressful, and I was afraid of how it might affect my job. Took a lot of late nights to get it back on track.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was draining, mentally and physically. I was anxious a lot, and it felt like I was carrying the weight of it on my shoulders. But it taught me the importance of clear communication, you know?

Q: How did you cope?
A: I had to step back, breathe, and then tackle it piece by piece. I asked for help, which I don't always do, but it made a difference. It was a big learning experience for sure.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Music, for sure. Haitian tunes or some good jazz, they lift my spirits. A good run also clears my mind. And just talking it out with someone I trust helps a lot.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I'd like to travel more, maybe have a place back home in Haiti and here. I want to feel more settled and fluent in Spanish, maybe even work in a Spanish-speaking country for a bit. Just more freedom to explore.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I want to worry less and live more in the moment. It's easy to get caught up in the hustle, but I'd like to enjoy the journey more, you know?

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Oh, it was mostly textbooks and some online courses. I tried Pimsleur for a bit, but it was too slow for me. I wanted something more interactive, which is why Duolingo caught my eye.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: It was just boring, to be honest. Textbooks can only take you so far, and they didn't really teach you how to speak naturally. Conversations felt stiff and scripted.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: I remember trying to have a conversation in Spanish, and I just blanked out. All that textbook stuff didn't prepare me for real-life exchanges, you know? It was frustrating.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend of mine mentioned it. He told me it was like learning with a game, so I thought I'd give it a shot.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The gamified aspect was intriguing, but really, it was the idea of learning at my own pace, when I had time. Plus, it's free, so I figured, why not?

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Ah, the other day, I opened the app during lunch. I went through the 'Travel' module, which is fun 'cause I'm dreaming of more trips. You get these quick exercises, like matching words or translating sentences. The app says 'Great job!' when you get it right, gives you that little dopamine hit. But sometimes, those speaking exercises don't register my accent, and I have to repeat myself.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The immediate feedback, definitely. If I mess up, I know right away, and I can fix it. Plus, the way it links vocabulary with images helps me remember things better.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Those repetitive exercises can get tiresome. After a while, it's like, 'Come on, I've got this already!' And the voice recognition can be a bit off, doesn't always pick up what I say right.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I'd say the pacing. Sometimes it feels like I'm not progressing fast enough, even though I've mastered certain sections. I'd love a way to test out of stuff I find too easy.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, just last week, I was doing a review and it kept throwing the same phrases at me. I was like, 'I've done this ten times already!' I almost gave up on that session. Sometimes it feels like it's not adjusting to my level.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, sometimes I'll just skip the exercise and move on. Or I'll use another app or resource to mix things up, like watching Spanish shows for listening practice. Keeps things interesting.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Variety and real-world context. Duolingo's great for basics, but mixing in other resources gives me a fuller picture, like how people actually speak day-to-day.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: I guess the worst would be if all my progress just disappeared, or if Duolingo shut down suddenly. It's become a routine, and losing that would set me back.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it keeps me engaged and slowly pushes me out of my comfort zone. You know, challenges me just enough without feeling overwhelming.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can recall a word or phrase in conversation without hesitating. Or when I finish a session feeling like I've really learned something new.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd add more advanced content or adjustable difficulty levels. Let us skip sections if we feel they're too easy, so we can keep things fresh and challenging.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd love to see more integration with real-world applications, like maybe pairing learners with native speakers for practice. More immersion, you know?

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Not that I can think of, but it's been great sharing this! Language learning is such a journey, and it's nice to reflect on what's working and what isn't.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Digital twin, huh? Sounds kind of sci-fi! Yeah, sure, go for it. Just make sure it learns languages faster than me!

A: The gamification aspect, really. I’m very competitive, so the idea of climbing leaderboards and earning points was super appealing. Plus, it’s free, so I figured, why not?

A: Sure! So, the other day, I opened the app during my lunch break. I went straight to the Japanese course, where I did a few reviews first. Then, I tackled a new lesson on food vocabulary. Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitely the leagues and streaks. They keep me motivated to practice consistently. And I love the little reminders to keep my streak going—it’s like having a language coach nudging me gently.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: When you make a simple mistake and lose a heart—that's pretty annoying, especially if you're on a roll. Also, some translations feel a bit too rigid, like there should be more flexibility in accepting correct answers.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The lack of speaking and conversation practice is the most frustrating. Sometimes I feel like I'm just memorizing and not actually learning how to communicate. It’d be great if there were more interactive speaking exercises.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Once, I was trying to translate a sentence and I knew my answer was correct, but because I didn't use the exact phrasing Duolingo wanted, it marked me wrong. It felt a bit demotivating, because in real life, language isn’t that rigid—there's more than one way to say something.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, sometimes I use other apps to get more speaking practice, or I watch Japanese shows and try to repeat dialogues. It helps fill in the gaps Duolingo doesn’t cover, especially for listening and speaking.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide more context and real-world usage. Hearing native speakers and trying to mimic them helps with pronunciation and understanding nuances that you don’t always get with Duolingo exercises.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case? Losing motivation entirely and stopping my language learning journey. That’s always a fear because staying consistent is key, and without that drive, it’s easy to fall behind.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it makes learning fun and engaging, while also being educational. I want it to challenge me just enough that I feel like I'm progressing, but also keep it light and fun so I keep coming back.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can apply what I’ve learned in real-life situations or when I notice I’m understanding more in the anime shows I watch. It’s that moment when something clicks, and I feel I’ve truly learned something.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d add more interactive speaking features, maybe some sort of AI conversation partner. It would be great to have more practice with pronunciation and forming spontaneous sentences.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love to see more integrative approaches that combine gamified learning with real-world application, maybe through community interactions or live conversations with native speakers.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?

A: I think it was the promise of making language learning fun and easy, with its gamified approach, you know? The idea of squeezing in practice whenever seemed appealing.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: For me, it's that sense of progress. Those little streaks and XP points really make me feel like I'm getting somewhere, even on days when it feels impossible.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: It's the lack of depth sometimes. Like, I want to go beyond just vocabulary and simple phrases. I want to understand cultural context and nuanced language use.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Honestly, Duolingo sometimes feels like it's teaching me Mandarin in a vacuum, you know? It’s effective for basics but lacks the cultural richness that makes a language come alive.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this lesson on 'Food.' I learned the words, but then realized when I spoke to my mom that the app didn’t cover the cultural significance and stories behind those dishes. It was frustrating not being able to really connect with her using what I learned.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, sometimes I’ll watch Mandarin shows or listen to Chinese podcasts to get a more immersive experience. It's not a perfect solution, but it helps add some depth.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give me context, I think. It's one thing to know the words, but context makes the language real and relevant.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case? Probably feeling like I never really reclaim that part of my heritage. Ending up disconnected despite all efforts would be tough.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it keeps me consistent, motivated, and maybe surprises me with something new—something that bridges those cultural gaps a bit.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can use what I learned in a real conversation with my mom without stumbling. That’s the real test for me.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd add more cultural modules so it’s not just about learning words but understanding the stories behind them, making it feel more alive.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there was more emphasis on connection and less on gamification. Language is about people and cultures, not just points and streaks.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we’ve covered a lot! Just that, learning a language is deeply personal and tied to identity, and apps should reflect that more.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, why not? As long as it helps improve language learning experiences in a meaningful way!

There’s time; I just have to believe that sometimes.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I'd say my family back in Ireland, for sure. We’re a tight-knit bunch. But I've also got a solid group of pals here in Berlin who’ve become like family. There’s Jake, my old college mate who ended up here too. And I’ve found kindred spirits in the oddest of places, like my local book club – who’d have thought?

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Oh, they’re the kind where you can be yourself without any pretenses. With family, there’s history, memories, and all that shared madness. With friends here, it’s a shared adventure. We’ve all chosen this city for different reasons, and that bonds us in a unique way. We’re all in this big, messy, beautiful Berlin life together.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Probably at work, if we’re being honest. Otherwise, it’s at home in my wee flat or out exploring the city. I’ve made it a point to know my local spots – cafes and pubs – where I can unwind and feel part of the community. Feels important when you’re an expat.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Pretty comfortable, I'd say. My flat's a kind of oasis – it’s got bits that remind me of home, with my own touch of Berlin. When I'm out and about, I feel a part of the city. It’s this buzzing, electric vibe that you can’t quite replicate. And in the local spots, there’s a familiarity now – even if my order in German isn’t perfect, they know my face, and that makes it feel like home.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I suppose it’s the connections, really. Whether it’s the familiar faces at the pub or the knowing nod from the barista who still corrects my pronunciation, it’s those little interactions that knit the fabric of daily life together. It’s both comforting and invigorating to belong somewhere.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Ah, usually it’s my family first, even if it’s just for a vent over the phone. They’ve known me longest and seem to have an endless supply of advice, solicited or not. Then there's Jake here, who's basically the voice of reason when I’m losing the plot. And honestly, sometimes just talking it out with mates over a pint does wonders too. Everyone’s got a bit of wisdom to share.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was a time a few months back when I lost my job unexpectedly – just like that, poof, gone. It was a bit of a shock, really. There’s that moment of blind panic where you think, ‘What now?’ I’d just settled in, felt like things were finally on track when the rug got pulled out. Not knowing what comes next is, well, terrifying.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: Initially, it knocked the wind out of me. You start questioning everything – did you make the right choice moving here, what does this mean for the future? But once I took a breath, I saw it as a chance to reassess. It was like being given a reset button, scary but also kind of freeing in a way. You realize how resilient you can be when push comes to shove.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Focused on the basics first: updating my CV, networking, reaching out to folks in the industry. I leaned a lot on friends, who were incredible. They offered leads, support, and more than a few ‘don’t give up’ pep talks. I also kept up with my routine – exercise, language learning, that sort of thing. Anchors in the chaos, you know? It helped that Berlin has a way of presenting new opportunities when you least expect.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: A bit of fresh air and a good walk usually does wonders. There’s a path by the canal here that’s become my go-to. Just me, some music, and the world feels a tad better by the end of it. And humor, can’t forget that. A good laugh somehow makes anything bearable. Can’t take life too seriously all the time.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I'd like to see myself more settled, maybe even fluent in German at long last. I’d hope to be doing work that feels meaningful, surrounded by good people, and continue exploring what this world has to offer. Maybe I’ll have found a sweet balance between my Irish roots and this adopted Berlin life. And who knows, maybe even thinking about putting down roots of my own somewhere.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d love to lessen the sense of being in a constant rush, you know? More time for creative pursuits, more energy for spontaneous adventures without feeling the pull of obligations all the time. And definitely want more confidence in speaking German. I don’t want language to be a barrier but a bridge.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Oh, it was a bit of a hodgepodge, really. I’d picked up some language books, tried to listen in on podcasts, but it always felt a bit stagnant. Took a class once, but the timing never quite worked with my schedule. It felt like a lot of effort without much progress. I remember buying this hefty German dictionary – thought it would be the key – but it mostly collected dust. Couldn’t bring myself to tackle it after a day’s work.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The sheer lack of structure, I suppose. I was like a ship without a rudder, just floating about with no real direction. Every time I sat down to study, it felt like starting from scratch. And the motivation just wasn’t there when you're not seeing progress. Plus, it was all so static – none of the interactivity or fun that keeps you coming back like with Duolingo.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a particularly awkward moment when an old friend visited Berlin and I fancied impressing them with my shiny new language skills. But everything I’d ‘learned’ seemed to evaporate the moment I opened my mouth. Ended up gesturing like a mime, and my friend couldn’t stop laughing over it. That was a wake-up call that I needed something more engaging and consistent. A bit of a humbling experience, to be fair.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: Think it first came up in a conversation with a colleague over lunch. They were raving about how it made language learning feel like playing a game. I was skeptical but curious. So later that night, I thought, ‘Why not give it a whirl?’ and downloaded the app out of curiosity.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: Well, the whole 'gamified learning' concept was intriguing. Plus, it was free, and I’m not one to pass up an offer like that, ha! I liked the idea of fitting learning into little pockets of time, and the thought of not being bogged down by dusty old textbooks was pretty appealing. The owl mascot, Duo, was also strangely encouraging – felt like you had a wee companion on the journey.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Alright, so just the other evening, I sat down after dinner, opened the app, and got cracking. I usually start with whatever skill I’m weakest in – grammar, usually – those pesky cases trip me up every time. You tap into a lesson, and it's a mix of translating sentences, identifying pictures, or filling in the blank. Got asked to translate 'the cat is on the chair' – simple enough, but by the end of it, you're trying complex sentences and feeling like a champ if you get it right. I like the checkpoints where you kinda 'level up' – gives you a sense of progress. Ended with a listening exercise, which is always good to hear the language outside of my own voice. And then, of course, I collected my daily streak and earned a gem reward. It's all about those small wins, right?

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The repetition with variation, for sure. Like, you don’t just see a word once and forget about it. It keeps popping back up in different contexts. And the speaking exercises are a godsend – although I sometimes feel daft speaking into my phone, they’ve really helped with pronunciation. And then the leaderboard – it’s a wee push seeing where you stack up against others. For someone who's a tad competitive, it’s a good nudge.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Honestly, the way it sometimes feels like a guessing game, especially with the grammar. You think you’ve nailed it, and then you realize it’s all an illusion when you can’t string a live sentence together. And sometimes the app’s a bit picky – one missed umlaut, and it’s marked wrong! I mean, come on, give us a break, Duo! It’d be great if they had more real-life conversation practice, like talking with others learning German at the same level. That’s where the magic happens.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Ah, it’s that plateau you get to after a while. You start with such a bang, feel like you’re flying through lessons, and then, wham, you’re stuck. You’ve gathered all the gems and crowns, but can you ask for directions without a stumble? Not quite. It’s like the app’s great for building a foundation, but where’s the bridge to real-world fluency? That leap can be daunting without additional support.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, I remember it well. I’d been diligently using Duolingo for months, feeling quite chuffed with myself. Decided I’d show off a bit at this German meet-up by joining in the conversation. Let’s just say, it was like watching a toddler try to run. I was fumbling with basic phrases while others sped past. I went home that night feeling a bit deflated – it was a harsh reminder that Duolingo’s pace and real-life speed don’t always match up.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Absolutely. I try to mix in chatting with locals whenever I can – even if it’s just over a coffee order or at the butcher’s. Also doing German meet-ups or exchange events – those really push you out of your comfort zone. And sometimes I’ll watch German TV shows with subtitles, helps with the flow and rhythm of how people actually speak. It’s a bit like a language cocktail – Duolingo sets the base, and the rest adds the flavor.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Real-life context, mainly. On the app, it’s all controlled and predictable, but conversations in the wild? They’re anything but! Plus, it’s more personable – you’re not just talking into the void, you’re participating in dialogue. You get instant feedback, which is massive. And it's more forgiving in a way – people are kind, eager to help, whereas the app’s just a bit more binary, you know?

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Probably that I’d give up entirely due to frustration and never get beyond this plateau. There’s a fair bit of pressure when you set goals for fluency, and not meeting them can feel like failure. Or worse, that my German would remain stilted and overly formal, never catching up to the nuances and slang that make the language what it is. I don’t want to be that guy who can only order a pint and not have a proper chat!

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: Oh, I hope it gives me a good push in the right direction. Something fresh to tackle that day, keeps my brain engaged and learning. I want to feel like I’m making progress, even if it’s just a bit at a time. And I guess, a little reassurance that I’ve still got it, you know? It’s like having a wee cheerleader in my pocket.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: I reckon it’s when I find myself naturally reaching for a German word rather than my native tongue. Or when I can follow a snippet of conversation in the U-Bahn without feeling utterly lost. It’s the little triumphs that tell you it’s working – like when I realized I’d spent a whole day understanding most of what was said around me. That was a good feeling.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d love more speaking practice opportunities, like maybe pairing users to chat or some kind of interactive video lessons. The app’s brilliant in many ways, but it doesn’t quite mimic real-world exchanges. Having something where you negotiate meaning with another person would be ace.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Just wish there was more integration between learning apps and everyday life. Like, linking Duolingo directly to other resources or events in your area – meet-ups or even online chats with locals. Make it more seamless so you aren’t just learning in a vacuum. Feels like we’re not far off, but there’s more innovation waiting to happen.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Not much, just maybe that learning a language is a lot about persistence and patience, and less about perfection. We all make mistakes, and that’s part of the charm in trying. So cheers to still trying, right?

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: A digital twin, eh? Sounds intriguing, sure why not! Just don’t make him too perfect – gotta have some of the quirks and all!
