Q: Intro greeting
A: That sounds good, thanks. I’m happy to talk about it, I’ve definitely had a whole journey with language learning and Duolingo.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: I’m 19, a college student, and I’ve always been a high-achiever: honors classes, APs, test prep, all of it. Most of my life so far has been built around goals and deadlines—do well on the next exam, get into the next program—so when I get interested in something, I tend to go all in right before a big milestone and then completely cool off afterward.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a big city in the U.S. in a family that valued education and 'using your time wisely.' There were always activities, tutors, and some kind of performance metric in the background.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was exciting and competitive—lots of opportunities, but also lots of pressure to stand out. I learned early on that cramming before big events worked for me in school, so that mindset kind of spilled over into everything, including learning languages.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: A turning point was when I prepped like crazy for a big standardized exam and hit the score I wanted, but then felt weirdly empty afterward. I realized I’m really good at sprinting for a goal, but not great at sustaining habits once there’s no exam or trip on the calendar.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It made me notice that my whole identity was wrapped around 'the next big thing.' Once I hit a target, I didn’t really know how to engage with the subject just because I enjoyed it, and I started to see that pattern in how I used apps like Duolingo too.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Initially I celebrated and then crashed, but after a while I started experimenting with smaller, maintenance-style goals. The truth is, I still slip back into cram mode whenever a big deadline shows up—it’s a hard pattern to break.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now I care most about setting myself up for future opportunities—study abroad, internships, maybe working internationally. Language fits into that because it feels like this lever I can pull to unlock travel, grades, and career stuff.

Q: Why is that important?
A: I’m very outcome-driven; I like seeing tangible proof that my effort turned into something—scores, acceptance letters, achievements. Learning a language feels valuable, but I still subconsciously treat it like another thing I’m supposed to 'win' at instead of an ongoing process.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: On a really good day, I’m on top of my assignments, I’ve knocked out my studying, and I’ve over-prepared for whatever’s coming up. I like that feeling of being ahead of the curve and seeing all my 'progress bars' filled—grades, to-do list, Duolingo tree, everything.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I can look back and see that I made measurable progress—finished chapters, checked off tasks, kept streaks, advanced in skills—that’s a good day. I like the visual satisfaction of things being complete or 'on track.'

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I usually look at how it lines up with my long-term goals, like, 'Will this help my resume? Will this help my grades? Will this help me study abroad?' Then I weigh how much effort it will take and if I can fit it into my schedule without crashing.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I’m definitely more of a planner, but with bursts of chaos. I’ll plan everything out and then end up doing most of the work in a concentrated push closer to the deadline.

Q: Example showing that?
A: For a recent midterm, I made this beautiful study schedule two weeks out, but I seriously started grinding three days before the exam. Same with Duolingo—before a trip, I’ll suddenly do tons of lessons a day to 'catch up' and fill out my skill tree, even if I’d been pretty inactive right before that.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I think about how much it could move the needle for me if it works versus the hit I’ll take if it doesn’t. If the upside is big—like a scholarship, opportunity, or unique experience—I’ll usually go for it, even if it means a short-term cram-fest.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical weekday is classes during the day, a mix of lectures and labs, then studying and group work in the afternoon or evening. On calmer weeks, I sprinkle in Duolingo sessions, but on heavy weeks I basically switch into 'exam mode' and ignore anything that doesn’t feel urgent—until something like a trip or test brings the language back into the 'urgent' category.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Classes and coursework take the bulk of my time, but mentally, managing deadlines and planning what to cram for next is the most draining. I’m always triaging which subject or task gets my intense focus next.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more steady energy for things that don’t have hard deadlines—like actually maintaining my language skills. I’d love to be someone who practices a little every day instead of someone who goes into hyperdrive before trips or exams and then drops it.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Time and mental bandwidth have been the biggest constraints. There’s always another assignment or project, so things like consistent language practice get pushed down the list until there’s a big reason to care again.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: Honestly, I’ve mostly been doubling down on prioritizing whatever’s closest on the calendar. That works short-term, but it means longer-term goals like 'maintain my Spanish' end up in this weird limbo where I only give them attention in bursts.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I’m closest to my roommate, a couple of friends from high school who are also in college, and my parents. They’re all used to me disappearing a bit when I’m in cram mode and then resurfacing after exams or trips.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Supportive, slightly chaotic, and very understanding of my student brain. They tease me about how I suddenly become obsessed with a topic and then go quiet once the big event passes.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Most of my time is split between campus, my dorm, and my laptop. A lot of my world lives on screens—school portals, study tools, and apps like Duolingo.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I’d say a mix of supported and stressed. Campus is a place where everyone’s pushing themselves hard, so it’s normal to be in grind mode, but it also means I constantly feel like I should be doing more.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: There’s this unspoken competition around who is the most productive, most involved, most prepared. Seeing other people post about their streaks or achievements, whether it’s Duolingo or grades, feeds into that feeling that I need to be 'maximizing' everything.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to Google or classmates first for practical solutions. If it’s more of a 'what am I doing with my life' kind of problem, I’ll talk to my parents or a close friend.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: A tough moment was juggling finals with planning for a study-abroad application. I wanted to show strong language progress on my application but had barely touched Duolingo during the semester, so I suddenly tried to ramp up like crazy while also studying for exams.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: Day to day, it meant late nights and this constant feeling that I was behind on everything. I was blasting through Duolingo lessons to fill out my tree and rebuild a streak, but I knew it wasn’t the same as consistent practice, and that bothered me.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I powered through by creating a tight schedule and basically living by it for a few weeks. After it was over—after the exams and application—I crashed, took a break from anything that felt like studying, and, as usual, Duolingo was one of the first things to fall off.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: It helps to zoom out and ask, 'What actually matters this week?' and let myself drop some things temporarily. I’ll also try to do one or two tasks that give me quick wins, like a short assignment or a single Duolingo lesson, just to feel less stuck—though sometimes I avoid Duolingo if I feel too behind.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: A few years from now, I hope I’m living or working somewhere where I actually use the language I’ve been learning—not just telling stories about how I 'almost' studied abroad. I’d like to have a more sustainable rhythm, where I don’t rely on cramming and can treat learning as part of my life rather than a temporary project.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to break out of the all-or-nothing mindset. Right now, if I fall behind or mess up a few lessons, I feel like the whole thing is ruined and I don’t know how to re-engage without starting over, and that keeps me stuck.

Q: Before PRODUCT, how did you handle the core job?
A: Before Duolingo, I learned languages mainly through school classes, exam prep books, and some YouTube. I’d study intensely before a test or a trip, then drop it almost completely once the event was over.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The most painful part was realizing how much I forgot between those cram periods. It felt like I was constantly rebuilding the same foundation over and over instead of progressing, which is frustrating when you’ve put in so many hours.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Before a trip, I crammed phrases for weeks, felt kind of confident, and then still froze in real conversations. I remember thinking, 'I studied so much, but without steady practice, it didn’t stick the way I expected.'

Q: How did you first hear about PRODUCT?
A: I heard about Duolingo from classmates and social media, especially people sharing screenshots of their streaks and completed trees. It looked like a way to turn language learning into a game with visible progress.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of building a long streak and filling out the skill tree really appealed to me. I liked the thought of seeing a complete tree and a big streak number as proof that I was 'on top of' my language, especially leading up to trips or exams.

Q: Walk through a recent PRODUCT use.
A: Recently, before a short trip, I opened Duolingo after being away for a while and saw my streak was gone and some skills were cracked. I felt a pang of regret, then decided to do multiple sessions in a row—reviewing cracked skills, unlocking new ones—until the tree looked more 'full' again; afterward, I felt oddly satisfied by the visuals but also aware that I’d basically done another cram session.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The most helpful part was the structured review of older skills; it reminded me of things I hadn’t thought about in a while. It was nice to see that, under the rust, I still remembered a fair amount.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: It was frustrating to see so many signs that I’d been inactive—broken streak, cracked skills, the tree not looking 'perfect' anymore. Once it looks messy, I start to feel like the app is ruined and I don’t know how to casually re-engage without feeling like I have to fix everything at once.

Q: Most frustrating part of PRODUCT overall?
A: The most frustrating part of using Duolingo is that it visually tracks every gap in my consistency—streaks, cracked skills, incomplete sections—so when I fall behind or mess up, it feels like I’ve broken the whole thing. I love seeing a long streak and a full skill tree, but once it’s not perfect, I kind of emotionally check out.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: One specific time was after an exam period when I hadn’t opened Duolingo for a couple of weeks. When I finally did, my streak was gone, several skills were cracked, and new units were locked; I stared at the screen and thought, 'This whole thing looks ruined now,' closed the app, and didn’t come back until I had another trip to prepare for.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: I sometimes use separate vocab lists in Google Docs or Notion for words I care about, especially before exams or travel. I’ve also taken screenshots of a 'clean' tree and a high streak number because it feels good to look at, even if I know it’s not current.

Q: What do workarounds give you that PRODUCT doesn’t?
A: The vocab lists feel more targeted to what I need for specific situations, like trips or tests, while Duolingo can feel more general. The screenshots are almost like trophies—they let me remember that there was a time my tree was full and my streak was high, even if the app doesn’t show that anymore.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: The worst-case scenario is feeling like all my effort only counts if the streak and tree look perfect—and the moment they don’t, it feels like I wasted my time. Emotionally, it’s like, 'I put in all this work, and now because I fell behind, it’s ruined and I have to start over or walk away.'

Q: When you open PRODUCT, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping Duolingo will help me get to a level where I can handle real interactions on trips and not feel lost, and maybe support me for exams. On a more emotional level, I’m also hoping it will give me a sense of visible progress—like a full tree and a strong streak—that makes me feel like my effort is paying off.

Q: How do you know PRODUCT worked?
A: If I finish a set of lessons, see skills get strengthened, and the tree looks more 'filled in,' I feel like it worked that day. I also feel good if I recognize phrases later in real life and can tie them back to what I practiced.

Q: One thing you'd change about PRODUCT?
A: I’d change how it handles falling behind—maybe a way to 'reset the visuals' or enter some kind of 'rebuild mode' without feeling like everything is broken. I want a clearer path for re-engaging after a gap that doesn’t make me feel like I ruined the app and have to start completely over.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love if language-learning tools were designed with realistic student patterns in mind—that people will cram, pause, and come back—and offered more structured ways to recover after intense periods instead of just punishing gaps. Right now it feels like you either stay perfectly consistent or accept that your progress will look messy and 'wrong.'

Q: Anything important we didn’t cover?
A: I genuinely enjoy languages and I actually like Duolingo a lot when I’m 'on a roll.' The problem is that once I fall behind or mess up a few lessons, I look at the broken streak and cracked skills and feel like the whole thing is ruined, and I honestly don’t know how to re-engage without some kind of big dramatic reset.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Yes, that’s fine with me. If my patterns can help design a better way to come back after gaps, that would make it a lot easier for people like me to stick with the language long-term.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The overall problem with Duolingo be say sometimes e no feel real. I dey struggle to connect the lessons to real-world situations, you know. I want more application type thing.

A: There was this one time I dey try learn how to order food in a restaurant, but the sentence constructions no feel natural. I just take the lesson with a pinch of salt, and I no trust myself to use the sentences in real life.

A: Worst-case scenario be say after all this effort, I go Netherlands and struggle to hold even small conversation. That one go hurt, because language be key o.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?

A: When I fit recall a word or phrase from what I learn, and use am in a conversation or understand it when I hear 'am in real life. That's the real test for me.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I go like make the speaking exercises more interactive. Maybe add some feature wey mimic real-life conversations better. That one go help some more.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Access to more interactive resources for learning. I dey imagine something like virtual reality immersion for language, you know. That one go change the game.

A: Oh, that one be fine. If it go help improve the app or language learning in general, then why not?

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: It would be great if language learning resources were more integrated. Like having a platform that combines, um, Duolingo's gamified approach with real-world practice, videos, podcasts—all in one place, so it’s more comprehensive.

A: I think it was the, um, idea of it being game-like and interactive. Like, I thought if I could get hooked on games, why not language? Plus, it was easy to access on my phone, so I could practice during my breaks, which made it more practical for my schedule.

A: I love the bit where they, um, remind you of your past mistakes and you get to fix them. It’s like, just the right amount of challenge without being overwhelming. Plus, hearing the words pronounced helps my listening skills grow a lot.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Honestly, sometimes it feels repetitive, like I'm not really learning how to use the language naturally. I wish it had more cultural context, like how these words fit into daily life. It's like learning just words, not the music or the soul of the language.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I’d say it’s the lack of real conversation practice. I mean, they have exercises, but it doesn’t quite capture the flow of a real dialogue or help me understand colloquial expressions. Conversations in real life aren't broken into neat little sentences!

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Yeah, once I tried talking to my uncle using what I learned from Duolingo, and he’s like, 'You sound like a textbook!' It was pretty awkward because I realized I couldn't keep up with the natural pace and the slang. It was a bit of a wake-up call that I needed more than just Duolingo.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: I guess it's, um, getting stuck in the app cycle without ever moving beyond it. Like, never feeling confident enough to actually use the language socially or culturally, which would kinda defeat the whole purpose for me.

A: I hope it gives me, like, a little boost in confidence, reinforcing what I know and slowly expanding my vocabulary and understanding. It's like hoping each session nudges me closer to being conversational, you know?

A: When I can, like, recall words or phrases without really thinking about them, especially in real-life situations. Also, when I can use learned phrases naturally in conversations, that feels like a win.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?

A: They’re built on trust, history, and mutual support. We’ve been through a lot together, and it’s like having a safety net. We celebrate each other’s successes and support one another through challenges.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Most of my time is spent at work or at home with my family. Both places are where I feel productive and where I can relax and be myself.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: At work, it’s a mix of focus and camaraderie. You know, we push each other to get the job done. At home, it’s warmth and comfort. It’s where I can unwind and spend quality time with loved ones.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The people, definitely. My coworkers and I share jokes and stories, and my family fills our home with love and laughter. Both create an environment where I feel encouraged and supported.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to my wife first. She has a great way of listening and offering perspective. Depending on the situation, I might also reach out to close friends or family back in Jordan for advice. Different perspectives help a lot.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: I’d say adjusting to a new role at work was challenging. It required a lot of learning and adapting, especially communication-wise with my Spanish-speaking colleagues. It was stressful at first, trying to balance learning with my other duties.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a bit overwhelming, to be honest. I felt like I was constantly playing catch-up. But it also sparked my interest in learning Spanish more seriously, which is a positive outcome. Challenges often push us to grow, after all.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I took it step by step. I started using Duolingo daily to build my language skills. I also reached out to coworkers for help and tried to engage in language exchanges. Feeling like I was making progress really helped ease the stress.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a break and spending time with my family is always refreshing. I also find that a good walk or a cup of Arabic coffee can clear my mind. Sometimes just zoning out with some music helps too. It's important to recharge.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to be more fluent in Spanish and maybe even have visited some Spanish-speaking countries. I’d like to continue growing professionally, while also enjoying more leisure time with my family. And, inshallah, more travel experiences with them.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I wouldn’t mind having less rigid work hours, to have a bit more flexibility. Also, more opportunities to engage in cultural exchanges, whether through work or in the community. It’s important to keep growing and learning in different ways.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I tried a few textbooks and some language CDs, but it wasn’t very engaging. I even tried attending some evening classes, but with work and family, it was hard to keep up with the schedule. It felt more like a task than fun.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The rigidity of the schedules and how dry the materials felt. It was hard to stay motivated with just drills and repetition without much interaction or feedback. It felt like I was memorizing rather than really learning.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time I tried to follow along with a language CD during my commute. I just couldn’t keep focused, and it ended up being more distracting than helpful. It was a clear sign that method wasn’t going to work for me.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend of mine mentioned it during a chat about learning new languages. They were using it for German and spoke highly of its interactive approach. I was intrigued, so I decided to give it a shot.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I was impressed by how accessible and user-friendly it seemed. It was free to start, and the idea of it being like a game really appealed to me. I thought, why not turn learning into something enjoyable?

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure! So, just yesterday, I logged in and noticed I had a 50-day streak going, which was a nice motivation boost. I started with a practice lesson in the 'Shopping' unit. It was fun matching the words with images and speaking out loud the phrases. Even got a couple of them wrong, but the app just shows you the right answer, which helps it stick. I love how each lesson feels manageable, and those little animations and sounds when you get it right make it fun. So, after about 15 minutes, I felt like I’d made good progress.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitely the 'Speaking' exercises. They really push you to pronounce words correctly and get comfortable speaking. It’s like having a mini conversation partner, which is fantastic because it builds confidence. Plus, the instant feedback is really valuable.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes the app penalizes you for tiny errors, like missing an accent or a misplaced word. It can be a bit frustrating when you feel like you understood the concept but still get it marked wrong. But it’s a small bump in an otherwise smooth experience.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: It would be the ads in the free version. After a few lessons, they can become quite intrusive. I understand they have to fund the app somehow, but it does break the flow sometimes. Maybe a smoother transition or less frequent ads would help.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was a day I was on a roll, doing lesson after lesson, then suddenly, a long ad popped up. It made me lose my momentum just when I was really getting into it. It’s hard to regain that focus once it’s broken, especially after a full day at work.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, sometimes I listen to Spanish music or podcasts to enhance what I’m learning on Duolingo. It’s a good way to immerse myself in the language outside of the app, and it provides context you don’t always get from lessons alone.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They offer more of a cultural context, which is crucial for understanding how language is used in real life. Music and podcasts help with listening skills and expose me to different accents and slang, which is very practical.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: The worst would be losing motivation and dropping the language learning altogether. It’s easy for that to happen if the learning process becomes too tedious or if I encounter too many barriers, like the app not meeting my learning needs.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it engages me with interesting lessons and keeps me motivated with its gamified setup. I also look for it to challenge me just enough so I feel like I’m learning without being overwhelmed.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can use a phrase I’ve learned in a real conversation, that’s when I know it worked. Or when I recognize something in a Spanish song or show, it’s like a light bulb goes off. It’s a great feeling!

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d make the app’s ads less intrusive or offer more interactive ways to engage with them so they feel like part of the learning process rather than just breaks. Maybe some language-related offers or short, educational snippets.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love to see more integration between language apps and cultural experiences. Like offering virtual reality tours of cities where the language is spoken, combining learning with cultural context. It’d make learning more immersive and compelling.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we covered a lot! Just to add, the community aspect of language learning is important. Engaging with people who are learning the same language can really enhance the experience.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Absolutely, as long as it’s helping to improve language learning experiences for others, I’m all for it. Go right ahead!

Q: Intro greeting
A: That’s fine with me. I’ll be honest about what works and what doesn’t, especially when it comes to exam prep.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: I’m 22, a university student, and my life so far has revolved a lot around exams—entrance exams, standardized tests, all the usual checkpoints. I’m practical by nature: I don’t mind working hard, but I want whatever I’m doing to map clearly to results, especially when scores are on the line.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a mid-sized town and then moved to a bigger city for university. My family is pretty education-focused but not over-the-top about it.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was stable and fairly structured—school, extra classes, and a lot of talk about getting into a good program. I learned early that exam scores open doors, so I got used to thinking in terms of test strategy more than learning for fun.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: A turning point was taking a big standardized test for university admissions and seeing how much difference good prep made. I wasn’t the smartest person in the room, but I outperformed a lot of people because I treated it like a system to master instead of a mystery.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It made me realize that a lot of things that seem intimidating are really about understanding the format, the patterns, and the expectations. That mindset now shapes how I approach language exams and the tools I use.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I doubled down on structured prep—past papers, targeted drills, analysis of mistakes. Since then, I’ve been pretty skeptical of anything that feels too fluffy or fun without being clearly tied to exam performance.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now I care most about finishing my degree strong and hitting the language scores I need for scholarships and potential grad programs abroad. The language exam isn’t an abstract goal; it’s directly tied to money and opportunities.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because those scores literally change what options I have and what I can afford. I don’t have endless financial safety nets, so I care a lot about tools that truly move the needle on exam performance.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: On a good day, I attend classes, work through a planned set of practice questions, and finish knowing exactly what I improved. If I can see progress in my mock test scores or timing, that’s satisfying.

Q: What makes you say 'this was a good day'?
A: If I can point to something concrete—like I improved my listening accuracy by a certain amount or I finally nailed a specific grammar point—I feel like it was a good day. Vague 'I studied' without measurable progress doesn’t do much for me.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I gather information and compare options: cost, time, and expected impact. Then I usually choose the option that gives me the best return for the effort, even if it’s not the most exciting.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely a planner. I like knowing what I’m doing this week and why I’m doing it.

Q: Example showing that?
A: When I registered for my language exam, I immediately made a study plan mapped to the test sections—reading, listening, writing, speaking—and slotted in which days I’d do mock tests versus drills. Duolingo is in the supplement part of that plan, not the core.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I look at the worst-case scenario and the potential upside. If the risk doesn’t jeopardize something important like exam performance or finances, I’m more flexible; if it does, I’m cautious.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical weekday is classes during the day, then a block of focused study in the evening. I usually prioritize exam-type practice—timed reading, listening, writing—then, if I have a bit of leftover energy or time, I might open Duolingo for some light vocab or sentence review.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Classes and targeted practice sessions take the most time and energy. I don’t have a lot of patience for scattered or low-yield activities because my schedule already feels full.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more energy for sustained, high-level reading and listening in the language—like articles or podcasts. Those feel closest to the real exam demands, but they also require a lot of focus.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Time and mental bandwidth have been the biggest constraints. There’s a constant tradeoff between coursework, exam prep, and everything else, so anything that feels like 'cute but not useful' gets cut fast.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I prioritize ruthlessly. I keep a few core resources that I trust for exam prep and treat everything else, including Duolingo, as optional extras that can be dropped without guilt if needed.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I’m closest to a couple of classmates who are also preparing for language exams, plus my family. We compare scores and prep strategies more than social gossip sometimes.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Practical, supportive, and a bit nerdy. We talk about test sections and prep resources the way some people talk about TV shows.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly at school and home, with a lot of time online for study materials and practice tests.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I’d say focused but somewhat stressed—there’s always another exam date or assignment on the horizon. I feel supported, but there’s a constant awareness that the clock is ticking.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The environment is very exam-centric; everyone is talking about scores, deadlines, and applications. It’s motivating, but it also makes it obvious when a tool is just entertainment dressed up as learning.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: First I check official materials or trusted prep books. If it’s still unclear, I might ask a teacher or a friend who’s already taken the exam. I don’t usually turn to casual apps for real answers.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: A tough moment was getting a mock test result back that was lower than I’d expected after weeks of studying. It made me question whether I was spending time on the right kinds of practice.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: For a while, I became even more selective about what I used. I cut down on anything that felt like busywork and focused more on reconstructing my mistakes and drilling weak areas in test-like conditions.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I analyzed the mock test in detail, identified patterns in my errors, and adjusted my study plan. Emotionally, it was frustrating, but it also reinforced my skepticism about tools that feel fun but may not correlate strongly with exam performance.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Breaking things into specific, manageable tasks helps—like doing one reading passage and reviewing it thoroughly. Seeing clear, targeted progress is calming for me.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: A few years from now, I hope I’ve used these language scores to get into a program or job that lets me live or work abroad. Ideally, language will be a tool I use confidently, not something I’m constantly testing.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to be past the phase where everything is dictated by exam dates and score reports. Right now, a lot of my decisions are filtered through whether something will help with the test.

Q: Before PRODUCT, how did you handle the core job?
A: Before Duolingo, I relied on textbooks, official practice tests, and some online courses specifically aimed at my exam. It wasn’t exciting, but it was very aligned with what I’d actually be tested on.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The annoying part was that it could be monotonous and mentally heavy. After a long day, jumping straight into dense reading or timed listening wasn’t always realistic, even if it was the most efficient option.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Not exactly failed me, but it did burn me out at times. When all your study tools are serious and intense, it’s hard to keep going day after day without something lighter to mix in.

Q: How did you first hear about PRODUCT?
A: Like most people—friends, social media, and the general buzz of 'you should try Duolingo, it’s fun and free.'

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I was looking for something lighter to do on days when I couldn’t face another full mock test. Duolingo looked like an easy way to keep the language in my head without committing to a full study session.

Q: Walk through a recent PRODUCT use.
A: Recently, after a long day of classes, I didn’t have the energy to do a full exam section, so I opened Duolingo instead. I did a few lessons, matched pictures with words, tapped through some sentences, and by the end I thought, 'Okay, that was mildly useful review, but honestly, this is too cute for real test prep,' then I closed it and wrote down what topics I needed to drill properly the next day.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The vocabulary and basic sentence exposure was somewhat helpful, especially on a low-energy day. It’s better than doing nothing, and it keeps the language from feeling completely distant.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: The frustrating part was feeling like the app was more focused on animations, streaks, and little characters than on the skills I’m actually tested on. I kept thinking, 'This is too cute for real test prep,' and wishing I could flip a switch into a more no-nonsense mode with harder drills and fewer distractions.

Q: Most frustrating part of PRODUCT overall?
A: The most frustrating part of Duolingo is the gap between how serious my goals are and how playful the app feels. For someone preparing for standardized exams, it often feels like a children’s workbook—too cute for real test prep—when what I want is something that looks and behaves more like a test environment.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: One time I tried to use Duolingo as my main study tool for a week, just to see. At the end of the week, I took a timed practice test and my performance barely changed; I remember thinking, 'Okay, this is fun, but it’s too cute for real test prep,' and I went straight back to more traditional resources for the heavy lifting.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: I sometimes jot down words or structures from Duolingo that show up often and turn them into my own drills or flashcards. But honestly, most of my serious exam prep happens outside the app using more targeted materials.

Q: What do workarounds give you that PRODUCT doesn’t?
A: My own drills let me control difficulty, format, and timing so they match the test. Duolingo doesn’t give me that level of control; it keeps everything in a friendly, gamified wrapper, which is not how exams feel.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case is walking into the exam feeling busy but not prepared—having spent a lot of time on things that look like practice but don’t translate into higher scores. I can’t afford to confuse 'doing something in the language' with 'training for the test.'

Q: When you open PRODUCT, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping Duolingo will give me some light reinforcement of vocabulary and patterns on days when I can’t tackle full test sections. Part of me also wishes it had a serious exam mode, but right now I mostly treat it as a side dish, not the main course.

Q: How do you know PRODUCT worked?
A: If I can remember specific words or phrases later in my real practice and they come to mind faster, then I’d say it worked. If it just felt like tapping through cute exercises for a streak, it doesn’t register as meaningful progress.

Q: One thing you'd change about PRODUCT?
A: I’d add a no-nonsense mode specifically for exam-focused learners—harder drills, fewer animations, less gamification, and more tasks that look and feel like real test questions. Basically, less cute, more serious.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d like more tools that explicitly bridge the gap between fun, casual learning and high-stakes exam prep. Right now, you either get cute apps or dry test books, and there’s not much in between.

Q: Anything important we didn’t cover?
A: I’m not against Duolingo—it has its place. But as someone preparing for standardized exams, I keep finding myself saying that it’s too cute for real test prep, and I wish I could switch it into a more serious mode without all the extra distractions.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Yes, that’s fine. If my perspective helps you design a more exam-focused, no-nonsense option, I’d consider actually using Duolingo more regularly.

Q: Intro greeting

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, you see, I was born in Chennai, India, and moved to the US about 20 years ago. I've been in the IT field, you know, all that tech stuff, for quite some time now. Married with one son who loves anime. So, now I am trying to learn Japanese with him. It's a bonding experience, you see.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Chennai, you know, the capital of Tamil Nadu, in India. It was a bustling city but still had its own charm, like a good masala dosa.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was quite lively, I must say. Lots of street cricket, festivals, and, of course, the delicious food. My fondest memories are of celebrating Pongal with the family, all those colors and sweets, you know.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Moving to the US was the big one, I think. It was quite a leap, like halwa falling into hot sambhar! But it was also quite exciting, new culture, new opportunities. I went to Houston first before settling here.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, you see, it changed everything. Career-wise, it gave me opportunities that I didn't have back home. Personally, it was a big adjustment, adapting to a new culture and lifestyle. But, you know, it made me and my family stronger.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Oh, a lot of learning on the job, so to speak. I just tried to keep an open mind, you know. Made some good friends along the way who helped me understand the nuances of living here.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I think it's family time, yeah. I mean, work is always there, but these moments with my son, learning Japanese together, those are precious. It's like, who needs a TV when you have such live entertainment at home, right?

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because, you know, time is flying. One day he’ll be off to college, and I don’t want to miss these opportunities to bond and share experiences that we can laugh about in the future.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? Oh, that's when I can finish work on time, maybe cook a nice Indian dinner, and then sit down with my son for some anime and a bit of Duolingo, just winding down without stress, you know.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: I think it's when I go to bed content. When I know the day had balance, a bit of work, a bit of family, a bit of learning, and, of course, some laughs.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: Ah, big decisions need a big cup of chai, you know. I usually mull over them, discuss with my wife, make a pros and cons list, and sometimes a little prayer for good measure.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Oh, planner, definitely. I like to know what's coming, you know. Even in movies, I sometimes check online how it ends before watching!

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, when we planned our last family vacation to California, I had an itinerary ready, down to the T. Even scheduled in 'flexible times' for surprises. My son teases me for that one.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk, I see it like spicy food. You enjoy it but handle it carefully. I try to evaluate, understand the worst-case scenario, and then decide how spicy I want it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Ah, let's see. I get up early, maybe around 6:30, start the day with a bit of yoga if I'm not too lazy. Then it's breakfast, helping my son with online school setup, then I dive into work. IT work can be quite demanding, so there's a lot of meetings. We try to have dinner together, and then some Japanese lessons or Duolingo sessions. We wind down watching an anime episode or two.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: I think it's the juggling part, you know. Balancing work and family, especially with remote working, it gets tiring. Meetings, emails, and then shifting to family mode, it can be draining.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: More time for personal projects, I suppose. I've been wanting to, you know, dabble in some coding side projects or maybe learn to play the guitar. But the day just gets over too quickly.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: I think time was the biggest constraint, especially with the pandemic. Working from home sounds nice, but it blurred the lines between work and personal life. Suddenly, work hours were all over the place.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: Ah, it's like managing a big traffic jam, you know. I started setting stricter boundaries, making sure I finished work by a certain time, and keeping weekends for family only. Even Sundays are no-screen time, at least till evening.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: Definitely my family, my wife and son. And I've got a couple of close friends from college, we still chat and video call regularly. I guess it's the shared history that keeps us close.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Supportive, fun, and honest. We can talk about anything, you know. There's no judgment, just reliability. Like the old saying, 'a friend in need is a friend indeed.'

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: These days, mostly at home, actually. Thanks to the remote work culture. In the living room or my little home office corner I set up.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Oh, it's comfortable, but sometimes it feels a bit like the same scenery over and over again, you know. So, I try to add small changes, like new plants or rearranging furniture.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I think it's the routine, the lack of travel and going outside lately. It's like eating your favorite dish every day—it gets monotonous.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Mostly my wife. She's got a good head on her shoulders and usually has a different perspective. And if it's work-related, I'll talk to close colleagues or my old college friends.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Well, last year, my mother in India fell ill. Being so far away was tough, you know. I felt pretty helpless, and all I could do was make video calls and speak to doctors remotely with time zone differences.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was stressful, honestly. I felt this sense of guilt and worry continuously. It's not easy, juggling time between work, family here, and worrying about family back home.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I learned to prioritize and set small goals each day. Also, I leaned more on my friends and wife. They were my sounding board and helped me stay positive during a difficult time.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a break helps, going for a walk or doing some meditation. Sometimes, just watching a silly comedy with my son to laugh it off. Laughter really is the best medicine, I say.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I would like a bit more balance, you know, between work and personal life. Maybe travel more with the family, see new places, and, of course, be somewhat fluent in Japanese by then. Wouldn't that be something?

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I hope to be less caught up in work. It's important, yes, but family time should be higher on my priority list. Also, I want to dedicate time to hobbies, become more well-rounded, not just Rajesh-the-IT-guy.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Oh, before Duolingo, we tried a book-based approach, you know, those 'Learn Japanese in 30 Days' kind of books. But they were more amusing paperweights than learning tools, I tell you. We also tried watching anime with subtitles to pick up phrases, but it was so random. Nothing seemed to stick!

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: It was not engaging, that's for sure. The books were very dry, and I would often find myself dozing off. Plus, the lack of interaction made it feel like a one-sided conversation, you know?

Q: Time it really failed?
A: One embarrassing moment was when I tried to use what I learned from the book at a Japanese restaurant. I ordered 'konnyaku' thinking it was some kind of special sushi but ended up with a jelly-like dish that my son teased me about for weeks!

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I first heard about it from a colleague at work. He was using it for Spanish and kept saying how fun it was. So, I thought, why not give it a try?

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of learning while playing a game, honestly. My son and I are big on games, so anything that combines learning and fun is worth a shot. Plus, it's free, so there wasn't much to lose.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: So, let me think, just yesterday, my son and I sat down after dinner with the Duolingo app. We did a session on phrases, like 'konnichiwa' and 'arigatou'. The app gives you these little bursts of lessons, with matching words to pictures or repeating phrases. At the end, they have this funny sound for right answers and the owl mascot doing a dance. It’s quite amusing. My son loves it when we get a streak going, and he likes seeing our progress on the leaderboard.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The quick lessons and immediate feedback, you know, especially when you match words with pictures or hear the correct pronunciation. It feels like solving a puzzle. Plus, doing it together with my son makes it competitive and fun.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Ah, sometimes the repetition, I tell you. It’s like the app doesn’t believe I’ve learned 'konnichiwa' yet. It keeps throwing it at me like confetti. And if you make a mistake, no mercy, back to square one!

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: It must be the heart system, really. You make mistakes and lose lives, like in a video game. But here, it’s more annoying because sometimes the mistakes are typos or misclicks. Then you have to wait or pay to continue. Such a spoil sport, that owl!

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Just last week, I was practicing 'shopping' vocabulary, and one little typo got all my hearts drained. I was like, come on, give me a break, don't be such a strict teacher! My son found it hilarious, but I had to take a break and recharge my hearts before continuing.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, yes, we do. Sometimes, if I know it's getting repetitive, we'll switch to watching an anime episode for some 'real-world' practice. Or use flashcards or other language apps for variety.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give variety, you know. Sometimes you need a change of scenery. The other apps or shows provide context and help connect words to situations better. Remembering vocabulary in real conversations, I think, is more effective that way.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: I guess the worst thing would be, you know, if the fun and engagement are lost. Like if my son suddenly doesn't want to learn anymore because it feels like 'school' instead of fun time. That would be quite disappointing.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it makes learning feel like an adventure, like we are on some anime quest. And I hope we both can laugh and learn without feeling overwhelmed or bored. Something we look forward to every day.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: Ah, when my son and I manage to throw a few Japanese phrases in our daily conversation, you know it's working. Or when we recognize words while watching anime and give each other high-fives, that's definitely a win!

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I think maybe more focus on conversational practice, you know. Less 'fill in the blanks' and more dialogue simulations would be great. Make it feel like we're actually in a Japanese market asking for directions!

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd love if language learning tools were more integrated, like connecting to cultural content—animes, food, music. Make it a full experience, like how we learned languages growing up, through life, not just books.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we covered quite a bit, haha. Just that it's been a wonderful experience learning with my son, and I hope more people see language learning as a way to connect and enjoy, not just study.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Oh, sure, as long as it doesn’t have to work overtime like me, ha! Go ahead, you have my permission.

Q: One turning point in your life?

Q: Why was that a turning point?

Q: What is a good day for you?

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?

Q: Which parts take the most energy?

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?

Q: Biggest constraint last year?

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Always family first. My daughter, she is wise and knows so much. We solve problems together, with her husband too. And, um, my church friends, they are like family also, always listening when I need.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Ah, it was when I had to go for surgery. I was scared, you know? Hospitals, they are not much fun. It was hard because, um, I worry about language, if doctor understand me. But family, they were there every step, so I not alone.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It make me, um, realize importance of health, and how lucky I am to have family support. It was scary time, yes, but it also show me strength I have inside and remind me, life is precious.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I pray lot, kept busy with little things like knitting, to keep mind from worry too much. And, um, I talk with family daily. They give me strength, you know? Once surgery done, I focus on recovery, little goals each day like small walks.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking deep breaths, sitting quietly with tea, or maybe small prayer helps. Usually I call my daughter, we talk. Talking things out makes me feel, um, lighter. And sometimes just, uh, baking bread and smelling it, that simple thing help too.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to be healthy, see grandkids grow, achieve their dreams. Maybe learn English more, be confident to hold conversation anywhere. I'd love to travel more, see more of America, maybe visit Ukraine again too.

Q: What do you want to be different?

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: It was, um, slow and not interactive. I mean, reading books, repeating lines, it gets boring, yes? Also, trying to learn without, um, feedback, you never know if you say right or wrong. It felt lonely, no connection.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Oh, I remember once, I try to order in restaurant, use English from book. But, waiter, he did not understand me. I was embarrassed, but also, it was, um, wake-up call that I need better way to learn. That's when I start looking for options.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: My grandkids, they are savvy with these things. They come to me and say, 'Babushka, try Duolingo, it’s fun, like game!' and they helped me set up on phone. Such smart kids!

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: When my grandkids say it's like game, and when I see how it remind me daily, I thought, 'Okay, Olga, it's time to try something new.' Also, they were excited, and I want to join their excitement, you know?

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Ah, let's see, last time I open Duolingo, it say 'Olga, ready to learn?' I pick lesson on food, 'cause I love learning kitchen words. It start with picture of apple, then sound plays, and I repeat, 'apple.' Then it ask to match pictures with words. I got two wrong, but not worry, I learn. Later, small green owl appear, say, 'Great job!' and I feel good! Then, I earn some lingots, which, um, feel like little victory. Each lesson is like, yes, step closer to mastering English!

Q: Most helpful part?
A: I think, um, the structure. It keeps me on track, like little bird in forest path. Reminders, they help too, say, 'Olga, time to learn!' It very encouraging. Also, hearing pronunciation is very good, teach me how to say words right.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, words I learn, they don't, um, seem useful. I mean, like, tricky words, not kitchen or family words, you know? And when I get it wrong, it make me feel, oh, bit silly. But, I tell myself, 'Keep trying, Olga.'

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I think, maybe not enough real conversation practice. I learn, but talking with people, it’s different story. Also, app sometimes, it move too fast, like it's in hurry. I wish it slow down, let me catch breath.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Ah, yes. Once, I try to use word I learn in grocery store. But, um, cashier, she not understand me. I felt, like, oh, I need more practice! Words on app are one thing, but real people, they talk fast, with emotion. I need more real world practice, you know?

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Sometimes, I, uh, ask grandkids to practice with me, like small role-play. Also, I use, um, sticky notes around house with words. It help to see them daily. And, sometimes I watch English shows, repeat what they say.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give me, um, context, and, how you say, real life application. I mean, practice with family, it's more natural. Plus, I can ask questions, get instant answer, which Duolingo cannot do. It's, um, more interactive, personal.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case, I guess, is, um, not understanding important conversation, like at doctor, or missing something grandkids say. It, um, makes me feel isolated, like I miss piece of life here. That's why I keep learning, don't want that happen.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it help me feel more confident in English, like each lesson build my skills. I want it to be fun, not just, um, like school. And I hope, it bring me closer to talking freely with people outside.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can, you know, have small talk with cashier, or understand part of conversation on TV. Also, when grandkids say, 'Wow, Babushka, you said that right!' It feels like win.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would like, um, more conversation practice, you know, real scenarios. Maybe option to, uh, chat with other learners. It would be nice to hear more natural speaking, like in real life.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Oh, I think, more community support, like groups of learners in same boat as me. We could meet, share struggles, practice together, maybe drink tea. It make learning less lonely, you know?

A: I think we talk lots today. I just, um, want to say, learning is journey. Must be patient, enjoy process, even when hard. And thank you for listening to my stories!

A: Oh, I don't know what that is, dear. But if it help someone learn, then sure, you have my blessing!

Q: One time that frustration showed up?

Q: Do you use workarounds?

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love for language learning tools to integrate more cultural context, like understanding idioms or cultural references that native speakers use. It’s these little details that make a language truly functional and relatable.

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey, how's it going? I'm Tyrone.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, I grew up in a small town in Mississippi. Joined the military right outta high school, traveled all over. Did 30 years serving, retired a while back. Now, I'm tryin' to make the most of my time, pick up some new skills—like Arabic—since I love to travel.

Q: Where did you grow up?

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Quiet, you know, everybody knew everybody. Real close-knit, but not a lot going on. Lots of time to dream about getting out and seeing more of the world, which is what I eventually did when I joined the military.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Joining the military was the big one. It changed everything—got me out of Mississippi, made me who I am. It's where I learned discipline, met folks from all walks of life, and realized the world's a big place.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It opened doors I didn't even know existed. Gave me purpose, taught me responsibility, and gave me a chance to serve my country. Plus, it sparked a lifelong love of travel and learning.

A: Handled it like I do most things: head-on. Took on every challenge they threw at me, learned from each experience, and kept pushing myself to be better.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Important cause I spent so much of my life working hard. Now I want to enjoy the fruits of that labor by exploring the world. Plus, I think it’s important to keep learning, keep pushing, even now.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day is when I feel productive—got my exercise in, maybe learned a bit more Arabic, and spent some quality time with the family. Just having that balance, you know?

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I hit the sack and feel accomplished. Like I used the day well, didn't waste it. It’s that satisfaction of getting things done.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I weigh the pros and cons, look at all angles, and then trust my gut. Spent years in the military making decisions under pressure, so I rely on that experience too.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I’m a planner, for sure. Especially from my military days, planning’s kind of drilled into you.

Q: Example showing that?

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Carefully. I assess the situation, see what’s at stake. I’m not afraid of taking risks, but I prefer calculated ones, you know? But sometimes, you gotta just trust yourself and go for it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Wake up early, go for a run or hit the gym. Then, breakfast and check on my to-do list. I spend a couple hours on learning—Arabic included, of course. Rest of the day varies—might be catchin' up with buddies, doing odd jobs around the house, or planning my next trip.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I'd like more time for travel. Balancing everything can be a challenge, and sometimes there just aren’t enough hours in the day to plan big trips.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: Patience and planning. When stuff's outta your control, you gotta adapt. Focused on things I could do at home—learning more Arabic, prepping for trips when they happen.

Q: People you feel closest to?

Q: How did it affect you?
A: Kind of threw me off for a bit. You put effort into planning and then have to shift gears. It’s frustrating, but I’ve learned to be flexible, adapt when needed.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Turned my attention to learning more Arabic. Figured if I couldn’t go there physically, I could at least prepare better for when I could. Gave me something to focus on.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Exercise, definitely. Clears my head. Also, breaking it down—taking things step-by-step. When you’re overwhelmed, you just focus on the next small thing you can do.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: Ideally, I’d be traveling more, maybe even living abroad for a bit. Just soaking in different cultures, using what I’ve learned. And still having that strong connection with my family, wherever life takes us.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I wanna be more spontaneous. Always been a planner, but sometimes I think life could use more of a mix, you know? More spur-of-the-moment adventures.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Tried a bit of everything. Rosetta Stone, Pimsleur—those programs, but they felt kinda rigid and not all that engaging. I'd lose interest after a while, which wasn’t great for learning.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Probably how outdated and slow some of them felt. Learning should be dynamic, you know? But those old programs, they just felt like being back in school—staring at screens and repeating after a robot.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: I remember trying to have a basic conversation in Arabic with a friend and just blanking. Realized what I’d learned wasn’t sticking cause it wasn't real-world stuff, just exercises.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I think a friend mentioned it to me. Said it was free and pretty good for practicing on the go, so I figured I’d give it a shot.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The fact that it was free was a big draw, and I liked the idea of having a mobile app. I wanted something I could use whenever, wherever, and that seemed like a no-brainer.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure, so the other day, I jumped on Duolingo before breakfast. The app started me on a vocabulary lesson, you know, matching words with pictures. After that, it was onto some sentence building exercises. I like when it makes me speak the phrases out loud—helps with retention. Wrapped up with a review quiz to see how much stuck. Worked through it in about 20 minutes.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The speaking exercises, definitely. They force me to actually use my voice, and I think saying the words out loud helps me remember them better. Plus, it’s good prep for real conversations.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes it feels too much like a game. I mean, I like the badges and all, but it can be distracting. At times, I wish it pushed more on grammar and real-world use, like beyond just short phrases.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Probably when it seems too repetitive. You get stuck on the same words and phrases. I get it's for retention, but sometimes I need more variety to keep engaged.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh yeah, had this lesson where I kept seeing the same noun over and over, like I’d mastered it months ago. I wanted to move on, learn new words, but it kept dragging me back. Felt like I wasn't progressing fast enough.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yup, I started using YouTube videos and language podcasts to supplement. I’ll pause to practice pronunciations and get a better feel for conversational flow.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give me that real-world context. Hearing native speakers in real situations helps me understand slang, different accents, and how the language flows in conversation.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case, I spend all this time learning and still can't communicate effectively during my travels. That would be a real letdown, considering the effort put in.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping it'll challenge me, keep me engaged, and make the learning stick. I want it to be thorough enough that when I step into a new country, I don’t feel lost.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I see progress in real life, like if I can read a sign or understand bits of conversation in Arabic. Or when I feel more confident trying to speak the language.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d make it focus more on practical conversation and grammar. Give us more realistic dialogues instead of just isolated phrases.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Greater integration of real-world content—news, culture, slang. Make language learning immersive, so you’re not just learning words, but also the context of where, when, and how to use them.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Not that I can think of. Just hoping my experiences help shape better language tools for folks like me.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, go ahead. If it’ll help improve language learning tools, I’m all for it.

Q: Intro greeting

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, I grew up in Poland, small town near Wrocław. Moved to UK about ten years ago for work, you know, better opportunities. Been driving trucks all over, mostly between UK and Europe. It's like, always on the road. Recently trying to improve my English more seriously.

A: Grew up in Poland, little village close to Wrocław. Quiet place, lots of countryside, very peaceful.

A: Well, it changed everything—job, language, lifestyle. Before, I never left Poland. Now, I'm always on the road, meeting people from everywhere. It's like life opened up, you know?

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: At first, struggled a lot with English. So, I focused on learning from every interaction, picking up words and phrases during work. It was sink or swim, really.

A: Right now, improving my English is important. Makes job easier and life in UK better. Also, I care about staying fit, you know, long drives can mess with health.

A: Better English means better work opportunities and understanding what's around me. Plus, health is everything, especially when driving long hours—got to be sharp and in shape.

A: When I go to sleep and feel I learnt something, even just a bit, and had good conversations at truck stops. That feels like progress.

A: When I can recall and use a phrase or word in a real conversation without hesitating. That, and when I see my streaks and feel confident in my progress—both are reassuring.

A: Losing touch with English because I can't practice effectively. It's, um, hard to imagine going backward after all the progress I've made.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it, uh, challenges me a bit, introduces new words, and, like, helps make my English feel more natural.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can use what I've learned in real conversations, even if it's just a small part. It's when I understand more in movies or what the cashier is chatting about at the store.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Maybe, uh, have more interactive speaking exercises with different accents. That way, I can get used to how English sounds in various contexts.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd like to see, you know, more community-based learning where people can come together more often to practice in person and share experiences.

A: I think we've covered a lot, love. Just, um, maybe to say that learning is a journey, not a destination. It's about enjoying the process, too.

A: Oh, sure, I suppose! As long as it promises to be as patient as that little Duolingo owl, I'm fine with it.
