Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there, how's it going? I'm Quinn, nice to meet you!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, I grew up in Dublin, always dabbling in a bit of art, you know. Went to art school there and then found myself drawn to the vibrant, eclectic vibe of Berlin. Now I'm here, trying to learn German and figure out how to sell a painting or two, ha!

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: Ah, classic Dublin, you know? Born and bred on the north side, with all its charm and, um, quirks.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was grand, full of character. Every street had a story, people had a way with words, and the music, don't get me started. There’s a sort of friendly chaos that just gets under your skin.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Deciding to pack up and move to Berlin was a big one. It was a leap into the unknown, but I needed a change, and honestly, Berlin's art scene was calling my name.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It was like jumping off a cliff and hoping I'd learn to fly on the way down. It was terrifying but also exhilarating. I had to figure things out from scratch, which, in a way, was freeing.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I kind of just... winged it. Tried to connect with fellow artists, make my presence felt in galleries, and also, um, got a bit obsessed with Duolingo to get my German up to scratch.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's about cultivating my art and making sure I can, you know, communicate effectively here in Berlin. German's essential if I want to get my art out there and really be a part of this community.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Communication's everything, isn't it? If I can't share my thoughts or understand others, I'll just be floating on the surface, not really diving in. Plus, art's about connection, and language is a huge part of that.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Oh, a good day would be starting with a cup of strong coffee, maybe a bit of successful painting, discovering a new phrase in German, and catching up with mates at a gallery opening.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I've created something new, learned something, and shared laughs with friends, that's pretty much the jackpot for me.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to mull things over a lot, chat with friends, and, um, listen to my gut. There’s a lot of instinct involved. Sometimes you just need a pint to break it all down, you know?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely more go-with-the-flow. Plans are great until life throws a curveball, then you just roll with it.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Moving to Berlin was very much a 'see what happens' kind of thing. I had a rough idea, but nothing like a solid plan, and somehow, it all worked out—or is still working out, I should say.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I sort of embrace it. I mean, being an artist, you're always taking financial risks, aren't you? You just have to trust that it'll pay off, or at least you'll learn something from it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Well, I usually start with a quick Duolingo session while the coffee brews. Then it's into the studio, where time sort of bends—could be hours, could be minutes. Maybe I meet a friend for lunch, then back to painting. Evenings are either chill at home or out at some event.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Honestly, dealing with the admin side of art—emails, submissions, that lot. It takes the soul out of creating sometimes, but it's part of the gig.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I've been wanting to explore more of Germany, you know. Get a better feel for the culture outside Berlin, maybe find some new inspiration.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: It's probably balancing my art with learning German. Both demand a lot, and sometimes it feels like there's just not enough time in the day for both.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I try to combine them where I can—like listening to German music or podcasts while I paint. It's a sort of multitasking, but not quite.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My family back in Dublin, of course. Then there are a few artist mates here in Berlin who've become like a little family away from home.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They're all about support and banter. It's like having this safety net of people who get what you're going through.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Probably in my studio or at different galleries and cafes around Berlin. I like to keep the inspiration alive.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Comfortable and inspired, mostly. They're like my second home, where I can just let ideas flow without interruptions.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the freedom to create without judgment, and being surrounded by like-minded people who are also chasing their passions.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Usually my artist friends here or, if it's something bigger, I'll call my mum back home. She's always got the best advice, even if it's just to have a cup of tea and breathe.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Ah, there was a time when I almost ran out of funds. I was between commissions, and it got a bit nerve-wracking. I thought I'd have to pack it all up and head back to Dublin.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was pretty stressful. I mean, you start doubting your choices, questioning if you've got what it takes to make it work. It shook me a bit, but also pushed me to hustle harder.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Well, I took on a few odd jobs, anything to keep the lights on, you know? And I tried to focus on my art as an escape, hoping it would eventually pay off.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Honestly, a bit of humor goes a long way. That and stepping back to remind myself why I'm here, doing what I'm doing. A good chat with a mate doesn't hurt either.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I'd love to see my art reaching more people, maybe have a few solo exhibitions under my belt. Being able to speak German fluently would be a huge bonus too.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: Honestly, more financial stability would be nice. Just enough to not worry about the next month, you know? And perhaps a bit more balance in my schedule.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: I tried classes at some point but, you know, rigid schedules never suited me. Then there were books and podcasts, but it was all very sporadic and lacked the consistency I needed.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Probably the lack of immediate feedback. I mean, you'd go back and forth in a book without knowing if you'd actually learned anything until you tried to use it in a real conversation.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time I tried to order something in a cafe, thought I'd nailed it, but ended up with a completely different order. The barista's face was priceless, and I was left sipping a sauerkraut smoothie—never again.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: Oh, it was through a friend back home. They knew I was struggling with German and said, 'Why not give that owl a go?'

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I liked the idea of bite-sized lessons that I could fit into my day. Plus, the whole gamified approach seemed like a bit of craic, to be honest.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure! So, I open Duolingo on my phone, and the little owl cheers me on. I usually pick a skill I haven’t practiced lately, like 'Clothing' or 'Food'. I love that it starts with a recap of what I might've forgotten. As I go through the exercises, there's a mix of translating sentences, matching pairs, and speaking challenges. The speaking ones are my favorite, even if I sound daft. Some of the sentences are ridiculous, like 'The bear wears a hat', but hey, it sticks!

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The interactive exercises are great. They make me feel like I’m actually engaging with the language, not just passively absorbing it. And the daily streak is a surprisingly good motivator.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes it gets a bit repetitive, you know? Like you swear you’ve done the same exercise twenty times over. And some of the phrases are so odd, they're hardly practical.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Probably when I know I’ve pronounced something right, but it doesn't register. You end up shouting at your phone, 'I said it perfectly!' But the owl doesn’t budge.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was a time I was doing a pronunciation exercise on 'Eichhörnchen'—tricky word, right? I must've said it ten different ways, and it still wouldn't accept it. I was losing my mind and laughing at the same time, but ended up letting it go.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Sometimes I record my voice exercises and play them back, just to see if I’m actually off. And watching German films with subtitles for context helps fill in the gaps.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They add a bit more context and realism, which Duolingo sometimes lacks. Real conversation doesn’t always follow the script, you know?

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case? I'd probably get stuck in a never-ending loop of repeating a lesson I can’t pass. That, or the streak pressure could turn me into a hermit solely focused on maintaining it.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it gives me something new to chew on. A fresh perspective or phrase that I can drop casually in conversation and see the surprised look on a local's face.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can toss out a sentence in German with ease, or when I catch myself thinking in German without realizing it—that's when I know it's sinking in.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd love more real-world applications, like situational role-plays. Also, having the option to practice more diverse conversations would be great.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd make language learning less about ticking boxes and more about cultural immersion. Something with a bit more soul, if you know what I mean.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Maybe just that language is art in itself. It's another form of expression, and it's been interesting to see how it influences my own work.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Ah, why not! Just make sure it appreciates good art and doesn't embarrass me too much, haha.

Q: Why is that important?

A: It made me realize how quickly things can change on the road. I felt a bit powerless and frustrated, not knowing when I'd move again. Made me think harder about preparation and patience.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I reached out to other drivers, shared information about what was happening. That helped ease the stress. I used the time to practice German on Duolingo and catch up on rest. Tried to stay positive and focused on what I could control.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking deep breaths and reminding myself it’s temporary—it’s worked in the past. Music helps too, especially when I’m stuck in traffic or at a standstill. A good song can change the mood entirely.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I’d like to have more time at home, maybe manage my own small fleet of trucks. Still on the road but not as intensely, more balanced. Being more fluent in German would be nice, opens more possibilities.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: The amount of time away. It would be great to not miss family events. And maybe a bit less paperwork on the road, that’s always a drag. Less stress, more quality time.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: I mainly used phrasebooks and a bit of Rosetta Stone, but it was tough. The books weren’t practical for real life, and Rosetta Stone was too slow for me. Often, I just picked up bits from conversations. It worked, but not very efficiently.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The phrasebooks didn’t fit real-life conversations. They taught me how to ask for a train station but not negotiate delivery terms. And Rosetta Stone needed too much time, which I didn’t have.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Once, I had to explain a delivery issue to a German client. My phrasebook had nothing useful, and I ended up using a mix of English and gestures. It was awkward, and I felt unprepared.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A fellow driver mentioned it on a break. He was learning Spanish and said it was handy, so I figured, why not try for German?

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of learning in short bursts seemed perfect for my schedule. That and it was free! I didn’t have much to lose by trying, and I needed a faster way to learn.

A: Sure. So, I was parked at a rest stop in Bavaria, just had lunch. Opened Duolingo, started with a few practice exercises. The app threw some vocabulary at me about vehicles—nice touch. Did a couple of quick lessons on sentence structure. I like how it repeats words I struggle with, helps them stick. Finished with audio exercises, trying to match what I hear. By the time I was done, I felt like I had a mini lesson on the road.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Having the app available anytime. It fits into the small breaks I get, and the gamification keeps it engaging. I like the quick correction on mistakes, helps reinforce learning before I forget.

Q: Most frustrating part?

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: I was trying to ask a local about a detour and realized the phrases I practiced weren't clicking. The app taught me the words, but not how to use them naturally in conversation. Had to fumble through it.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it gives me lessons that stick, engaging exercises that help remember words and phrases I actually use on the road. Plus, quick wins that motivate me to keep learning.

A: When I successfully use a phrase I learned in a real conversation, or I can read German signs and documents better. It’s those moments when you understand without needing to translate everything.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd add more practical language lessons, like business or transport-specific content. Things a truck driver actually encounters—more practical, less random sentences.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: More integration of language learning with practical, real-world settings and scenarios. Tools that mimic natural conversation and help tackle real situations would be game changers.

A: I guess just that language learning needs to keep realistic. Theoretical knowledge is good, but practice and context matter just as much.

A: Sure, go ahead. If it helps improve language learning, I'm all for it.

Q: Intro greeting

Estoy trabajando en mejorar mi inglés para asegurarme de poder comunicarme efectivamente en este mercado.

Q: Why was that a turning point?

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Ahora mismo, estoy enfocada en mi carrera. Quiero hacer un impacto en los medios aquí, y parte de eso es asegurarme de comunicarme de manera efectiva en inglés. También quiero conectarme más con la comunidad latina y compartir nuestras historias.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Pienso que en un mundo tan globalizado, es crucial que se escuchen nuestras voces y se representen nuestras perspectivas. Además, fortalecer mis habilidades lingüísticas me dará más oportunidades para crecer profesionalmente.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Un buen día es cuando he escrito algo que me enorgullece o he tenido una entrevista que realmente conectó. Al final del día, con un cafecito en la mano, si siento que he aprendido algo nuevo y he contribuido de alguna manera, esa sensación es invaluable.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?

Q: How do you make big decisions?

Q: Typical weekday?

Q: How did you cope?

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: Quisiera estar establecida en un medio de comunicación influyente, con un buen equilibrio entre la vida laboral y personal. Sueño con escribir algo más profundo, quizá un libro, y seguir conectando con la comunidad latina aquí.

Q: What do you want to be different?

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Era muy frustrante la falta de interacción y practicidad. Los libros eran teóricos, y al no tener un interlocutor real, era difícil saber si realmente estaba mejorando. Sentía que estaba aprendiendo en una burbuja sin poder salir a practicar.

Q: Time it really failed?

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: Creo que fue hace unos años, lo vi recomendado en línea por un amigo en redes sociales. Decía que era muy accesible y fácil de usar en cualquier lugar.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: La posibilidad de poder practicar en el teléfono, en los trayectos o cuando tuviera un momento libre, me atrajo. Quería algo que complementara las formas más tradicionales de aprendizaje y que me mantuviera motivada diariamente.

A: Bueno, el otro día, usé Duolingo mientras tomaba un cafecito por la mañana. Abrí la app y vi que había una nueva actualización de unidades. También hay los recordatorios diarios que me mantienen al tanto. Aunque, si debo ser honesta, a veces siento que las lecciones son un poco repetitivas.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Diría que la portabilidad de la app. El hecho de que puedo usarla en cualquier parte es genial. Me gusta la manera en que proporciona ejercicios para practicar la pronunciación. Es práctico para reforzar lo que ya sé mientras estoy en movimiento.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: A veces, la falta de profundidad me frustra, especialmente cuando necesito aprender vocabulario más avanzado. También siento que no se centra mucho en contexto, que es crucial para mi trabajo. Es como aprender palabras sueltas sin entender cómo se usan realmente.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: El enfoque repetitivo en las mismas estructuras básicas es un poco fastidioso. Y la gamificación es buena al principio para enganchar, pero a largo plazo, necesito contenido más serio, más adulto. Me falta esa profundidad como un buen libro o una clase intensiva podría ofrecer.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Recientemente, mientras intentaba preparar un artículo en inglés, necesitaba entender mejor el uso de ciertas expresiones profesionales. Intenté buscar una lección en Duolingo que me ayudara, pero nada abordaba lo que necesitaba. Fue frustrante no poder encontrar el recurso correcto dentro de la app.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Sí, a menudo complemento Duolingo con otras herramientas. Uso apps como Babbel para gramática más compleja y veo videos de YouTube para escuchar diferentes acentos y aprender vocabulario en contexto. También, leo mucho en inglés para tener esa exposición diaria.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Me dan profundidad y variedad. Puedo practicar ejemplos de la vida real, como situaciones que enfrentaría en un entorno profesional. Además, me ayuda a mantener las cosas interesantes, porque a veces Duolingo se siente un poco repetitivo.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Que dependa demasiado de una herramienta y termine estancada, sin progresar en el lenguaje. Si no busco más allá y no ejemplifico con situaciones reales, podría fallar en comunicarme efectivamente cuando más lo necesite, especialmente en mi trabajo.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: Espero que me ofrezca algo nuevo, que me rete, pero también que sea divertido. Que me dé un panorama de temas que realmente usaría en conversaciones cotidianas o en el ámbito laboral.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: Me doy cuenta cuando me cruzo con palabras o expresiones que repasé en la app y puedo utilizarlas correctamente en una conversación o al escribir. También ayuda cuando puedo entender más rápidamente las cosas que leo o escucho en inglés.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Integraría más contenido para usuarios avanzados, especialmente para aquellos que quieren usar el idioma profesionalmente. Quizás crear módulos especializados o permitir un nivel de personalización más alto en las lecciones.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Haría que las plataformas fueran más integradoras, conectando los aprendizajes con situaciones reales, como prácticas de conversación con hablantes nativos o simulaciones de situaciones laborales.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Creo que hemos tocado los puntos claves. Quizás solo añadir que es importante tener en cuenta diferentes estilos de aprendizaje y cómo estos pueden ser atendidos por plataformas educativas.

Q: Intro greeting
A: Olá! It's really lovely to be here, sharing a bit of my story and, uh, my love for languages with you. I'm excited!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Oh, where do I start? I was born in Lisbon, steeped in the soulful rhythms of fado, you know? I always felt this pull to express emotions through music. My journey has taken me from the narrow streets of Alfama to the bustling cafés of Paris, where I'm now trying to sprinkle a bit of French into my performances. It's like adding a new color to my musical palette, and it's been quite the adventure!

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Lisbon, in the beautiful neighborhood of Alfama. It's a place full of history and, um, music at every corner.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was magical in many ways. Alfama is all cobblestone streets and hidden corners, you know? It's where fado really breathes. Growing up there was like living in a musical—there were always voices singing, guitars playing. It taught me to feel deeply and express those feelings through music.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: I think moving to Paris was a huge turning point for me. I mean, leaving Lisbon and starting over in a new city, with a new language—it was daunting but exhilarating. It opened my world. Suddenly I was performing my fado in these intimate little venues in Montmartre and hearing French all around me. It made me want to blend these worlds, um, to sing fado in French as well.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it pushed me out of my comfort zone, you know? I was used to singing in Portuguese, in my language. Paris made me realize that, um, music doesn't have to be confined by that. I could share my stories and emotions in French too, and it made me fall in love with language all over again.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Well, it was a lot of, uh, embracing the unknown, I guess. I started taking French lessons and tried to immerse myself in the culture. It wasn't easy—I made mistakes, got frustrated, but I also learned to laugh at myself. Music was my anchor, my way to connect with people.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I'm really focused on, um, perfecting my French so I can, you know, perform seamlessly here in Paris. I want to write original fado songs in French too. It's important to me that I, um, respect and understand the nuances of the language.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because language is more than words, you know? It's a way to connect with people on a deeper level. When I sing in French, I feel like I'm not just using a tool, but I'm part of the culture. It's a way to honor where I am and the people who are listening to me.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Hmm, a good day? Well, it usually starts with coffee at a little café, maybe jotting down some lyrics or ideas. Then I’d have a rehearsal or maybe a performance in the evening. If I can get a good language practice session in with Duolingo or chatting with locals—oh, and maybe catch a sunset over the Seine—then, yeah, that's a good day.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel fulfilled, like I've learned something new or touched someone with my music. It's the small victories, like mastering a tricky French expression or having an audience member say they felt my song, even if they didn't understand every word.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I, um, tend to go with my gut. I think it's the musician in me—so much of music is about feeling. But I also weigh my options, talk to friends who know me well. It's a blend of intuition and practical thinking, I guess. I ask myself: does this move me forward or open up new possibilities?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'd say a bit of both. I like having a plan, especially with my music and performances, but I'm also open to where the day takes me. Life is, uh, unpredictable, and sometimes the best things happen when you aren't looking, you know?

Q: Example showing that?
A: Oh, like, there was this time I had a performance planned in Paris, everything set. But then I got an invite last-minute to join another artist on stage, completely unexpected. I, um, decided to go for it, and it turned out to be one of the most magical nights. The chemistry on stage was amazing, and the audience loved it. Sometimes you just have to, like, embrace those surprises.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk can be, you know, a bit scary, but I think it’s essential. I weigh the pros and cons, try to see if the risk aligns with my goals. But at the end of the day, I believe—like in music—you have to take a leap of faith sometimes. That's where the magic often happens, in those uncertain spaces.

A: It changed everything—my perspective, my career, how I see healthcare, really. It's like starting fresh but with all the experience I gained back home. It opened doors to understanding different cultural approaches to health.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Well, it was a bit daunting, but I threw myself into it. I leaned on my nursing experience and made an effort to learn about Maori culture and language—it helped me connect with patients more deeply.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I'd say integrating Maori language and culture into my work as a nurse. It's something I feel very passionate about—showing respect and providing care that acknowledges the cultural identity of the people I'm treating.

Q: Why is that important?
A: It's about more than just language. It's about showing respect and understanding—making sure patients feel seen and valued. It helps in building trust and delivering holistic care, which is crucial.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day is one where I feel I've made a difference—whether it's by comforting a patient or successfully using my growing Maori vocabulary to connect with someone. And if the weather's nice, ending with a walk along the beach wouldn't hurt!

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I head home and feel a sense of accomplishment. It's those little moments, like seeing a patient's face light up when they hear me speak Maori, even just a wee bit.

A: I tend to weigh things up carefully. Being a nurse, you get used to making decisions under pressure, so I like to gather all the facts, talk it through with people I trust, and then go with my gut feeling.

A: I'm definitely a planner, but I try to be flexible too. Nursing teaches you that things rarely go exactly as planned.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?

Q: How do you make big decisions?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?

Q: How do you handle risk?

Q: Typical weekday?
A: My weekdays are pretty packed. I start with checking emails and planning my content for the blog. Then it's meetings, photo shoots, and a bit of French practice. I usually end the day with some editing and perhaps a cozy dinner with friends. It’s busy, but I love every bit!

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Definitely in cafés or walking through the Parisian streets, camera in hand. I also spend a lot of time in my little apartment, editing photos and writing.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Cafés are my creative zone. There's something about the ambient noise and aroma of coffee that fuels my inspiration. My apartment is like my safe haven, a place where I can unwind and let my creativity flow.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I think it’s the mix of history and modern life in Paris. The old buildings with their stories and the vibrant city life—it's all so inspiring and revitalizing.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually call my mom. She always knows how to make me feel better, even when I’m miles away. And my best friend here; she gets my fashion dilemmas and helps brainstorm solutions.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: A long walk along the Seine always helps. It clears my mind. Also, a good phone call with my family to remind me of who I am and what I’m here to achieve.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I see myself having mastered French and possibly adding another language. My blog and style influence would have expanded to a global audience. Maybe even design my own fashion line that reflects my Moroccan roots and Parisian flair.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d love to have a stronger command over fashion-specific language in French. And, maybe a bit more stability in my routine to focus on personal growth alongside professional pursuits.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of consistency and focus. Audiobooks were too passive, and language meet-ups were so hit or miss with the crowd. Sometimes it felt like I was going nowhere.

Q: Time it really failed?

A: Sure! So, yesterday I was waiting for a friend in a café. I opened Duolingo, chose the French course, and started a new lesson on verbs. Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitely the listening exercises. They help me get familiar with the Parisian accent, which is so essential. Plus, the app's reminders keep me on track, so I don't skip any days.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: The most frustrating part is when it doesn’t provide enough context for advanced vocabulary or specific phrases, especially in fashion. Like, I need to know how to discuss textures and styles in detail, and Duolingo just doesn’t go that deep.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I’d say the rigidity in how it expects you to learn. Sometimes I feel like it's too linear and doesn't adapt to my specific needs or areas where I struggle. It could do with more personalized learning paths.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Like, last month when I was trying to refine my blog content in French, I needed exact terms for different fabrics and cuts, and Duolingo's vocabulary seemed too basic. I ended up searching elsewhere, which broke my learning flow.

A: Oh, yeah. I frequently use fashion magazines and watch French fashion shows to get the vocabulary I need. I also attend fashion events to immerse myself with the language in context.

A: The real-world application, for sure. Hearing and seeing the language in use within the fashion industry gives me the context and depth that Duolingo lacks. It’s like getting a sneak peek into how real conversations happen.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case would be if Duolingo doesn’t evolve to include more specialized content, I might outgrow it and lose a convenient way to practice daily. That would mean more effort tracking down different learning resources.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it gives me a quick, effective boost in language skills that I can apply immediately in my day-to-day life in Paris. Something that feels rewarding and progresses, even if it’s just in small steps.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: I know it worked when I can actually use a new word or phrase in a conversation with a friend, or when I navigate a situation in French without feeling lost. It's about those little victories, you know?

A: I’d add more advanced options and industry-specific vocab, especially for areas like fashion. Also, maybe some virtual conversation meet-ups to practice speaking with others.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd love to see more integration between digital learning and real-life application. Like, apps that tie in with local events or cultural experiences where you can practice what you've learned in a supportive environment.

A: I think we covered a lot! Just that language learning is a journey, and apps like Duolingo are a piece of a much larger puzzle involving experiences, culture, and personal growth.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure thing, as long as it captures my flair for fashion and my passion for perfecting French!

A: Well, media is a big part of football these days, right? I want to represent myself well, be able to communicate my thoughts. It builds a better connection with people off the pitch too.

Q: What is a good day for you?

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?

Q: How did it affect you?

Q: How did you cope?

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I'd like more stability, you know? Feel completely settled in my career and language abilities. Also, more time to enjoy life outside football and connect with people on a deeper level.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Ah, the slow progress, definitely. Felt like I was learning random bits with no real context. Plus, textbooks can be boring, not something I looked forward to after a long day of training.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: I remember trying to follow a conversation in a café, and I was just lost. It hit me then that knowing words wasn’t enough. I needed to understand how they fit together in real speech. That was a wake-up call.

A: A teammate mentioned it during a flight to a match. Said it was fun and easy to use, especially when you don’t have much time.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of short lessons was appealing. Like, I could fit it in between training or on the bus. Plus, my teammate said I could learn in a game-like format, which sounded way better than textbooks.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure, uh, so last night, I opened the app after dinner. I did a few vocabulary lessons, the ones with pictures where you match words. I like those because they're visual and stick better. Then I tried the speaking exercise, repeating phrases. It's pretty good for pronunciation, even if it's not always perfect. I finished with that little progress bar filling up, which is satisfying. It feels like scoring a goal when you finish a lesson, you know?

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Honestly, the repetition is key for me. It’s like training drills, you do it until it’s second nature. The speaking exercises help with my accent too, which is super important.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Hmm, sometimes the translations feel too textbook, you know? Like, it’s not how people really speak in daily life. I’d like more realistic conversations.

A: I guess it’s the lack of deeper conversation practice. As someone who needs to engage with media, I'd love more realistic dialogue that feels more like what I hear in interviews or public speaking.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this one time I was preparing for an interview, tried to use some phrases from Duolingo, and it didn’t fit right. It wasn’t how the anchor spoke at all. Made me realize I needed more conversational practice.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, sometimes I listen to French podcasts or watch TV shows. It helps to hear how words are used naturally. I also try to engage in conversations with locals whenever I can.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They give me context and cultural nuances, which are crucial. Language isn't just words, it's about feeling the rhythm and tone, which you can't get from an app alone.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case? Probably preparing wrong for a big media event. Like, failing to express myself clearly on-camera because I stuck by the book too much. That’s a nightmare, especially with so many viewers.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it reinforces what I've learned, maybe teach me something new and useful. Something I can actually use in a real conversation, you know?

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can recall a word or phrase easily during a conversation, that’s how I know. Or when I'm able to follow French commentary during a match, that feels like progress.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: More conversational practice, definitely. Like, simulated interviews or dialogues that mirror real-life situations more closely.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I guess more integration of culture with language. Learning isn't just about words, it's about understanding the people who speak it, their way of life.

A: I think we covered a lot! Just that, you know, continuous improvement in language tools is key for people like me.

A: Yeah, sure, as long as it helps improve learning experiences for people.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: The worst-case scenario would be feeling disconnected from my heritage because I can't fully grasp the language in a meaningful way. It's important to me that learning Portuguese helps bridge that gap and not just be a bunch of words I can't practically use.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it helps me learn something new every day, even if it's just a small thing. Like, adding a piece to a puzzle. I want to feel like I'm getting closer to speaking and understanding Portuguese better.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: I know it's working when I recognize words in Portuguese films or when I can string together a sentence without too much hesitation. Seeing my daily streak grow is also a nice confidence boost.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would add more cultural content—like videos or stories from native speakers. Something that makes it feel a bit more real and immersive, you know, beyond the exercises.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there were more platforms that integrate cultural learning with language practice, especially for diasporas like myself. It's not just about words; it's about connecting with roots and communities.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we've covered quite a lot! But, um, I just want to say how thankful I am for tools like Duolingo. It's really helping me on this journey of rediscovery.

A: Oh, sure, if it helps improve experiences for people like me, then why not?

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hola! Nice to meet you! I'm Carmen, and I'm excited to chat about my language adventures here in Japan.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Ah, well, I grew up in Seville, in the heart of flamenco. The rhythm, the colors, they are part of my soul. I started dancing flamenco as a little girl, and I knew it was my path. Many years later, I found myself moving to Japan to teach flamenco, and now I'm here, learning Japanese to connect better with my students and the beautiful culture here.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Seville, Spain. It’s a city full of life, with flamenco in every corner and the sun shining brightly most of the year.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Growing up in Seville was like living in a festival, you know? The Feria, Semana Santa, flamenco... it was vibrant and loud with family gatherings, and always filled with music. It shaped my spirit, my movement, and how I express myself today.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Deciding to move to Japan was a huge turning point. I had this opportunity to teach flamenco... in Kyoto! It was terrifying and thrilling all at once. I left behind not just a city, but my close-knit family and traditions to step into a completely different world.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It was a turning point because it forced me out of my comfort zone completely. I had to adapt to a new culture, learn a new language, and rebuild my identity outside my Spanish roots. It was like learning a new dance, with unfamiliar steps and rhythms.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Well, I embraced it with as much passion and openness as I could muster. I started taking Japanese lessons, sometimes feeling like I was fumbling through words like I first fumbled in dance. I made friends and let my flamenco spirit guide me in forming connections here.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's balancing my flamenco teaching with learning Japanese. I want to fully communicate with my students, capture every nuance of their expressions. It's important because my art depends on that connection and understanding.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because language, to me, is as much a part of the dance as the music or the steps. It’s a paso doble between my passion and my new life. I believe understanding the language will enrich my teaching and deepen the connections I have with my students.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day involves a dynamic flamenco class, where my students and I are in sync, moving gracefully. Then maybe a quiet moment sipping tea while practicing Japanese, and ending with a warm chat over dinner with friends.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel like I’ve expressed my soul, either through dance or language. If my students leave with smiles and I've conquered a tricky part in Japanese, that's the feeling, you know?

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I listen to my intuition, that flamenco rhythm inside, but I also discuss with my family and friends. I weigh the pros and cons, but in the end, I trust the feelings that move me.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Oh, I'm definitely more of a go-with-the-flow kind of person. Life has its plans, and sometimes you just need to dance along with it.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Like when I moved to Japan. I didn’t have everything figured out, but I felt the pull of an adventure. I had a rough plan, sure, but mostly I trusted the journey and let things unfold.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: With a bit of fear, honestly, but also a thrill. I mean, it’s like performing a new flamenco piece. There’s always a chance of failing, but the possibility of something beautiful is worth it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical day? Well, mornings are for Japanese study over breakfast. Then I might prepare lessons or do some admin work for the studio. Afternoons are noisy with classes filled with clapping and footwork. Evenings are quieter, maybe some yoga or a stroll, followed by dinner with friends, often trying my best on konbini Japanese conversation.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: The teaching, definitely. Flamenco is passion and storytelling. Getting that across in another language, with all its culture, really takes a lot of my physical and mental energy.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time for personal flamenco practice. Between teaching and language lessons, my own dancing sometimes gets put aside. I miss the deep personal connection that comes from losing myself in the dance.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: The language barrier was the biggest constraint. There were moments in my classes where I couldn't express exactly what I wanted. It's frustrating when the words don't flow like my dance does.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: Duolingo helped, surprisingly. It’s like having a little tutor on my phone. But I also attend language exchanges and practice with friends, mixing Spanish warmth with Japanese politeness.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My family back in Spain, of course, and my new friends here in Japan. We share laughs, meals, stories… it almost feels like a mini community, a little piece of home mixed with new flavors.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They're like a dance – give and take, sometimes leading, sometimes following. With my Spanish family, it’s grounded in tradition. Here in Japan, it’s more about shared experiences and learning from each other.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: In my studio. It’s my sanctuary, my stage. It's where I express myself the most, where my passion and work come to life.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I feel alive, invigorated. The studio is where I pour out my heart, where my students and I share energy and stories. It's a place of transformation for both them and me.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The energy of movement, the sound of footwork, the clapping – it’s the heartbeat of flamenco that creates an environment of pure expression and connection.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I turn to my family or my friends here. They’re like my support network, offering advice, a listening ear, or even just a distraction with a silly story or a good night out.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was a time when I had difficulty conveying a complex flamenco concept. I was frustrated and doubting my own skills, feeling the gap in my language ability acutely.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It made me question my effectiveness as a teacher. I felt like maybe I was losing that cultural depth that I so dearly wanted to share. It shook my confidence a bit, you know?

Q: How did you cope?
A: I doubled down on my Japanese studies, talked to other bilingual teachers for advice, and also reminded myself of my strengths. I learned to be patient with myself, to embrace the process like a slow, evolving dance.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Dancing, of course! It clears my mind, centers me. And talking to a friend over a glass of Rioja doesn't hurt either. Those moments of connection and movement are my therapy.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I would love to have a bilingual flamenco school, teaching and performing across both cultures. I want to feel at ease with Japanese and maybe explore other parts of Asia while sharing the beauty of flamenco.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to feel more fluid in Japanese, like the language is as natural to me as Spanish. Also, I'd love more time for personal creativity, to choreograph new pieces that reflect my experiences here.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: I started with traditional classes and textbooks, but it felt rigid, you know? I also tried language exchange meetups, which were fun but not always consistent. Sometimes it felt like dancing with a partner who had two left feet.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of practicality. I'd learn words I could never use in daily life or in the studio. It felt disconnected from what I needed. Plus, the grammar drills were dry, with no rhythm or life.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Once, I tried to use a phrase I learned from a textbook in a supermarket, and the clerk just looked at me confused! It made me realize textbooks sometimes lack the nuance and flow of real conversation.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend mentioned it over tapas back in Spain, saying it was a fun way to learn new languages. I was intrigued by the idea of learning on the go with some gamification.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of learning through short, engaging exercises was appealing. Plus, the little owl mascot, Duo, seemed encouraging. It was a way to incorporate language learning into my busy life without too much formality.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Just yesterday, between classes, I opened Duolingo on my phone. I started with a quick revision of some kanji and then moved into a lesson on polite phrases – something essential in Japan! I love how it gives you a sentence, and you have to pick the right words. At the end, when Duo cheered for me with its little sound, it felt like a mini-victory dance. And those streaks! They’re addicting, like trying to keep a rhythm in a dance performance.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The interactive nature and the repetition. It helps solidify new words, kind of like practicing a flamenco sequence till it’s second nature. The immediacy and feedback make learning feel alive and dynamic rather than static.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, it feels a bit repetitive, or like it’s not quite going deep enough into the context. You can remember vocabulary, but mastering the language needs more than just words—it’s about the rhythm, the subtleties, things that an app can't always capture.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The lack of real conversational practice. It can sometimes feel as if I'm just memorizing rather than truly engaging in the music of the language. I wish it could simulate real-life dialogue more effectively.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this time when I had just finished a lesson on polite Japanese phrases, and I tried to use one during a meeting with other teachers. It didn't land right because the app had left out some cultural nuances. It reminded me that learning a language is more than just vocabulary and syntax; it’s about cultural context too.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, I often supplement Duolingo with language meetups and try to read Japanese manga to get a feel for the language's flow. It's like adding layers to a performance, ensuring every detail feels authentic and connected.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide context, nuance, and live interaction. It’s like switching from practicing to performing on stage, where everything blends—the rhythm, the audience, the movement. Those interactions add the spice that an app alone can't provide.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: That I'll never quite feel fluent, always missing that one word or phrase at the crucial moment. It’s like forgetting a step in a dance routine—throws the whole performance off! I fear that gap might keep me from fully integrating here.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it offers me something new, engaging, something that challenges me a bit. I want to feel like each session adds a step to my fluency dance, moving me closer to expressing myself completely in Japanese.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can slip a new word or phrase into my day-to-day conversations, or when I don’t even realize I’m thinking about something in Japanese. That’s the magic moment, like muscle memory in dance.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d add more real-world conversational practice, maybe through interactive dialogues that simulate real-life situations, more than just phrase matching. Let’s bring the cultural music into the mix!

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Integrate more cultural immersion into language learning apps, connecting learners with native speakers or cultural experiences. Make the language dance across borders, so to speak, blending technology with real-world emotion.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I suppose just how grateful I am for the little victories in this journey. Even in frustration, there’s growth. Learning a language is a never-ending dance, and I'm thankful for every step.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, as long as it captures the passion and rhythm of who I am!

A: Overall, it's the lack of depth in cultural context. I wish it would offer more scenarios that reflect real-life conversations in Vienna—a bit less 'tourist phrases' and more local, everyday dialogue.

A: There was this one time, I was about to meet a friend's family for the first time, and I needed some phrases to sound more natural in a family setting. A: I hope it, like, gives me a fresh challenge, something that makes me feel I've stepped forward—whether it's a new phrase, a tricky sentence, or just the satisfaction of advancing in my skills.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: I know it's worked when I can catch a phrase in conversation that I practiced or when I can string together sentences more confidently without second-guessing every word.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would, um, love it if Duolingo incorporated more immersive exercises. Maybe scenarios that reflect more complex social interactions or cultural contexts specific to the regions where the language is spoken.

A: I wish there were more integrated platforms that combine the best of apps like Duolingo, with real-world cultural experiences, perhaps using augmented reality to simulate interactions.

A: Hmm, that's interesting! I guess so, as long as it respects my journey and privacy.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I come home feeling tired but happy, yeah, that’s a good day. Like, when everything flows, from the waves to the conversations. You just know it when you feel that inner peace.

A: I’m more of a gut-feeling kind of guy. I mean, I like to think it through a bit, but usually, if something feels right, I just go for it. Like, when I moved to Australia, it just felt like the right call.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk is part of life, especially in skiing. I try to assess it as best I can, knowing when to push it and when to, you know, step back. A bit like skiing down an unknown slope, you have to trust your training but also respect the elements.

Q: Typical weekday?

Q: Describe those relationships.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time when I completely missed a class because the slopes were just too good to leave. That, uh, kind of put me behind and it was hard to catch up. It’s tough when life pulls you in different directions.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend back in France mentioned it to me. He was using it for English and said it was like having a mini teacher in your pocket.

A: I was curious about having something flexible, that I could do in short bursts between ski sessions. And, um, the idea of it being kinda game-like sounded fun. Learning shouldn’t always be serious, right?

A: Worst case? I guess, lacking real progress and confidence due to misunderstanding fundamentals. It would be, like, trying to ski with only one ski—just wouldn’t work well in the long run.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it keeps me on track and teaches me something new. Even if it's just a small detail, it’s encouraging to feel like I've advanced a bit in my language skills.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: I know it works when I recognize new words in a conversation or when something I struggled with suddenly makes sense in real-life usage. That’s, like, a little victory dance moment.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d say improving its explanations when you get things wrong. Like, a little more feedback or maybe a short grammar tip could help bridge the understanding gap.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there were more immersive, like, interactive experiences that blend with daily life. Learning should be more contextual, so you can instantly apply it to real-world scenarios.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we've covered a lot. Just, um, the importance of balance, I guess—between work, learning, and enjoying the journey. It’s all connected.

A: Sure, why not? As long as my digital twin embraces the slopes as much as I do!

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hej! Cześć! Uh, hello there! I'm Marta, nice to meet you.

Q: Short version of your life story?

I’ve been learning Swedish to better communicate with patients—it's super important for my work!

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a town just outside Kraków. It's a lovely place, with lots of greenery and very friendly people.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Growing up there was quite nice, really. It's small, so everyone knows each other. I spent a lot of time outdoors with friends. We’d play until the sun went down. I was very close to my family, and we had this strong community feel. It feels very grounding, you know?

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Moving to Sweden was definitely a big turning point. It was, like, a huge change, moving from everything familiar. But, um, it was an opportunity I couldn't pass up. The healthcare system here is fantastic, and it’s a chance to grow professionally.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, leaving Poland meant leaving behind my family, friends all my life... And I had to adapt to a new culture and language. It changed my perspective, and I had to become more independent, you know? Relying on myself in a new country was both scary and empowering.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Oh, it wasn't easy! I relied a lot on technology and language apps to get by. I also, um, made an effort to connect with other Polish expatriates and local Swedes. Building a network here helped tremendously. Plus, lots of coffee and determination!

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, my focus is on mastering Swedish, particularly for healthcare. I want to ensure that I can communicate effectively and empathetically with my patients. Language is key, you know? Being able to understand and be understood—it’s crucial in my line of work.

Q: Why is that important?
A: In healthcare, communication is everything. I mean, you have to connect with patients to provide them with the best care. If I miss something because of a language barrier, it could affect their health and trust in me.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? Hmm, it's one where I feel I've made a difference, even a small one, in someone's life. If a mother leaves feeling confident and safe after talking to me, that's a success. And if I can sneak in some effective Swedish learning time, that’s a bonus!

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: It's when I leave the hospital with a smile, knowing I helped someone. And when I have those little victories in learning, like finally remembering a tricky word or phrase in Swedish—I think, yes, I’m getting there.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: Oof, big decisions… I make lists, pros and cons, you know the drill. I also talk to my husband and closest friends. They help me see things from different angles. I tend to sleep on it, too—things are clearer in the morning!

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely a planner. I like to know what's happening, you know? Especially with work and studying Swedish. But I try to leave room for spontaneity because life doesn’t always go as planned!

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, like when we decided to move to Sweden. I planned everything down to the last detail—from the paperwork to finding a place to live. But when our flight got canceled last minute, I had to adapt quickly. It taught me to handle things as they come, you know?

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I try to assess it carefully, weighing the potential benefits and drawbacks. I’m not, um, super impulsive. But I also remind myself that some risks are worth taking, like moving here. It’s about finding that balance between caution and adventure.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Let's see... I usually start early with a cup of Polish tea, then head to the hospital. My day is filled with patient consultations, delivering babies, which is amazing! Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the hospital shifts. It’s both physically and emotionally demanding, especially the night shifts. Also, the mental energy of switching languages is a lot—like, talking in Swedish when your native tongue just flows easier.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time for language practice and maybe a hobby or two. Sometimes I feel I'm doing just enough to keep up, instead of really pushing forward. Oh, and visiting family back in Poland more frequently!

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Balancing my work with learning Swedish, definitely. There’s only so much time in a day, and sometimes I feel torn between my professional responsibilities and my study goals.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I try to integrate learning into my day, like listening to Swedish podcasts during my commute. Plus, I set very specific, small goals, like learning five new words a day, which feels more manageable.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My husband and our close group of friends here in Sweden. And, of course, my family back in Poland. Even if we’re apart, we talk often; our conversations keep me grounded.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: These are relationships where we support each other unconditionally, you know? They’re the people I can be myself with, who understand my journey and challenges, and who share my joys and frustrations.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly at the hospital, honestly. It’s like my second home. And at home with my family, those are my two main spaces.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: At the hospital, I feel purposeful, like part of a team making a difference. At home, I feel relaxed and, um, loved. It’s my safe space where I can recharge and be myself.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The work we do at the hospital, it’s challenging but so rewarding. And my family, their support and love—it’s everything. They keep me going.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: My husband, definitely. He’s my rock. Also, my close friends here and back in Poland. They give me perspective and sometimes, you know, just listening helps.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: When one of my patients had complications during delivery. It was, um, very intense and stretched my Swedish skills under pressure. It was scary, but being able to communicate effectively was crucial.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a wake-up call, realizing how important language skills are in those critical moments. It made me more determined to improve, but also more cautious about relying solely on what I think I know.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I talked it through with colleagues and mentors. They were supportive and shared similar experiences. I also revisited specific medical Swedish terms and scenarios to make sure I’m better prepared next time.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a step back and, um, breathing helps. Sometimes just a walk in nature or calling my family in Poland grounds me. Also, silly as it sounds, cooking—just focusing on something unrelated for a while.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I’d like to be fully fluent in Swedish, working as a midwife with even more confidence. I’d love a balance, maybe a little garden and more regular trips back to Poland. Definitely more stability, both professionally and personally.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I hope to feel more integrated here in Sweden, like, a part of the community. More time for personal growth too, outside of work and language learning.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: I started with books and online resources, like YouTube videos and podcasts. But, um, it was hard to stay consistent. I’d often get frustrated without regular practice partners. Sometimes, I’d try speaking with Swedish colleagues, but it felt intimidating with my limited vocabulary.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of feedback, really. It’s hard to know if you’re improving and getting the nuances right without interactive practice. Also, finding time to sit with a book was tough—life is so busy, you know?

Q: Time it really failed?
A: Oh, there was this one time when I tried to order food in Swedish and the waiter just switched to English. I felt embarrassed and realized I needed more structured learning and confidence building.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend mentioned it to me, actually. They were using it to learn French and recommended it as an easy-to-use app with a fun approach.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I was looking for something that fit into my schedule. When I saw how Duolingo could be done in small doses, like just ten minutes here and there, I thought, why not? Plus, it was free, and that's always a bonus!

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure! So, I usually open the app during a coffee break. The home screen is colorful, with lesson circles, and I like that it shows progress bars. I recently did a module on 'Medical Swedish'—it’s a mix of vocabulary and fill-in-the-blank sentences. There are these cute little picture exercises too, like matching words to images of medical instruments, which is so helpful for me. I appreciate the 'speaking exercises' where I repeat phrases—it helps with pronunciation, which is tricky in Swedish.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The most helpful part is the repetition; it really drills those medical terms into my head. And the little, like, congratulatory sound when you complete a lesson—it feels good! Keeps me coming back.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes Duolingo feels like it's too generic, you know? Like it doesn't cover the specific healthcare phrases I need. And occasionally, the translations seem a bit off or too literal, which can be confusing.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I’d say it's the lack of real-life context. I mean, they do a great job with basics, but I wish there was more focus on real conversations, especially in healthcare settings. Like, how do I tell a patient to breathe calmly during labor in Swedish?

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Ah, there was this lesson about food, and I was thinking, 'I really need more medical terms!' I spent time learning words for vegetables when I was more anxious about phrases for patient care. It made me wish for a more specialized module.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, definitely. I sometimes supplement Duolingo with healthcare-focused podcasts and YouTube channels. Also, chatting with colleagues helps—real conversation is indispensable.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide context and nuance, which Duolingo sometimes lacks. Listening to professionals use the language in real scenarios fills in the gaps where the app falls short.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Hmm, worst-case? If I had a communication mishap with a patient because I misunderstood something crucial. But thankfully, with Duolingo and other resources, I'm getting more confident!

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it challenges me just enough to learn something new but not overwhelm. And that it focuses on the vocabulary I need most at the moment, especially medical terms.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can recall phrases during patient consultations without hesitating. If I can carry on a conversation with a patient smoothly, I know all the practice is paying off.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d introduce more interactive dialogues, maybe even simulating real patient conversations, to practice in a context closer to what I experience at work.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: More resources tailored to specific professions, like healthcare. It’s essential for us to have language tools that serve the precise needs and dialogues we encounter daily.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Um, no, I think we covered pretty much everything! Just grateful to tools like Duolingo for making language learning more accessible and, uh, less daunting.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, that sounds interesting! I hope it captures my Polish determination and the compassion I bring to my work.

Q: Short version of your life story?

Started out in my late twenties in the Barossa Valley, made a name for myself there before deciding to take the plunge and head over to France. Been here for a good number of years now, running a small winery and trying to get my French up to scratch as it’s, well, crucial for business.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Lovely spot with great wines and even better people.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was just fantastic. Tons of open space, vineyards around every corner, and a close-knit community. We had heaps of family gatherings and a laid-back lifestyle. I reckon it’s a great place to raise a family, really taught me to appreciate the beauty of nature and good wine, of course.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Deciding to move to France, without a doubt. It was a massive leap with plenty of unknowns. But the desire to challenge myself and learn from the best in the world of wine was too strong to pass up.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it meant leaving everything familiar behind and starting fresh in a new country. It's not just the technical side of winemaking; it's the culture, the language, you know, embracing a whole new way of life. It really pushed me out of my comfort zone.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I dove in headfirst, really. Tried to learn as much as I could, both about French wines and the language. It was a bit rough at first, with plenty of missteps, but I threw myself into the community and slowly started picking things up.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's about refining my craft and keeping the winery afloat in, you know, a competitive market. But also making sure I’m communicating effectively with my team and our customers, which is why I’m focusing on improving my French.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Well, wine isn’t just about the drink itself; it’s about the story, the heritage. If I can’t share that with people in their native tongue, I feel like something’s lost. Plus, it’s hard to do business if you can’t fully understand or express yourself.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day is when the sun’s shining over the vineyard, I’ve nailed a particularly tricky blend, and I’ve had a positive conversation with a customer or colleague in French where, um, I actually understand it all. Might seem simple, but it’s the small wins that make it.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I finish the day with a sense of accomplishment, whether it’s in the cellar or out in the field, and I can sit back, enjoy a glass of our wine, and think, ‘Yep, nailed it today,’ then that’s a good day.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I’m more of a gut-feel kind of bloke, but I do like to weigh up the pros and cons. I’ll have a yarn with people I trust, get their perspective, and then I try to balance my instincts with their advice. It’s important to have both the heart and mind in the right place.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I’d say I’m somewhere in between. While the wine industry demands a fair bit of planning, you’ve also got to be adaptable because Mother Nature doesn’t adhere to schedules.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, last season there was a sudden cold snap during what should’ve been a warm period. I had plans laid out for the harvest, but we had to push everything back, adapt quickly. We ended up doing things a bit differently, but it worked out well in the end. You’ve got to roll with the punches sometimes.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: In winemaking, you deal with risk all the time—weather, market trends, and so on. I try to mitigate what I can, like diversifying our product range, but I’ve learned to accept that some things are out of my control. I focus on what I can influence.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Weekdays are a mix of vineyard work, cellar management, and business operations. I’m usually up early, checking on the vines, then sorting production schedules. Afternoons might be spent on tastings or meetings with distributors. And somewhere in between, I try to squeeze in some French lessons on Duolingo or chatting with locals to practice.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the physical work in the vineyards and keeping up with the admin side of things. And of course, learning the language—it really drains you when you’re not naturally inclined toward it, like me. But it’s all part of the job.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?

Q: Why is that important?

Q: What is a good day for you?

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The textbooks, for sure. They felt lifeless and failed to keep up with my learning pace. And the tutoring, while beneficial, was costly. I felt bogged down by the structure and the rigid nature didn't quite gel with my creative spirit, you know?

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time when I had prepared a small talk in German for an event, all from textbook phrases. Once I delivered it, people looked at me like I was from another century! It was embarrassing and made me realize the gap between textbook language and real-life conversation.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A fellow singer mentioned it during a rehearsal break. They were using it to learn French and spoke highly about how interactive and musical it felt. It intrigued me—a language app with a bit of flair!

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: Honestly, it was the idea of a more flexible, gamified way of learning that caught my attention. Plus, the thought of earning 'lingots' and tracking progress seemed fun, almost like playing a game. I thought, why not bring some joy to my language journey?

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Okay, so yesterday, I opened the app and started with my daily lesson. The home screen had these cute icons like a tree growing with each lesson completed. I jumped into a session on German vocabulary. The app gave me sentences to translate, and I typed my answers. There's this little green owl—Duo—that cheers me on! It even had audio sections, so I listened and repeated the phrases aloud. And when I got something right, there was this delightful chime, like a mini-celebration. It ended with a review of what I learned, which is always useful for solidifying new words.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The interactive nature and the repetition have been great. Also, the audio is really helpful because I can hear the pronunciation and mimic it, which kind of aligns with how I learn music—by listening and repeating.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, the sentences feel a bit artificial, or very out of context. Like, when am I ever going to say 'the penguin writes a letter'? And sometimes, the app insists on very specific translations, even when alternatives are acceptable in conversation.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The rigidity in accepting answers can be a bit much. If I type something that should be right, but it doesn't exactly match the app's preferred translation, it counts as wrong. It can be discouraging, especially when the essence is correct.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, I remember this one lesson where I was translating a sentence about animals. I used a different word order that was technically correct. The app marked me wrong, and it was frustrating because it felt less about learning and more about rigidly matching a single answer. It made me question if I was understanding German or just Duolingo's version of it.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, sometimes I'll cross-reference with other language resources or online forums if something doesn't make sense. I'll jot down the correct answers after getting a question wrong, and practice constructing my own sentences outside the app to ensure I'm learning contextually.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide context and validation. Language is alive, flexible, and sometimes the app feels like it's in a bubble. The workarounds remind me that language isn't just about strict rules but communicating ideas and emotions effectively.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Probably if the app became even more rigid, pushing learners into rote memorization without context. I fear it could deter passionate learners like me, who need that blend of structure and creativity to thrive.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it ignites curiosity and reinforces my knowledge with engaging tasks that feel like a puzzle I want to solve. I want it to feel as exciting and rewarding as hitting a high note in a performance!

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can recall words and phrases effortlessly in conversation—or if I manage to impress my German friends with a perfectly pronounced sentence. It's in those little victories where I see progress.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would love more contextual lessons, like scenarios I would actually encounter living in Germany. Oh, and maybe more music-related vocabulary—imagine singing your exercises!

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd love to see a blend of technology with real-life conversation opportunities, like virtual exchanges. Language is so much more than words on a screen; it's about people and connections.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we've covered a lot! But perhaps, just the idea that language, much like music, is a journey. It's a lifelong passion, and it's beautiful even when it's challenging.

A: Ah, a digital twin of me? As long as you capture my passion and dramatic flair, I suppose it's fine!

Q: Intro greeting

Q: Short version of your life story?

Q: What was it like growing up there?

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Definitely moving to Japan. It's a whole different world from Kenya. I had to adapt to not just the culture but learning a new language too. It really pushed me out of my comfort zone but in a good way. It's broadened my perspective and built my resilience.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it wasn't just about running anymore. It was about communicating, understanding people, and integrating into a new way of life. It made me realize how language is such a powerful tool, you know? For connecting, for learning, and for racing, which I didn't fully appreciate before.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I just, like, took it one day at a time. I started with the basics, of course, like greetings, numbers, and 'where's the bathroom?' phrases. Q: What do you care most about right now?
