Q: Why is that important?
A: Well, if I can communicate effectively, I can train better, understand race strategies more deeply, and, um, just connect better with people around me. It's like having two feet solidly on the ground as opposed to hopping on one, you know?

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day starts with a solid morning run. Then, getting through my language practice without forgetting everything I learned the day before. If I can squeeze in some chill time and maybe a good meal with friends, that's perfect.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When the training feels strong and I've had a breakthrough in Japanese, like understanding a phrase or even holding a longer conversation. That sense of accomplishment, you know? That's everything.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I usually weigh the pros and cons, maybe chat with a trusted friend to get another perspective. But, um, ultimately, I trust my gut. It's led me to some pretty amazing experiences.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely a planner. My training schedule is planned to the minute, and I try to apply that to other areas of my life too. It just keeps me focused and less stressed.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, last month, I planned a weekend trip to Kyoto—everything from the train schedule to places to eat. I didn't want to waste time figuring it out on the spot, just wanted to enjoy the sights and sounds.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I guess I weigh the potential outcomes, think through what's manageable. Running itself is taking risks—pushing your limits, but with calculated decisions to avoid injury. I approach life sorta the same way.

Q: Typical weekday?

Afternoons are for more training—speed work or endurance runs. I try to end the day with some downtime, maybe watch a Japanese show with subtitles to reinforce what I'm learning.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: I'd say the language learning, honestly. I mean, running is physically demanding, but language learning requires a lot of mental stamina, especially when you're trying to master a language as different from English as Japanese is.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: Probably for more cultural experiences here in Japan. There's so much to explore and learn outside of my immediate focus areas, and I sometimes feel like I'm missing out on embracing the full Japanese experience.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Definitely adapting to living in Japan during the pandemic. It was tough balancing restrictions, training, and learning Japanese without the same social interactions I might have otherwise had to practice.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Comfortable, honestly. They're like arenas of growth for me. I feel focused and motivated in these places to be my best version. It's where I can channel my energy into improving.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The routine, I guess. It's like a rhythm I understand well, whether it's the pace of my run or the progress in my language skills. It's familiar and empowering.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Mostly to my coach here in Japan or my family back home. They provide different perspectives—my coach knows what it's like to, you know, be in a foreign place competing, and my family offers that grounding emotional support.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?

A: It was kind of frustrating. I was worried about my performance, and without running, I felt my stress levels rising. It also dampened my motivation for language practice since I didn't have that usual routine.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Focused on rehab and maintaining my mental health. I picked up more Japanese reading, which was actually helpful. And I leaned on my family and friends for support—they reminded me that setbacks happen and the comeback is what's important.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Getting outside for a walk or a slow jog. It clears my mind. Meditation's been a new find too, just a few minutes of quiet can reset my mood. And, listening to some inspiring podcasts or music also does wonders.

A: I'd love to see myself fluent in Japanese, not just for races but in daily life. Running-wise, I hope to have achieved some personal bests in major marathons. I'd like to be a voice for empowering other athletes, maybe by sharing my experiences and insights.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: Hmm, maybe a better work-life integration with time for family and travel. I'd also like to have more cultural experiences, not just through running, but by immersing myself more deeply into Japanese culture.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Oh, it was piecemeal, mostly phrasebooks and some online classes. I'd write words on flashcards and repeat them during my runs, but it lacked the structure I needed. It was frustrating not being able to track my progress properly.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The inconsistency, really. Like, I'd know a word one day and forget it the next. And it was hard to, um, integrate what I learned into complex sentences or conversations. It felt like I was only operating at a surface level.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: When I tried to order food at a restaurant and completely blanked. I had the sentences in my head, but panic took over. Made me realize learning words wasn't enough if I couldn't apply them in real situations.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I think a friend mentioned it, actually. Said it was good for keeping language skills fresh and, uh, had this game-like approach which sounded interesting.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of daily reminders and streaks caught my attention. I mean, it's like training—consistency is key, right? Plus, it was free to start, so I thought, why not give it a shot?

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Alright, so the other day, I booted it up in the morning after my run. I went through a lesson on food vocabulary—lots of tapping and matching exercises. Then, there was a speaking exercise where I had to repeat phrases. I kinda like how it gives immediate feedback, you know, whether I got it right or wrong. I ended with a few practice questions to test what I recalled. It felt, um, like a solid session.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitely the immediate feedback. It's helpful to know right away if I've said or chosen something wrong. Also, the streak feature keeps me accountable, just like a running log. Feels like I'm progressing.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes it can feel repetitive, like I'm drilling the same words over and over. And, uh, the voice recognition isn't always accurate—I might say something correctly but it marks it wrong. That's a bit frustrating, especially when you're sure you got it right.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I'd say it's the lack of real-life conversation scenarios. Like, I'm learning phrases, but it doesn't always translate to the fast-paced exchanges I need during races or everyday interactions. I need more spontaneous, situational practice.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, at a sports store I wanted to ask about a specific pair of shoes. I had the vocabulary, but when the conversation shifted, I struggled to keep up. Duolingo hadn't prepared me for that kind of exchange, and it was a bit embarrassing fumbling through it.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, sometimes I use language exchange meetups or apps to practice speaking with actual people. It pushes me out of my comfort zone, which is better for real-life prep. I try to watch Japanese shows too; it helps with hearing the language in context.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They, uh, provide that authentic speaking practice and the unpredictability of real conversations. Duolingo's great for vocab but doesn't simulate a dynamic dialogue. Plus, it helps with my listening skills, which is a biggie when you're out in the world.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Honestly, it's getting to a race or important event and not being able to understand critical instructions or make myself understood. That'd be tough, especially if something urgent comes up and I can't communicate effectively.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it solidifies my vocab and, uh, gives me those incremental improvements I need. I also hope for some challenge, like new types of exercises that engage different skills or help me think on my feet.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can recall phrases and words during conversations or when I'm out and about. If I make it through a lesson without feeling baffled by the end, that's a good sign. Plus, if I notice improvement in my listening skills, that's key.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Uh, I'd add more conversation simulation scenarios, maybe where you respond to dynamic prompts or have to, like, navigate a virtual day in Japan. That'd really help in making the learning process more immersive.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Hmm, probably more integration of language learning into daily activities, like through augmented reality. Something where I could point my phone at things and learn words on the go, reinforcing everyday language interaction.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we covered a lot, but just to emphasize, learning a language is a journey—like a marathon, really. It's not always easy, but it's rewarding in so many ways.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Uh, sure, that sounds interesting. If it helps improve language learning tools, I'm all for it!

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there! Lovely to be chatting with you today.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, let's see, um, I grew up in Johannesburg, always been a bit wild at heart. Ever since I was a child, I had a fascination with animals, you know, the Big Five and all that. So naturally, I became a game ranger. It's quite a life, really - living in the bush, surrounded by the wildlife. Recently, I started learning Swahili because I'd love to work more in East African reserves. It’s all about feeling more connected to the land and the people, hey?

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Johannesburg, South Africa. It's a big city but with easy access to gorgeous natural parks. Quite a unique place 'cause you get the urban and the wild.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was a real mix of hustle and bustle with a touch of wilderness. You'd have the city life with all its energy, but weekends were for getting lost in nature. My family would often visit Kruger Park. That's when I fell in love with the bush, you know, the thrill of spotting a kudu behind a tree.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: The big moment for me was when I decided to leave the corporate world behind and become a game ranger. I was working in an office, and honestly, I couldn't stop daydreaming about the African savanna. So one day, I just thought, 'Zelda, it's now or never!' I quit my job, trained as a ranger, and I've never looked back.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, it was the first time I chose passion over practicality. Leaving the predictable life of a steady job for the uncertainty of the bush was scary, but it was where my heart truly lay. I mean, what's the point of living if you’re not pursuing what makes your soul sing, right?

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I just took it day by day. There were challenges, of course, like adjusting to life away from the city comforts. But I surrounded myself with people who had the same love for nature. They were my mentors, teaching me everything from tracking animals to living sustainably. It was like being in a Nat Geo documentary!

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's about bridging the gap between wildlife conservation and local communities. Language plays a huge role, you know, being able to communicate with the local communities in Swahili can really make a difference. It’s about mutual respect and learning from one another, ensuring that both the animals and the people thrive.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because conservation isn't just about protecting animals; it's about understanding the whole ecosystem, including the people who live there. If they’re involved and benefit directly, they’re more likely to help preserve the land. Plus, it’s a way to honour the wisdom and traditions that have been part of African culture for centuries.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? Oh, that's waking up at dawn, hearing the birds chirping, and knowing I'm off to track some lions. If I can end the day with a chat around the campfire with fellow rangers, exchanging stories in Swahili, that’s perfect. It’s like living inside those nature documentaries I used to watch as a kid.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I’ve seen something new or rare, like a leopard making a kill or a family of elephants bathing. It’s those moments of pure, raw nature that make me grateful to be out there. Oh, and if I’ve managed to use a bit more Swahili in my conversations, that’s a bonus.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to go with my gut. It's like when you're tracking an animal and you have to trust your instincts. Of course, I'll weigh the pros and cons, maybe chat with some close friends, but ultimately, if it feels right in my bones, I'll go for it. Life in the bush has taught me to be adaptable and trust myself.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely more of a go-with-the-flow kind of person. The bush doesn’t exactly care for schedules, you know? You've got to be ready for anything, like a sudden storm or an unexpected elephant herd crossing.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Ah, just last week, we had a group of guests out on safari, and our vehicle got stuck in the mud. Instead of panicking, we all just embraced it, got out and pushed, and turned it into a bit of an adventure. You’ve got to take what nature throws at you and make the best of it.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I’d say I handle risk with a mixture of caution and excitement. In the bush, everything is risky, but that's what makes it thrilling. I always assess a situation, like checking for animals' behavior when approaching, but once I've done my checks, I'm all in. It’s part of the job, and I love it.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: My weekdays start before dawn. First light is the best time to catch the animals when they’re most active. We’ll head out on a game drive with the guests, tracking lions or elephants. During the day, there’s always something to do, like vehicle maintenance or planning conservation projects. In the evenings, it’s all about winding down with some Duolingo if I have the energy, trying to squeeze in a few Swahili lessons before the generator cuts out.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the early mornings and dealing with guests who might not be used to the bush lifestyle. It’s rewarding, showing them the beauty of the wild, but it can be draining to be 'on' all the time, especially when you just want a quiet moment with the nature around you.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time to dedicate to learning Swahili fluently. It's one thing to know the basics, but I’d love to be able to converse deeply with the local guides and hear their stories. It’s like when you miss an epic sighting because you were looking the other way; there’s a whole world in those conversations.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: COVID impacted us a lot, fewer tourists meant we had to tighten our belts. But it also meant more time to focus on conservation efforts and less disturbance for the animals. It was a bit of a double-edged sword, really, trying to find balance between financial constraints and conservation wins.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: We got creative, started offering virtual safari experiences which were a hit. Allowed us to share the bush with people stuck at home. And, on a personal level, I used the quiet periods to work on my Swahili and learn more about the ecology of the area. It’s about turning challenges into opportunities, you know?

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I’d say my fellow rangers and some of the local guides. We're like a family out here, supporting each other through thick and thin. And then there’s my family back home in Joburg, always rooting for me even if they don’t always understand the pull of the wild.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: With the rangers and guides, it's like being part of a pride of lions. We look out for one another, share the same passion for the land, and have a common mission. With my family, it’s more about love and support from afar, keeping me grounded and reminding me of home.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly out in the bush, on safari drives, or at the lodge. When I'm not out with the guests, I'm probably checking in on the animals, making sure everything's running smoothly at the camp.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: It’s a mix of awe and peace. There's something about the vastness of the savanna that makes you feel both small and significant at the same time. I feel alive, connected to the earth and the cycles of nature. It's a real privilege to call this place home, even with all its unpredictability.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I think it's the raw beauty of it all, you know? The colors of a sunset over the plains, the sound of lions calling at night, the freedom of just being out in the wild. It’s like being part of something much bigger than yourself.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: My fellow rangers for sure. We’ve got each other’s backs no matter what. And if it's something that requires more wisdom, I’ll lean on the local guides. They’ve got years of experience and a knack for finding solutions. It’s all about community support here.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: We had a major drought that really affected the wildlife. You could see the stress it put on the animals, and that’s hard to witness. It was difficult for us too because it meant re-evaluating how we managed the resources, ensuring both the guests and the environment were looked after.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a real emotional challenge, seeing the land struggling. You get attached to the animals, almost like they're extensions of your family. It made me rethink our impact as humans and the importance of sustainable practices, especially in the tourism industry.

Q: How did you cope?

A: Bonjour! Je suis Josephine. It's a pleasure to be here today.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Ah, where to begin? I was born in Kinshasa, Congo, but my journey brought me to Paris where I embraced the world of fashion. I've always been fascinated by design, colors, and fabrics, you know? In Congo, we have this rich fashion culture, and bringing that spirit here to Paris, it was like merging two worlds. Now, I'm working on perfecting my French so I can truly blend into the haute couture scene here.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Kinshasa, the bustling capital of Congo. It's vibrant, full of life, and has this unique rhythm to it.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Growing up in Kinshasa was an adventure every day! The community spirit, markets filled with vivid fabrics, sounds of Soukous music... it's a place that inspires creativity. But, you know, there were challenges too, like every place, but we found beauty in resilience.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Hmm, I would say moving to Paris. It was a dream of mine since I was a child, to walk the streets where fashion is like a second language. When I got the opportunity to study fashion design here, it transformed everything. It was scary, leaving home, but also exhilarating.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Paris, it's the heart of fashion, right? Being here opened doors to experiences and connections I never imagined. It pushed me to be more than a designer; to be an artist in a global fashion landscape.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: At first, it was overwhelming. I had to adapt quickly, learn the language better, and adjust to the fast-paced Parisian life. I relied a lot on my creativity, using it to express myself even when words failed me. Connecting with local designers and creatives helped, too.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, mastering French is vital for my career. I want to speak fluently so I can communicate my visions clearly in the fashion world, you know? Language is a bridge to deeper cultural understanding, and being in Paris, that's essential.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Well, in the haute couture industry, every detail matters. Speaking French well allows me to collaborate better, understand subtle cultural nuances, and ultimately, it's about respect for this place that inspires my work.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Oh, a good day... it starts with a fresh croissant and a strong café crème at my favorite boulangerie. Then, maybe sketching some designs, visiting fabric shops, and perhaps a call with my family back home. If I end the day with a little time on Duolingo or conversing in French with friends, c'est parfait!

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: It's when I feel creatively fulfilled and connected to both my work and the people around me. It's like the synergy of creativity and culture aligns perfectly.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I, uh, tend to go with my instincts a lot. I mean, of course, I weigh the pros and cons, but ultimately, I trust my gut and how something aligns with my passions. I also talk it over with close friends who understand my vision.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'm more of a go-with-the-flow kind of person. In fashion, things change rapidly, and being too rigid can stifle creativity.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Well, there was this one time I had a design review, and I had to scrap everything last minute because it just didn't feel right. Instead of panicking, I trusted my intuition and created a new piece overnight. It ended up being one of my best works.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risks are part of the journey. I try to see them as opportunities rather than obstacles. Of course, I get nervous, who doesn't? But if it's aligned with my goals, I take a deep breath and leap.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical weekday starts quite early. I like to start with a little morning stretch and breakfast, something light usually. Then, I dive into design work or meetings if I'm collaborating on a project. In the afternoon, I might visit a market for inspiration or materials. Evenings are for winding down, and I usually spend some time on Duolingo or watching French films to improve my language skills.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Designing can be quite consuming, especially when trying to bring a vision to life. Also, the networking part, which is crucial in fashion, takes a lot because you're constantly putting yourself out there.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: Honestly, I wish I had more time to explore Paris. I've been here for a while, but there's always something new to discover. Also, more time for learning French in a deeper, more immersive way would be amazing.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: I think the biggest constraint was balancing my career advancements with personal growth. There were so many opportunities, but not enough time to seize them all while also nurturing my language skills.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I tried to prioritize, selecting what aligned most closely with my goals. Delegating tasks when possible and staying organized helped too. And, I made sure to keep some time sacred just for myself.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I'm really close with my family back home in Congo. Here in Paris, I've formed strong friendships with other expatriates and creatives who share similar experiences. We support each other a lot.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They're like a second family. We laugh, share our challenges, and celebrate each other's successes. It's, um, a network of love and encouragement.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: I spend a lot of time in my small atelier, working on designs, or out in the city hunting for inspiration.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: In my atelier, I feel grounded and free to create. Out in the city, I feel invigorated and inspired. Paris has a pulse that just, uh, keeps you going.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the blend of history, style, and the constant hum of creativity everywhere. It challenges me to grow and express myself.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: First, I usually talk to my mother. Her wisdom is like a soothing balm. Then, I might chat with a close friend here in Paris who gets the fashion world and the pressures it brings.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Well, there was a time when I was preparing for a major fashion showcase, and everything just seemed to go wrong. From supply issues to, uh, design challenges, it was a storm.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was stressful, to say the least. I felt like I was constantly running against the clock. It tested my patience and resilience, but it also pushed me to be innovative in problem-solving.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I tried to take it one step at a time. Taking breaks to clear my head was crucial. I also leaned on my support network; friends brought me meals, and my mentor offered invaluable advice. It was about finding balance amid chaos.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Fashion aside, I love listening to music, especially old Soukous records from home. It reminds me of my roots and brings a sense of calm. Also, a good chat with a friend can work wonders.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I envision myself having a well-established fashion brand that celebrates African and European styles. I want to be fluent in French, contributing not just to fashion discussions but also cultural dialogues in Paris.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I, uh, hope for more balance between work and life. More time for personal growth and exploration, and of course, deeper cultural exchanges through language.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I mostly relied on language books and some online courses. They were okay, but, you know, it was hard to stay motivated without interactive elements. Plus, the materials often felt outdated and didn't help much with conversational French.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of immediate feedback, I think. With books, you can't ask questions or verify pronunciation. It felt like learning in isolation without any real engagement.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a networking event where I realized I wasn't as prepared as I'd thought. I struggled with the conversation, and it was clear the book approach wasn't enough to handle real-life dialogues.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend of mine in the fashion industry mentioned Duolingo while we were chatting about ways to improve our language skills. They swore by it for quick and effective learning.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I was really intrigued by how they described the gamified approach. It seemed fun and interactive, which was exactly what I needed to stay motivated. Plus, the idea of practicing a little every day seemed less daunting.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure, so yesterday, I opened Duolingo on my phone during lunch. I picked the 'Food' category because, you know, one can never know too much about food vocab in France! I worked through a few exercises that involved matching words with images, which helped me remember better. There were also speaking exercises where I had to repeat phrases, and it was nice getting instant feedback. I completed a few levels and earned some XP, which felt rewarding. I like that it tracks my daily streak; it's motivating.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: I love the speaking exercises. They help improve my pronunciation, which is crucial. And the instant feedback on correctness, I mean, it's like having a tutor right there with me.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, it feels a bit repetitive, like you're just repeating phrases without deeper context. I'd love more real-world applications or creative exercises integrated into the lessons.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: I guess sometimes it feels a bit too structured, and there's not much room for creative expression. I wish there were more conversational practice with longer dialogues or stories to weave language learning and creativity together.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this instance when I kept getting a phrase wrong due to a tiny error, and it didn't offer a detailed explanation on how to improve. It was a bit disheartening, especially when you're trying to be precise, but these are just the limitations of an app, I suppose.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, I do! I often combine Duolingo with watching French films or listening to French podcasts. It helps to hear the language in action, and it fills the gaps that Duolingo can't quite cover on its own.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide cultural context and real-life usage of the language. It's more dynamic and, um, brings the language to life, allowing me to practice comprehension and spontaneous speaking.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case would be staying stagnant with my language skills, unable to fully express myself in industry conversations. That would be detrimental to my growth and integration in the fashion community here.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it keeps me on my toes, offers something new to learn, and helps me improve steadily. Most importantly, I want it to be a step closer to fluency and confidence in French.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I'm able to understand and respond during casual conversations in French without, like, hesitating much, that's when I know it's making a difference.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would add more creative elements, maybe like role-playing scenarios or storytelling exercises, to weave creativity into the learning process, you know?

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish there were more integrated platforms that could combine structured learning with immersive cultural experiences to enrich language acquisition.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we covered a lot. Just, um, maybe emphasizing how language learning is not just about words, it's about connecting with people and cultures.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Uh, as long as it's respectful and keeps my creative spirit in mind, I suppose that's alright!

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there! I'm Idris, nice to chat with you.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Ah, where do I start? So, I grew up in Ghana, right? Always been passionate about tech. I ended up studying computer science, and after a couple of years in the industry there, I moved to the Netherlands to dive deeper into the startup scene. The tech ecosystem here is super vibrant, and I saw a lotta opportunities, you know? Now, I run my own startup focused on AI solutions, and learning Dutch is part of my plan to integrate better into the business scene here.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Accra, the capital of Ghana. It's a bustling city with a mix of everything – from traditional markets to growing tech hubs.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was lively, you know? The sense of community is strong, and people are always open to help each other out. The 'go-getter' attitude is everywhere, which kinda shaped my entrepreneurial spirit. We had this vibrant street life, full of energy, and that’s what I miss the most now that I’m in Europe.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: A major turning point was definitely moving to the Netherlands. It was a big leap, leaving my comfort zone and everything I knew behind. But I knew I had to make that move if I wanted to grow my career in tech. It was challenging at first, adjusting to a whole new culture and navigating the startup scene here.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, it forced me to adapt quickly, to become more resilient and resourceful. The opportunity to be part of such a dynamic environment opened doors for me. It changed my perspective on business and technology, shaped how I approach problems, and really cemented my passion for innovation.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I mean, it was all about networking and learning. I attended as many tech meetups as I could, sought out mentors, tried to understand the local market better. I had to learn Dutch too, which is why I started using Duolingo, to better communicate in business settings. It was all about immersion and not being afraid to make mistakes.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's about building my startup and making a real impact with our AI solutions. I’m also focused on mastering Dutch. Being able to conduct business fluently in Dutch could really open up new opportunities for my company here.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Business is all about connections, right? And language is a big part of that. Being able to speak Dutch fluently, especially in a business context, shows commitment and can really break down barriers. Plus, understanding cultural nuances can be a game changer in negotiations and collaborations.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? It’s when I can combine productivity with a bit of learning and personal growth. Ideally, I’d have a successful meeting with a potential client, make progress on a project, and squeeze in a Dutch lesson on Duolingo. Oh, and if I can fit in a good workout, that’s just cherry on top!

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel like I’ve moved the needle, you know? Made some tangible progress in my work, learnt something new, and felt connected with people – be it through a productive meeting or just a good chat with friends.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I usually assess the potential impact and weigh the pros and cons. I like to gather as much information as possible, maybe chat it over with a mentor or close friends. But honestly, there’s always a bit of gut feeling involved. Sometimes you just know what the right move is, you know?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I’m more of a planner, for sure. I mean, in the startup world, things are always changing, right? But having a plan helps me stay focused and adaptable.

Q: Example showing that?
A: For instance, when I was setting up my startup, I drafted a detailed business plan. It outlined our growth strategy, target market, everything. Yeah, some things didn’t go as planned – they never do – but having that framework helped guide decisions and keep the team aligned.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk is part and parcel of entrepreneurship, innit? I try to mitigate it by doing thorough research and analysis. But at the end of the day, you gotta be willing to take a leap. Balancing calculated risks with instinct, that’s key.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical weekday, hmm, starts with a morning run to clear my head. Then, I dive into emails and catch up on news, especially tech-related stuff. My day is usually filled with meetings, both internal and with potential partners or clients. I try to squeeze in some coding when I can because it keeps me sharp. And in between, I’d do a quick Duolingo session to brush up on my Dutch.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: I think it’s the meetings, especially when I have to present ideas or pitch to stakeholders. It’s exciting but also draining. Keeping up the energy to stay enthusiastic and persuasive throughout the day can be a lot, you know?

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: Honestly, I wish I had more time to explore creative ideas. Running a startup often means focusing on immediate concerns, but having time to just brainstorm and innovate would be amazing. And yeah, more energy to learn Dutch beyond just Duolingo levels.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Last year, it was definitely the pandemic disruptions. Things slowed down, and networking became harder. It was challenging to maintain momentum and morale. Plus, I couldn’t attend in-person events, which are great for learning and making connections in the market.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I pivoted a lot of our strategies to virtual platforms, made use of online networking tools, and focused more on digital marketing. We adjusted our product offerings to meet changing demands and kept the team engaged with regular check-ins and virtual team-building activities.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: That would be my family back in Ghana, even though we’re miles apart, and a few close friends I’ve made here in the Netherlands. We stay connected through calls and messages. They’re my support system, keeping me grounded and motivated.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They’re the kind of relationships where we can pick up right where we left off. With family, it’s that unconditional support, you know? And with my friends here, it’s about shared experiences and mutual understanding, especially in navigating life as expatriates.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly in my home office these days, thanks to the remote work trend. But I also spend quite a bit of time at co-working spaces, they're great for networking and keeping the creative juices flowing.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: In my home office, it’s comfortable but can get a bit monotonous, to be honest. Moving to co-working spaces brings a change of environment and energy. It’s refreshing to be around other creatives and entrepreneurs, which can be really motivating.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It’s the vibe, I guess. Seeing others hustling, being surrounded by people who are just as motivated creates a sense of community and belonging. Plus, those spaces often spark spontaneous conversations that lead to great ideas.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Firstly, my business mentor. He’s been in the tech industry for decades and provides invaluable advice. Then there's my network of entrepreneur friends who understand the struggles and can offer practical solutions or just a listening ear.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: I remember when we lost a major client due to budget cuts on their end. It was a big blow because we had worked hard to build that relationship. We had to quickly adjust our financial forecasts and find ways to make up for the sudden loss in revenue.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was quite stressful, honestly. I felt a lot of pressure to ensure the stability of the company and our team. But it also pushed me to think creatively about how we could pivot and find new opportunities in a challenging market.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I focused on strengthening relationships with our remaining clients and exploring new sectors. I also took the time to recharge personally – took a step back, reassessed our goals, and leaned heavily on my support network. Talking it out with my mentors and close friends was crucial.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a pause and re-evaluating priorities helps. Sometimes it’s a simple break, like a walk or listening to music. Meditation has been quite helpful too. And, of course, talking it out with someone who understands the pressures of running a business.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I’d love to see my startup thriving and making a real impact in the tech space, you know? More balance in work and personal life would be ideal, and mastering Dutch is definitely on that list. Maybe even start another venture or invest in new projects.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to have more time to focus on big-picture strategies rather than getting caught up in daily operations. Also, building a stronger local network in the Netherlands, both personally and professionally, would be fantastic.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I tried using language textbooks and attending a few local classes. But to be honest, it was tough keeping up. The classes didn’t always fit my schedule, and the textbooks felt dry, you know? I needed something more flexible and engaging.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Definitely the lack of flexibility. Classes were at fixed times which clashed with my work schedule, and I missed quite a few. Textbooks, on the other hand, were not interactive. It was all repetition without much feedback, which made it hard to stay motivated.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time I was supposed to have a meeting in Dutch, and I realized that my textbook knowledge didn’t cut it. I couldn’t keep up with the conversation. It was a wake-up call that I needed something more dynamic and closer to real life.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend of mine mentioned it. He was using it to brush up on his Spanish, and he said it was like playing a game. That caught my attention because I'm all about interesting ways to learn.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The combination of gamification and flexibility. I liked the idea of being able to learn in bite-sized lessons anytime, anywhere. Plus, it being free was a huge bonus, especially since I was already investing a lot in my business.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure thing. So, I usually fire up Duolingo in the evening, after wrapping up with work. The other day, I was on my tailored daily lesson – it started with some vocabulary revision, you know? Then it moved on to sentences, which I had to translate from English to Dutch. I like that it gives immediate feedback when I get something wrong, so I know right away what to focus on. Then there’s those speaking exercises – I was repeating phrases into my phone, and it checks my pronunciation. It’s kinda funny when my partner hears me randomly talking to my phone in Dutch from the next room.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The immediate feedback is gold. You make a mistake, and it’s on you right away, so you can correct and move on without waiting. It keeps the learning process active and engaging. Plus, the progression through different levels is motivating – feels like you’re unlocking new skills.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, the sentences feel a bit random or not practical for daily use. Like, when am I really going to say, 'The cat drinks milk' in a business setting, you know? I’d appreciate more context-specific lessons, especially focused on business Dutch.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: It's probably the lack of conversational practice. I mean, it's great for vocabulary and grammar but doesn’t push you enough into real-life situations. You can get a bit trapped in the loops of gamified challenges without stepping into actual conversations.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this instance when I joined a Dutch meetup group. The conversation was flowing, but I was stuck translating in my head at first. I realized then that Duolingo hadn’t fully prepared me for natural-speed conversations or the slang that people use casually.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, for sure. I try to supplement Duolingo with podcasts and Dutch news segments. And I practice speaking with a language buddy, someone who’s fluent and can give me real-time corrections and tips on how Dutch people actually talk.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Real-world application. They challenge me to use what I’ve learned in spontaneous conversations. I get exposed to different accents and natural speech patterns, which is crucial for understanding the language as it's really spoken.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: That’d be hitting a plateau in learning. You know, getting comfortable with a certain level on Duolingo without actually improving fluency. It could lead me to miss out on opportunities if I can’t communicate effectively in a business setting.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I'm hoping it keeps me engaged and motivated to learn. Each time, I look for that small piece of progress, whether it’s nailing a new word or sentence structure. I hope it continues to build my confidence in using Dutch beyond lessons.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I catch myself understanding a bit more of a Dutch conversation or when I construct a sentence without overthinking every word. It’s those small victories that show me it’s having an impact.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd add more context-specific modules tailored to professional language use. Business scenarios, formal email writing, negotiation terms – stuff that’s directly applicable to my industry.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love more integration between digital learning platforms and real-life practice opportunities, maybe partnerships with local conversation groups or language events that can complement the learning process.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I’d say the cultural aspect of language learning is really important too. Understanding idiomatic expressions and what makes Dutch culture unique would be super helpful.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Digital twin, eh? Sure, as long as it's for improving the user experience in language learning, I'm in!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Bueno, nací en Cuba, donde el ritmo y el movimiento son parte de mi ADN. Desde joven, me enamoré de la salsa, y eso me llevó a enseñar lo que es mi pasión. Hace unos años me mudé a México para expandir mis horizontes y perfeccionar mi español mexicano. Y claro, llevar la esencia cubana a estas tierras. ¡Es como mezclar dos ritmos y crear una nueva melodía! Ahora dedico mis días a enseñar salsa y seguir aprendiendo.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: Crecí en La Habana, Cuba, rodeado de música, baile y mucha cultura. Todo el mundo bailaba en las calles; era imposible no moverse al ritmo del son y de la salsa.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Ah, fue increíble. Imagínate, cada esquina una pequeña fiesta, una comunidad muy unida. El baile no era solo una actividad, era una forma de vida. Aprendí a bailar antes de caminar, y como dicen, 'mi casa era mi academia'. Los vecinos eran casi familia y siempre había alguien listo para un rumbón.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Yo diría que mudarme a México fue un gran cambio. Fue un salto de fe, dejar atrás lo conocido para abrazar lo nuevo. Vine por una oportunidad de enseñar salsa y también para mejorar mi español mexicano. Esa mezcla de culturas y ritmos ha sido enriquecedora, y cada día aprendo algo nuevo.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Cambiar de país no es fácil, dejar lo que amas por algo incierto. Pero al hacerlo, me di cuenta de lo importante que es salir de tu zona de confort. Me permitió expandir mi mente, mi creatividad, y me dio una nueva perspectiva sobre el mundo y sobre cómo el idioma conecta culturas.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Ah, con mucho baile, para ser honesto. Mantenerme en mi zona de confort cuando todo parecía nuevo fue clave. Me aferré a lo que conocía, como la salsa, y eso me ayudó a navegar por las diferencias culturales. También me lancé a aprender el idioma y la cultura local, lo que ha hecho que México se sienta como un hogar.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: La conexión humana, definitivamente. Como instructor de salsa, veo cómo el baile une a personas de diferentes orígenes. Y con el idioma pasa algo similar. Estoy muy enfocado en perfeccionar mi español mexicano para conectar mejor con mis estudiantes y la comunidad. También, al integrar la música y el idioma, se crea algo muy poderoso.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Porque el idioma es como una danza, ¿sabes? Permite que la gente se entienda, comparta ideas y emociones. Cuando enseño salsa, no solo enseño pasos, enseño historia, cultura. Quiero que mis estudiantes no solo aprendan a bailar, sino que también se enamoren de toda esa magia que rodea al baile.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Un buen día para mí es cuando puedo sentir que he hecho moverse a la gente, literalmente y con palabras. Empezar con un buen cafecito, clases de salsa llenas de energía, y luego unos minutos dedicados a mejorar mi español con Duolingo. Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: Uf, es complicado. Yo diría que sigo mi intuición, que es como cuando bailas y sientes que el próximo paso es el correcto. Consulto con amigos cercanos y reflexiono en cómo la decisión afectará mi enseñanza y mi vida en México. Al final, trato de pensar en cómo me hará sentir, porque si no tiene ritmo, no va.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?

Q: Example showing that?

Una vez, una clase terminó siendo una lección sobre la historia de la salsa cubana porque todos estaban curiosos. Eso es dejarse llevar, sin perder el ritmo.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?

Integrar estas experiencias no solo enriquecería mis clases, sino también mi propia comprensión del lugar donde vivo.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: Mis amigos del grupo de salsa con los que ensayaba en Cuba y algunos colegas que he conocido aquí en México. También, mi familia en Cuba sigue siendo muy cercana, gracias a las videollamadas. Esas conexiones, aunque sean a la distancia, son mi ancla.

Q: Describe those relationships.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: La mayor parte del tiempo estoy en el estudio de baile, mi segundo hogar. También paso tiempo en casa practicando y planificando mis clases. A veces, los parques locales también se convierten en mi espacio para ensayar nuevos pasos al aire libre.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: Me siento libre y auténtico en el estudio, es un lugar donde puedo expresarme y ser yo mismo. Los parques ofrecen un respiro, un lugar donde conecto con la naturaleza mientras practico. En casa, me gusta tener un ambiente tranquilo para crear y planificar, aunque el estudio es donde mi alma realmente se siente viva.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: Es el impacto del ritmo y la libertad de movimiento. En el estudio tengo la música a todo volumen y me pierdo en el sonido. En los parques, la brisa y el espacio abierto traen una sensación de libertad y posibilidades ilimitadas.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Normalmente hablo con mis amigos cercanos del grupo de salsa. Siempre tienen un consejo sabio o saben cómo animarme. También, mi hermano en Cuba es una gran fuente de apoyo. A veces, una buena conversación con alguien que entiende el baile y la cultura puede solucionar cualquier problema.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?

Me sentí como si me hubieran cortado las alas, pero al mismo tiempo, sabía que debía encontrar una solución.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: Fue un golpe duro, tanto emocionalmente como financieramente. Las clases de salsa son mi vida, mi manera de expresarme y de ganarme la vida. Sentía que una parte de mí se quedaba en pausa. Q: How did you cope?

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: Espero tener más tiempo para viajar y aprender de otras culturas. También, quiero mejorar las plataformas virtuales de enseñanza, haciendo mis clases más accesibles a personas de todo el mundo. Sería fantástico ver a más personas unidas por el amor al baile, sin importar el idioma o el origen.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?

Aprendí muchas cosas solo escuchando letras de canciones.

Había un desfase entre aprender del libro y luego intentar hablar con alguien, como un paso de baile sin música. También, los recursos eran limitados, y a veces los libros no reflejaban el español mexicano que estaba tratando de aprender.

Q: Time it really failed?

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitivamente la parte de comprensión oral y pronunciación. Me ayudó a captar el acento y las diferencias de pronunciación que existen en México comparado con Cuba. Me gustaría tener más oportunidades de practicar en tiempo real con hablantes nativos o tener algo más interactivo que las lecciones usuales. También, algunas veces las traducciones no son precisas al contexto, y eso puede ser un poco frustrante.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Es que, a veces, las frases se sienten un poco desconectadas de la vida cotidiana. Como si estuviera aprendiendo pasos de baile sin la música. Me gustaría que las lecciones fueran más inmersivas o que incluyeran más contextos culturales específicos. Porque, sí, aprendes la gramática y el vocabulario, pero la verdadera magia está en cómo lo usas día a día.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Recuerdo una lección que incluía una frase extraña, algo sobre elefantes en la biblioteca. No tenía sentido para mí y me distrajo bastante. Me dejó pensando que a veces sería mejor aprender frases que realmente podrías usar, especialmente en una cultura tan rica como la mexicana. Fue como querer hacer un paso de baile que no encaja con la música, desconcertante.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Sí, definitivamente. Me gusta complementar mis sesiones de Duolingo con conversaciones reales. A veces organizo pequeñas tertulias con amigos mexicanos para practicar lo que he aprendido. También, uso la música como una herramienta de aprendizaje. Escuchar canciones y tratar de entenderlas me ha ayudado mucho a captar modismos y expresiones locales.

A: Las interacciones reales y la música me brindan contexto cultural y emocional que no siempre obtengo en Duolingo. Está bien aprender vocabulario suelto, pero para mí, entender el lenguaje es como entender una coreografía completa, donde cada paso cuenta una historia. Las canciones y las conversaciones le dan vida a lo que aprendo, hacen que el idioma se sienta más auténtico y conectado a la realidad diaria.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Creo que el peor escenario sería estancarme y no poder comunicarme efectivamente, lo que afectaría mi capacidad para enseñar y conectar con mis estudiantes. Sería como perder el ritmo en una coreografía. El idioma es dinámico y siempre cambiante, y quedarse atrás en su evolución podría ser un gran obstáculo.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: Espero que me brinde una mezcla de aprendizaje ligero y oportunidades para desafiarme. Quiero sentir que avanzo, aunque sea un poco, en cada sesión. Es como practicar una nueva secuencia de pasos; cada vez que abro la app, quiero acercarme un poco más a la fluidez, sentirme más seguro con el idioma y, sobre todo, mantener viva mi motivación.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: Cuando puedo salir y usar lo que he aprendido en una conversación real, eso es cuando sé que ha valido la pena. Si me encuentro pensando en español o entendiendo a la gente sin tener que traducir en mi cabeza, entonces sé que el trabajo en Duolingo está dando sus frutos. Es como cuando un paso de salsa finalmente sale natural: ahí es cuando sabes que funciona.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Agregar más oportunidades para practicar conversaciones reales sería mi primera sugerencia. Algo así como 'Duolingo Live' donde puedas hablar con hablantes nativos o participar en conversaciones en grupo. Sería una fusión perfecta de aprendizaje estructurado e interacción auténtica.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: Pienso que deberíamos integrar más el contexto cultural en la enseñanza del idioma. Conectar cada lección con una pieza de música, historia o costumbre local haría que aprender sea más enriquecedor y relevante. Sería como aprender un paso de baile en el contexto de toda una coreografía, con su historia y significado incluido.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Quizás solo decir que, tanto en el baile como en el idioma, la clave está en seguir practicando y no perder la pasión. Me gustaría ver más programas que combinen ambos aspectos, porque es en la fusión donde ocurre la magia.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: ¡Claro que sí! Si va a ayudar a otros a aprender y a conectar tanto como yo, entonces adelante. ¡Muchas gracias!

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hi there! Oh, it's so nice to meet you. I'm Ursula, and I'm excited to share a bit about my journey with you!

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, let's see, I grew up in Germany, and ever since I was little, I was obsessed with the ocean. You know, I used to have these posters of marine life all over my room. Eventually, I pursued marine biology and now I'm in Costa Rica working on conservation projects. It's been a pretty wild ride... I never imagined I'd be here, surrounded by these beautiful creatures and trying to make a difference.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Hamburg, actually, a lovely city with a big harbor. It's a place where water really shapes the whole landscape and lifestyle, kind of prepared me for my current work, in a way.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was wonderful, you know? The city is vibrant with lots of culture, and there's this strong connection to the sea. As a kid, I was always at the harbor or at the aquarium. My parents, they nurtured my interest in marine life, taking me on little trips to the North Sea.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: I think it was when I got accepted into that internship program in the Galápagos Islands. It was like seeing all my childhood dreams come true. I remember feeling like I was exactly where I was meant to be, surrounded by the very creatures I'd been reading about for years.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: That experience, it really opened my eyes to the real impact of human activity on marine ecosystems. I mean, I had learned about it in textbooks, but seeing it up close, the effects of climate change, plastic pollution... it really hit home and pushed me to focus on conservation efforts.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I just threw myself into the work, you know? Every day was a learning opportunity, whether it was the science itself or communicating with the local community. I tried to absorb everything and applied it to my conservation projects back in Costa Rica.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's definitely conservation. I mean, the oceans are such a crucial part of our planet's health. Without them, we're really in trouble. So I'm focused on protecting these environments and, you know, trying to raise awareness about sustainable practices.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because, um, if we don't take care of our oceans, we're endangering countless species, including ourselves. The ocean, it's like the Earth's lungs, and we're choking it. And there's so much beauty and life down there that deserves our care and respect.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day is when I get to spend time in the field, you know? Observing the marine life, collecting data, and maybe even seeing a few turtles or dolphins. It's just so fulfilling. And if I can end the day with a swim or a dive, well, then it's pretty much perfect.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel like I've made a tangible difference. Whether it's successfully tagging a turtle for tracking or engaging with locals about conservation efforts. It's those small victories that motivate me.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to weigh things quite a bit, you know. I gather all the information I can, talk to colleagues or friends, and then there's a lot of reflecting. I mean, sometimes you just have to trust your instincts too, but I like to be informed first.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Oh, definitely a planner! I like to have a structure, especially when it comes to my work. But, nature has its own plans and teaches you to be flexible too.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Oh, once we had this big day planned for turtle tagging, and the weather just flipped on us, like on a dime. So we had to quickly adapt, switch to lab work instead, and it was actually quite productive. You learn to roll with it and make the best of the situation.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I approach it cautiously. Like with diving, there’s always a risk, but preparation is key. I plan, use my training, and rely on my team. And you know, the biggest risks sometimes lead to the greatest discoveries in the field.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Well, I usually start early. I check emails, then head out to the field if the day's projects require it—monitoring species, collecting samples. Afternoons might be spent analyzing data or meeting with my team. And I try to squeeze in language practice with Duolingo, usually in the evenings.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Fieldwork, definitely. It's physically demanding, with long hours in sometimes tough conditions. But it's also the most rewarding part, so it balances out, you could say.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time for community engagement. It's so important to involve and educate the locals about the conservation work we're doing, but there are only so many hours in a day.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Honestly, it was the language barrier. Being in Costa Rica, not speaking fluent Spanish initially was a hurdle. It limited my ability to communicate effectively with local partners and communities, which is crucial for conservation work.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: That's actually why I turned to Duolingo. It's helped build my vocabulary and gain some confidence. I also practice speaking with colleagues and locals whenever I can to improve my fluency.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My research team and a few friends back in Germany. The team here, well, we're like a family—supporting each other through the ups and downs. And my friends from home, they keep me grounded, you know?

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: It's a mix of professional and personal. With my team, we share a strong bond over the work we do. We're united by our passion for marine life. With friends, it's more about the shared history and the ability to be completely myself.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Definitely in the field or at the lab. That's where the action is and where I feel most inspired, working directly with the ocean and its inhabitants.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: It's like a mix of excitement and peace. Being in the field is exhilarating; there's always something new to learn. The lab is calming, allowing for reflection and deep focus on our findings.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the nature of the work. Being close to what I'm passionate about and seeing firsthand the impact of our efforts is incredibly fulfilling.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Usually, my team or my mentor from university. The team offers practical solutions, and my mentor provides a broader perspective and advice drawn from experience.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: We had this equipment failure right in the middle of a crucial research trip. It was frustrating because it delayed our data collection, and we had to scramble to find a solution without affecting the entire project timeline.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was stressful, for sure. It felt like all our hard work was at risk. But it also highlighted the importance of adaptability and teamwork in these situations.

Q: How did you cope?
A: We brainstormed as a team and borrowed equipment from a neighboring research group—luckily they were very accommodating. It taught me resilience and reinforced the importance of having a strong network and the ability to pivot quickly.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Honestly, a swim or a long walk by the beach. The ocean has always been my refuge—it helps me clear my mind and puts things in perspective. It reminds me why I do what I do.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I'd love to see the projects I'm working on make a significant impact, with healthier marine ecosystems and more public awareness about conservation. Personally, I hope for a good balance between work and life, maybe even learning another language.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I'd like to see more effective collaboration between scientists and policymakers. Sometimes it feels like we're speaking different languages, and bridging that gap could lead to more impactful results.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I tried classes, you know, the usual classroom setting with textbooks. It felt too rigid, and I struggled to keep up with the pace. It was hard to apply what I'd learned outside the classroom because it was very formal.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The lack of practical application was really frustrating. I'd learn grammar and vocab, but when it came to everyday conversations, I felt completely lost. It didn't give me real-life context or the confidence to engage with locals.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time I needed to liaise with local fishermen about a conservation project and I just couldn't follow their dialect or speed—rendering the whole conversation pretty much ineffective. That's when I knew I needed a new approach.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I think a colleague recommended it to me during a project meeting. She mentioned it was user-friendly and could be used on the go, which sounded perfect for my busy schedule.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I was drawn to the fact that it was app-based, so I could practice anytime, like between fieldwork and lab sessions. Plus, it was free, which made it a no-brainer to at least give it a shot.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Sure! Just the other day, I opened the app in the morning, during my coffee break. I went through a session focusing on conversational phrases, you know, the ones useful for small talks and introductions. It was quite interactive—matching voice exercises with text. I love the instant feedback, especially when it says 'Perfect!' It just sets a positive tone for the day.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The bite-sized lessons. They fit perfectly into my day, so I don't feel overwhelmed trying to learn too much at once. The way it gamifies the experience is also quite motivating, with streaks and rewards for consistency.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: I have to say, sometimes the exercises feel repetitive. Like, they drill the same words or structures without much context. It can be a bit monotonous, especially if you're seeking more conversational depth.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: It's definitely the lack of real-world speaking practice. I feel like I understand a lot, but when it comes to having a full conversation, I still struggle. It doesn't quite prepare you for the nuances of everyday Spanish here in Costa Rica.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, I remember trying to negotiate with a local vendor about supplies for a project, and I realized that the phrases I'd learned didn't quite apply to the fast-paced, colloquial exchange happening. I mean, it highlighted how textbook Spanish can fall short in real interactions.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, absolutely. I try to pair my Duolingo practice with real conversations as much as possible. I've joined local meetups where I can practice speaking, and I've even watched telenovelas for listening practice—it’s surprisingly effective!

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide context and fluency. Hearing the language in different scenarios helps me understand slang and regional expressions better. It's that real-world application that rounds out my learning experience, I think.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Not being able to communicate effectively could really jeopardize a project. Say, if there's an environmental emergency, you need to articulate your needs and actions clearly to avoid delays or misunderstandings.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it sharpens my vocabulary and gives me those quick wins of understanding grammar intuitively. But mostly, I look forward to it giving me enough confidence to speak more comfortably in real-life situations.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can understand and respond to someone without hesitating as much. It's those moments when phrases pop into my mind automatically that I feel like, yes, this practice is really paying off.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I would love for it to include more interactive speaking scenarios. Like role-playing activities that simulate real-life conversations, not just sentence repetition or translation exercises.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd bridge the gap between digital learning and community interaction more effectively. Maybe through integrated programs that connect learners with native speakers for mutual language exchange.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Maybe just the power of language in conservation. It's such a critical tool, and anything that can improve how we communicate this science is invaluable.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Uh, sure, as long as it's used for good, like improving language learning tools! I'm all for it.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
