Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there, how y'all doin'? Jackson here, ready to chat 'bout all things music and language.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Well, I grew up in the deep South, Mississippi to be exact. Got my first guitar at ten, and it was like finding a voice I didn't know I had. Played in juke joints and churches, then hit the road, chasing that blues dream. Ended up in France for the music scene—Paris, vibrating with energy, and decided I oughta learn French to connect better with folks. Been strumming and learning ever since.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in Clarksdale, Mississippi. It's a town rich with history and music, steeped in the blues.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was somethin' else, man. Music was everywhere, like air. We'd have folks gatherin' on porches, playin' guitars, singing. We were like a big ol' family, and music was our way of communicating things we didn't have words for yet.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: I'd say hittin' the road with just my guitar and a few bucks to my name. I was young, but I felt the call to take my music beyond our little town. That decision changed my life—it was like opening a door to a world full of melodies I'd only dreamed about.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It was a leap of faith, a chance to see if the world was ready for my kind of blues. Stickin’ with what you know is easy, but stepping out into the unknown, that's where I found my groove. I learned more about myself in those travels than any other time.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I took it day by day, you know. Played in bars and cafes, slept on couches or wherever folks would let me crash. I learned to trust the kindness of strangers and the power of music to bridge gaps and open hearts.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I'm all about connecting with people through both my music and learning the French language. I wanna be part of the Parisian scene in a real, soulful way. Music's my main voice, but French is startin' to give me new ways to express those same emotions.

Q: Why is that important?
A: It's like adding a new instrument to my band, you know. The more ways I can connect, the richer the experience. Language and music—they're both about communication, feeling something in your bones. It makes me feel more alive, more engaged with the world.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day is when I've strummed my guitar, maybe written a new lick or two, and had a chance to practice my French with the locals. If I can share a meal, swap stories, and end the night with a jam session, that's a day well-lived.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When there's music in the air and laughter around the table, when I've felt connected to the people and place. And a good coffee, can't forget that!

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I listen to my gut and the rhythms around me. I take some time, maybe go for a long walk with my guitar. I find that when I'm in tune with myself, the right choice usually comes to me.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'm more of a go-with-the-flow kinda guy. Plans are good, but life’s music has a way of improvising, and you gotta be ready to play along.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Like just last week, I was supposed to head to a gig, but met some folks on the Metro playin' their tunes. We ended up havin' an impromptu jam session right there. Missed the gig, but it was a real moment, one you can't plan for.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk is just part of life, part of playin' a good solo. I try to weigh it out, but sometimes you just gotta let the music take you, trust that the notes will lead you home.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: My days usually start with coffee and a quick Duolingo session. Then I practice my scales, work on new songs, or maybe head out for a lesson or gig. I'll try to catch up with friends or head to a cafe for some French practice, soak up the culture. Evenings are for jamming or performing, just losing myself in the music.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Honestly, learning French can be exhausting. It's like learning a whole new set of musical notes and trying to make music that feels right. Sometimes, just keeping up with how fast everything moves in Paris takes a lot outta me.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more time to dive deeper into the language and culture here. It's a rich tapestry, and balancing it with my music can be tough. Also, I'd love to sit with some of the old blues records I haven't spun in a while.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Well, COVID really shook things up. It put a damper on gigs and travel. Had to pivot a lot, do some online performances, which ain't the same as feelin' the crowd's energy live.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I leaned into home recordings, tried to reach out through virtual shows. Kept myself busy with creating stuff digitally, sorta translating live energy into something folks could feel through a screen.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I've got a few close buddies back home who are like family, and some fellow musicians here who share the same passion. They've become my crew, always there for a chat or a jam session.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: It's like a band, you know, always in harmony even when life gets noisy. We share the highs and lows, keep each other grounded.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: I'm either in my apartment, in a cafe for a change of scene, or at some music venue. Those places are like my own little world here in Paris.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I feel comfortable, like I can be myself. The cafes especially make me feel connected—just me, my thoughts, and a good cup of joe. Music venues, they're a whole different kind of alive.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the people, the vibe, the energy of it all. I get inspired just by watching the world go by, or hearing a new melody in the sounds of the city.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I talk to my friends, both back home and here. Sometimes just playing my guitar helps me work things out, too. It's like talking to an old friend who knows me best.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was a moment when a gig I was lookin' forward to got canceled last minute. It threw me off, 'cause I'd been countin' on it, you know. It's tough when you put so much heart into somethin' and it just vanishes.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a hit to the spirit, like playin' a wrong note in the middle of a solo. You gotta pause, regain your rhythm. But it made me more grateful for the opportunities when they do come.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I doubled down on writing new material, turning that disappointment into creativity. Worked on some recordings that I'd been putting off, and it turned into a creative streak that helped ease the frustration.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Music, always. And a walk through the city, soaking up the life around me. It's like hitting a reset button, helps me find my center again.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: In a few years, I see myself more rooted here, maybe even fluent in French, blending my music with new cultural flavors. I want to keep performing, connecting, and creating, bringing a little bit of that Southern soul to Paris.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I'd love more stability, especially with gigs. Navigating a consistent schedule in the music world is tricky, and a bit more predictability would be nice. Also, just feeling more at home with the language.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before, I'd just listen and mimic folks around me, try to catch snippets of conversation and practice with friends over coffee. It was kind of like learning a song by ear—not always easy to catch the right notes.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The thing was, it's hard to know if you're gettin' it right. Without real feedback, I often felt like I was playin' in the wrong key, you know? Plus, it was slow-going, and sometimes frustrating when folks spoke too fast.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: I remember tryin' to order at a cafe and askin' for somethin' completely different than what I intended. The server gave me this funny look, and that's when I knew I needed more structure in my learnin'.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: One of my buddies mentioned it over a beer. Said it was kinda like having a language jam session on your phone.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I figured givin' it a shot wouldn't hurt, especially since it was free. Plus, if somethin' can keep my attention like a good tune, it's worth a go.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: So, I fired it up the other mornin’, startin' with some basics to warm up. I like the little sounds it makes when you get something right—it’s kinda like applause. Worked through a few vocab exercises, tried some speech practice. Even though it was just me and the app, you get this sense of accomplishin' a little milestone.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The repetition helps, like playing scales on a guitar until they're second nature. The immediate feedback corrects me, so I don't keep hittin' the same wrong notes.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes it feels repetitive, like you're stuck in a groove that won't let you really jam. I need a little more flexibility, you know? Somethin’ that helps me improvise in conversation.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The lack of context can be a drag. You practice single phrases, but when folks in Paris start speakin' full throttle, it's like a different song entirely.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was this one time, I was tryin' to chat with some local musicians about improvin' a song, but I just couldn't keep up. I realized Duolingo hadn't prepped me for the real flow of conversation.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Oh, for sure. I'll listen to French music, try to translate lyrics, or watch movies without subtitles. It's like playin' along to a record till you get it right.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They bring in that real-world feel, givin' me context and rhythm. Language is music in its own right, and you gotta feel it more than just seein’ it on a screen.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Well, I reckon gettin' stuck, not improving on the nuances. I'd hate to miss out on meaningful connections and collaborations here in Paris 'cause I couldn’t quite get the language down.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it adds a layer to my language knowledge, fillin' in gaps and buildin' my confidence. It’s like adding a new riff to a song I’m still learnin'.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can stroll into a bakery, chat with the baker, and actually understand her response, I know it's workin'. It’s those small victories that tell me I’m on the right track.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Maybe more conversational practice, somethin’ that mimics real-life chats. You know, let it throw some curveballs like life does, not just stick to the script.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love if there were more ways to learn in context, like through personal stories or music. Language is alive, and sometimes apps feel a bit too rigid.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Y’all covered a lot! Just remember, learning a language is like learnin' to play the blues—it takes time, soul, and a whole lotta practice.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure thing, as long as it plays a mean guitar!

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Definitely moving to Portugal. It was a big decision to leave Brazil, my home, but I wanted to explore architecture here. The language and cultural differences were a challenge, but that’s also what makes it rewarding, you know?

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It forced me to, um, adapt and grow both personally and professionally. Learning European Portuguese was challenging, and it gave me a new perspective on how architecture can blend with culture. It pushed my limits.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Well, I dove into language learning headfirst. I used Duolingo, of course, and tried to immerse myself by talking to locals, attending events. I mean, I wanted to fully embrace the culture and language to enhance my work.

Q: What do you care most about right now?

And now, learning Italian is part of that artistic journey, you know?

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a small town near Prague. It's quite an artistic community with lots of old glasswork traditions, and it's nestled in this lovely landscape.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was quite, um, inspiring. I mean, surrounded by art and history, you know? The winters were cold and crisp, but we had warm hearts and lively gatherings. The local glass artists were like magicians to me, shaping molten glass into something so beautiful.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Moving to Italy was definitely a big turning point. It wasn't just a geographical change; it was about embracing a new culture and language. I remember the day I got the offer to work on Murano, it felt like a dream, blending Czech precision with Italian passion. That moment redefined my life, truly.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, it shifted my entire perspective on art and life. Suddenly, I was in this vibrant community where glass wasn't just a craft but a way of life. It challenged me to step out of my comfort zone, adapt, and become part of a new tradition.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I leaned into it, I guess. I started learning Italian immediately, trying to immerse myself into the Murano lifestyle. It was, uh, challenging but invigorating. I attended local workshops, spent time with fellow artisans, you know, just soaking it all in.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's about perfecting my craft while deepening my connection with Italian culture. I want to integrate the elegance of Italian design with my Czech roots. It's this blend that I'm passionate about sharing with the world.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because, um, it's like my art is a bridge between two worlds. By merging these styles, I'm creating something unique, something that resonates with both my past and my present. It's, like, paying homage to my heritage while embracing my new home.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day, let's see... It starts with a quiet morning walk through Venice, maybe catching the early light on the canals. Then I spend hours in the studio, working with glass. If I can have a genuine conversation in Italian without too many stumbles, it feels particularly rewarding. And ending the day with a lovely Italian meal... perfetto!

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I feel creatively fulfilled and connected with the people around me. You know, those days when language flows and my hands create what my heart envisions... that's when I know it was a good day.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to, um, reflect deeply and weigh my options. I consider what's meaningful to me and try to envision how the decision aligns with my artistic and personal goals. I also trust my intuition a lot, you know, that gut feeling.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'm a bit of both, honestly. I love having a plan, especially for my work, but I also embrace the unexpected. Sometimes the best art and experiences come from spontaneity.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Hmm, recently, I had planned a design for a glass piece, but when I started working, the glass took a different form altogether. Instead of fighting it, I went with it, and it ended up being one of my favorite creations. It's like life sometimes surprises you in beautiful ways.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I view risk as part of the creative process. In glass art, there's always a chance of something breaking. It's, uh, a bit nerve-wracking but also exciting. I try to see risks as opportunities for growth and discovery, even if they don't always work out.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: My typical day starts with an espresso, of course. Morning is my most productive time, so I'm usually in the studio by eight, prepping materials, sketching designs. By lunchtime, I like to take a break, maybe have a quick chat with local artisans. Afternoon is for refining pieces, and in the evening, I practice Italian. Sometimes I use Duolingo, sometimes I just sit at a café and listen to conversations. It’s a blend of work and cultural immersion.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the creative process itself. Working with glass requires focus and precision. Also, learning Italian can be mentally exhausting, especially when I hit those tricky grammar parts. It's rewarding but definitely takes energy.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more energy for language practice, really. There are days when I'm too tired after studio work to concentrate on Italian. Also, I’d love to explore more of the local arts scene but sometimes, you know, time slips away.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Language barrier, hands down. Even though I'm improving, conversations can still be challenging. I mean, there’s so much nuance in Italian, and sometimes I feel like my words don’t quite capture what I want to express in my art or everyday interactions.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I try to face it head-on. I engage in conversations whenever possible, and I use tools like Duolingo to fill in the gaps. Also, being around locals helps a lot, you know? They’re patient and encouraging, which makes it easier to learn.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My family back in Czech Republic and a few close friends here in Italy. There's also a fellow artisan on Murano who has become like a mentor. Each of these relationships brings something invaluable to my life.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They are, um, supportive and enriching. My family is always rooting for me, even from afar. My friends here provide a sense of home and community, and this artisan mentor? She's like a guiding light in both craft and life.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Mostly in my studio on Murano, it's like my second home. When I'm not there, I'm exploring Venice or spending time in local cafés, just soaking in the atmosphere.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: In the studio, I'm completely focused and at peace, you know, surrounded by tools and glass. In Venice, it's like a constant dance of inspiration and exploration. Both places fill me with a sense of belonging and purpose.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: I suppose it's the blend of creativity, history, and community. The studio is where I create, so it’s deeply personal. Venice itself is like a living canvas that keeps me inspired and connected to the Italian way of life.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: Usually, it's my mentor here or my family back home. My mentor has this uncanny ability to see a situation from a fresh perspective, and my family offers unwavering support and love. They all help ground me when things get tough.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Oh, definitely when a major piece I was working on cracked just before completion. It felt like all my efforts shattered with it. I had put a lot of heart into that piece, and seeing it break was, um, quite discouraging.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: Initially, it was a blow. I felt like I lost a part of my vision. But it also reminded me of the fragility of both glass and life, and eventually, it pushed me to reconsider my approach and expression in my work.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I took a step back, gave myself some breathing room to process. Talking to my mentor helped a lot; she reminded me that even in breaking, glass can create something uniquely beautiful. I used the pieces to create a new work, embracing imperfection, you know?

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: When I feel overwhelmed, I go for a walk along the canals or sit quietly in a garden. Sometimes, just watching the light play on the water calms me. I also find doodling or sketching therapeutic, as it helps me refocus my thoughts.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to have a more integrated life, where my art is recognized internationally but rooted in my Czech and Italian influences. I'd love to master Italian and maybe, who knows, teach or mentor young artists myself. A balance of personal fulfillment and professional growth would be ideal.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I wish for a bit more confidence in my language skills. I want to converse effortlessly, you know? It would make life and work smoother, especially in collaborations. Also, I hope to have more time for personal projects that blend both cultures.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I relied heavily on textbooks and some overly complicated grammar guides. I also attended a few language classes with mixed results. The textbooks were, uh, a bit dry and it was hard to stay motivated, especially with all the studio work that required my attention.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Oh, definitely the lack of engagement and, um, practical application. It felt like learning was happening in a vacuum. I could memorize words, but the moment I stepped outside and tried to use them, it was like my mind went blank.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was this one time I had to talk to a gallery owner. I thought I was prepared, you know, with all my vocabulary lists. But in the actual conversation, I got so nervous and lost track of what I learned. It was quite a reality check.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A friend here in Venice mentioned it to me. She said it was like a game and that I might enjoy the playful aspect. That caught my attention because I like the idea of learning being fun.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: I think the idea of bite-sized lessons was appealing. With my busy schedule, the fact that I could learn a little every day without feeling overwhelmed was really attractive. Plus, the app being free meant I could try it without much to lose.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Okay, so, yesterday evening, after dinner, I opened Duolingo. I chose an Italian lesson from the 'Arts and Culture' section. The session started with vocabulary matching, which is like a warm-up, then moved to forming simple sentences. I really liked the speaking exercises where you listen and repeat because they mimic real conversations. When I got a sentence wrong, the app corrected me and helped me understand the mistake. It was a 15-minute session, but it felt focused and fun.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: I’d say the repetition and immediate feedback. It's like having a coach beside you, correcting as you learn. Also, the feature that lets you listen to native speakers is incredibly useful. It helps with pronunciation, which is crucial, you know?

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes, the sentences are a bit odd or not really practical. Like, they don't always reflect real-life conversations. It's kind of like solving a word puzzle that doesn’t match the picture I have in my head of Italian dialogue.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Probably the lack of cultural context. While it helps with words and structure, it sometimes feels disconnected from the living language that I encounter in Italy. I wish it included more idiomatic expressions or cultural tips that mirror what I experience here.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Ah, yes, there was a time I learned a sentence on Duolingo and tried using it at a café. The waitress looked so confused. I realized later it was more formal or outdated than what people actually say. It was a bit embarrassing and made me question how much I could rely on the app alone.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Absolutely, I do. Sometimes I, um, use language exchange groups or listen to Italian podcasts. They offer a glimpse into casual speech, which is missing in the structured lessons of Duolingo. It’s like adding spice to a dish, you know?

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They offer context and authenticity. You can't learn the music of a language from an app alone. Hearing real people and engaging in actual conversation gives me nuance and cultural depth. It's that warmth and spontaneity that’s often missing in structured lessons.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst case? I suppose it's relying solely on the app and ending up with a robotic version of the language. That would mean missing out on the vibrant, emotional layers that make a culture come alive. It'd be like creating glass pieces without any color or texture.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it challenges me just enough to learn something new but not so much that it feels discouraging. Ideally, it reinforces what I've learned and adds a playful element, like a quick yet meaningful dive into the language.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I find myself using a word or phrase I learned spontaneously during the day. If I can understand a snippet of conversation or respond quicker, it’s like hearing an echo of the lesson in real life. That’s when I know it’s working.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d include more situational dialogues and cultural insights. Perhaps little notes on when certain phrases are used or tidbits about Italian customs. It would make the lessons feel more lived-in and relevant.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I think the whole language learning space could benefit from more integration with real-life scenarios. More partnerships with local businesses or cultural organizations would, um, bridge the gap between learning and living the language.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Just that language learning, like art, is an ongoing process. It's about embracing mistakes and finding beauty in the journey. And maybe, that Duolingo helps keep my journey playful, even if it’s not always perfect.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Oh, um, sure, as long as it captures my love for glass and culture, I'm fine with it.

A: Hola, bonjour! I'm Santiago. It's great to be here and talk a bit about my experiences. Merci beaucoup for having me.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: So, um, I grew up in Chile, you know, surrounded by beautiful vineyards. That's where my love for wine began. I, uh, worked hard and eventually became a sommelier. Then, I moved to France to specialize in Burgundy wines. I've been perfecting my French here, which is, you know, essential for my career. It's been a journey, combining my love for wine and my passion for languages.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a small town in Chile, um, near Valparaíso. It's a place where uvas, grapes, are part of life, and everyone knows the art of winemaking, you know?

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Aah, it was quite charming, actually. Very connected to the earth, the vineyards, y, um, family was everything. We celebrated harvests with these big fiestas. It instilled in me a deep respect for nature and the delicate balance that makes a great vino.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: I'd say moving to France was a major turning point. Leaving Chile and coming to Burgundy—it was quite daunting. But, you know, it opened a whole new world of wine for me, and pushed me to really master French. I had to adapt quickly, both in my profession and personal life.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it meant starting over in many ways. I had to build a reputation in a new place and learn the nuances of a new culture and language. It was like, um, trying to understand the complexity of a new assemblage, a new blend, and finding my place within it.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: Well, I immersed myself completely. I took every opportunity to mingle with locals, learn their customs, and, of course, taste as much wine as possible. Language-wise, I used apps like Duolingo, watched French films, joined local wine clubs—whatever helped me feel at home.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, my focus is on mastering French, especially the wine-related terminology. Being a sommelier in France, it's crucial to speak fluently. It's like having the perfect decantation, I need to bring out the full expression, the full bouquet, of what I know.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Porque, um, it's not just about communicating, it's conveying passion, knowledge, and respect for wine. In Burgundy, language is your key to appreciation and respect in the community. Knowing the right phrases, the cultural significance—it all affects how I'm perceived professionally.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: Oh, a good day? It starts with a perfect espresso, then visiting a vineyard with a beautiful terroir, learning something new about wine, and ending with a delicious dinner paired with a sublime red, preferably a Pinot Noir. And, of course, a bit of Duolingo practice in between.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I, um, feel I've appreciated the flavors of both wine and language. If I've learned something new, whether it's a tasting note or a French idiom, and shared it with others, entonces, that's a good day.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I try to balance instinct with deliberation. It's like selecting a wine—knowing its potential but also trusting your palate, your intuition. I weigh pros and cons, think of the long-term impact, but ultimately, I also go with what feels right in the gut, you know?

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'm more of a planner, definitely. But, um, in the wine world, things can change with a single tasting note, so I try to leave room for spontaneity too.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Just last month, I was planning a sommelier event, had everything detailed and organized. But then a rare vintage appeared unexpectedly, um, and I had to adjust my plans to include a special tasting session. It was hectic but exciting.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I approach risk like, um, tasting a new wine. You assess the potential, trust your experience, and sometimes you just have to take the plunge. It's essential to embrace it with openness and a readiness to learn, even if things don't go as planned.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: A typical weekday, um, starts with some Duolingo sessions, warming up with French vocabulary over breakfast. Then, I head to the vineyard or cellar, work on tastings, and meet clients. Afternoons involve managing stock or attending masterclasses. Evenings are for unwinding with friends over a good vintage, and perhaps a bit more language practice.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely, the tastings and client meetings. They demand full attention, perfect articulation of flavors, and a lot of interaction, especially when French isn't my first language. It's rewarding, but it can be draining, you know?

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: Honestly, I wish I had more time for traveling to different wine regions, exploring their unique profiles. And, um, more time to immerse in cultural experiences that go beyond just the wine, to really understand the people and history behind it.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: The biggest constraint was adapting to the changing rules due to the pandemic. It really, um, affected wine tourism and events, which are a big part of my work. There was a lot of uncertainty, especially with events being canceled or postponed.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I, uh, shifted focus to virtual tastings and online wine education. It was about staying connected with clients and wine enthusiasts from afar, keeping the passion alive even when we couldn't meet in person. Adaptation was key.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I feel closest to my colleagues in the wine industry. We, um, share a bond over the love of wine and the challenges of the trade. Also, my family back in Chile, they are always a phone call away, supporting me in everything.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: With my colleagues, it's like being part of a team of explorers, always learning together. With my family, it's a deep-rooted connection, like a well-aged wine that gets better with time, filled with warmth and wisdom.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Most of my time is spent between the vineyard and my small tasting room. Those are, um, my sanctuaries, where I truly feel in my element.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I feel, um, alive and inspired. Being among the vines, it's calming, revitalizing. In the tasting room, it's more of a performance, sharing knowledge and experience with others. Both spaces are, like, extensions of who I am.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the connection to the land, the history that's in every bottle. And, um, the interactions with people who appreciate what wine brings to life. It all makes me feel part of something bigger.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to my mentor in France. He’s, um, been in the industry for decades and has a wealth of experience. His advice is like a good reserve wine—rich and full of character. Also, I rely on my family for emotional support.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: There was a moment when, um, my biggest event of the year was postponed due to lockdowns. I felt quite lost without the anticipation and preparation. It was like waiting for a wine to mature, only for it to be corked, you know?

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was disappointing, it shook my confidence a bit. For a while, I felt like I had lost the rhythm in my work. But, it also taught me resilience and the importance of flexibility in this industry.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I, ah, turned to improving my skills. You know, I doubled down on learning French, even took up some new courses online. It kept me busy, gave me a sense of progress. Plus, I experimented with virtual tastings, which was new and exciting.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: A walk through the vineyard or a good glass of wine always helps clear my mind. And, uh, practicing breathing exercises, meditating. These little rituals, they help ground me when things get too hectic.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to be, um, fully fluent in French, running my own wine consultancy and hosting exclusive tasting events. I want to travel more and immerse myself in different wine cultures—each sip telling a new story. And, of course, maintain balance with friends and family.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to manage stress better, find ways to enjoy the present more instead of always planning for the next event. It’s about savoring the moment, like you would a fine vintage wine.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I relied heavily on, um, traditional language courses and textbooks. I also tried language exchange partners, but it was hard to find someone who fit my schedule. It was, uh, quite a challenge to keep it engaging.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The pace was, um, either too slow or too fast, never just right. I felt like, uh, lost without context, memorizing words I’d never use. Sort of like a dry wine without any depth.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was one time when, uh, at a wine tasting event, I couldn't follow a conversation about, um, biodynamic viticulture. It was embarrassing, and I realized then that my method didn’t equip me well for real-life discussions in French.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I first heard about Duolingo from a fellow sommelier here in France. He mentioned it over a glass of Pinot Noir as a great tool to refine language skills, especially in our industry.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea of, um, practicing on-the-go, whenever I had a spare moment, was really appealing. Plus, I loved the gamification aspect. It, uh, felt more like a game than study, which was exactly what I needed to stay motivated.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Well, um, I usually start with the Basics or Practice sections. The other day, I, uh, focused on the Food and Drink section, which is directly relevant to my work. It has exercises that involve writing and speaking sentences—I was saying things like 'Je voudrais un verre de vin blanc, s'il vous plaît'. It's very practical. The app gives immediate feedback, which I find crucial in catching pronunciation errors early. And, um, there's this little animation of Duo, the owl, cheering me on. It feels rewarding and keeps me coming back.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Honestly, the most helpful part for me is the pronunciation practice. It helps me, um, refine my accent, especially when dealing with terms that are specific to the wine industry. It’s like polishing a fine glass—each detail matters.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: The repetitive exercises can sometimes feel, uh, monotonous. And not all the vocabulary is applicable to what I need. Like, why would I need to say 'The cat drinks milk' when I’m trying to discuss vintage characteristics?

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Overall, I'd say, um, the lack of advanced conversation or cultural context can be limiting. I need to learn more about French idioms or phrases that are common in viticulture. Sometimes it feels like I'm only skimming the surface.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Oh, well, once during a tasting, I realized I didn't know how to express certain tasting notes in French. Like, I could describe the basics, but when it came to subtle notes or, um, terroir-specific terms, I was at a loss. Duolingo hadn’t prepared me for those nuances.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yes, definitely. I often supplement Duolingo with, um, wine-focused French courses and local French clubs. Also, I use French documentaries on wine as a tool to mix language learning with my passion, you know?

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: They provide, uh, cultural immersion and context that Duolingo lacks. I can learn how to express complex tasting notes and engage in deeper conversations about wine. It's like moving from a simple varietal to a grand cru.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: The worst-case scenario would be, um, not being able to communicate effectively during a major wine event, missing opportunities to connect with fellow sommeliers and connoisseurs. It would be like trying to open a wine bottle without a corkscrew—very limiting.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it helps me, um, build confidence in everyday French, and solidify the vocabulary I need for professional conversations. It's about reinforcing my skills, much like refining a wine blend over time.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can, uh, smoothly navigate a French conversation, especially about wines, and when I catch myself thinking or dreaming in French, then I know it’s working. It's like having a clear finish on the palate after tasting.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I'd add more specialized vocabulary, um, especially for professions like mine. And more complex dialogues, to practice real-life scenarios. It would make the app a fine-tuned tool, like a sommelier's knife.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I’d love to see, uh, more integration of cultural nuances and expressions in language learning. Language is about communication, but also about culture—like wine, it tells a story beyond mere words.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Just that, um, language learning is a journey, much like perfecting a wine. It's ongoing, requires patience and passion. I think that, sometimes, we focus too much on perfection instead of progress.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Oh, eh, sure, why not? As long as it captures the essence, like a good wine captures its terroir. Go ahead!

Q: Intro greeting
A: G'day, mate! Lovely to chat with ya.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Ah, well, grew up in Australia, right by the ocean. Always loved the sea, so naturally, I got into pearl diving. Worked with pearls for yonks—there’s just something magical about 'em. Met some folks from Mikimoto, and now I’m in Japan, diving and learning Japanese to better connect with the team. It’s been a real adventure.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a small coastal town in Western Australia. Just a stone's throw from the Indian Ocean.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Oh, it was fantastic! You know, loads of sun, surf, and sand. Spent most of me time out on the water. The community was tight-knit, and everyone looked out for each other. Simple life, but couldn't have asked for a better childhood.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: Probably when I got my first real diving gig. It was with a local pearl farm, and that’s when I realised I wanted to be around pearls for the rest of me life. It wasn't just a job; it was like finding a home in the ocean.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: It showed me that you can have a career doing something you genuinely love. Diving wasn't just a hobby anymore; it was a gateway to the world of pearls, craftsmanship, and luxury. It opened doors to places and people I never imagined meeting, like the folks at Mikimoto.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I just dove right in, honestly. Worked me way up, learned from the best, and took every opportunity that came me way. I was eager to learn, you know, and never shied away from a challenge. Every dive was a chance to get better.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's mastering Japanese. It's not just about the language; it's about really connecting with the Mikimoto team and clients on their level. I want to understand not just the words but the cultural nuances, especially in business settings.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Well, in the pearl world, relationships are key. Trust and respect build over understanding, and that means more than just knowing the language. It’s about showing respect for their culture, which really enhances collaborations and business opportunities.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day starts with an early dive, the water crisp and clear. Maybe find a few beauties, have a chat with the team, and then spend some time practicing Japanese. If I can finish the day watching a sunset on the water, that’s a topper.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I’ve learned something new, made progress with my Japanese, and felt a real connection with the ocean and the people I’m working with, that’s when I say the day’s been ace.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to weigh things carefully, like balancing air in your tank on a deep dive. I talk it over with me mates and mentors, mull it over a lot, and then I just sort of go with my gut feeling. It’s a mix of logic and instinct.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Bit of both, I'd say. I like having a plan, but I’m flexible enough to go with the flow. In diving, you have to be ready for anything, and I think life’s no different.

Q: Example showing that?
A: When I moved to Japan, it was a well-thought-out decision, but I arrived with an open mind. I had a plan to learn the language and integrate, but I’ve adapted a lot along the way as opportunities and challenges have popped up.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Working with pearls, you get used to assessing risk. It’s about understanding the stakes and having a backup plan. I think of it like calculating decompression stops on a dive; you have to be precise, but also ready to adjust if conditions change.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Starts bright and early with a dive session, looking over our oyster beds. Then, I’ll usually spend some time with the Mikimoto folks going over designs or quality checks. After that, it’s language practice with Duolingo or sometimes a tutor. In the evenings, I like to unwind with a bit of cooking or catching up with mates.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Honestly, the language learning is a big drain. It’s challenging keeping up with everything and practicing enough to see real improvement. Diving is physically demanding but in a more refreshing way, you know?

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I’d love to have more time to work on my Japanese and maybe dive deeper into cultural studies. Understanding the history and traditions behind what we do with pearls and Mikimoto’s role in it would be fascinating.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Probably the language barrier, especially in professional settings. It's tricky because I can handle basic conversations, but discussing technical specifics or nuanced topics in Japanese is still tough.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I’m constantly practicing. Using tools like Duolingo helps with daily practice, but I also meet with a tutor, and I try to speak with the team in Japanese as much as possible, even if it’s a bit rough at times.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My dive team back home and some close mates I've made here in Japan. We’ve all been through a lot together, and there's a bond that forms when you work underwater with someone. It’s like being part of a pod.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: Supportive and trustworthy. We look out for each other, share knowledge, and there’s always a sense of camaraderie. It’s about knowing someone’s got your back, whether it’s in the water or in life.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Either on the water or in the office. I split my time between diving and working on projects with the Mikimoto team, and then evenings are often spent studying or relaxing at home.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: In the water, I feel at peace, like I’m where I’m meant to be. The office can be a bit more challenging due to the language barrier, but it’s exciting too. At home, it’s relaxing and a bit of a sanctuary for me to unwind and recharge.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The water's familiar and comforting, like an old friend. The office has its challenges, but working with experts and seeing beautiful creations come to life is inspiring.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I often call up me mentor back in Australia or chat with colleagues here. They provide different perspectives and advice, and it’s good to have a mix of local and homegrown insights.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: We had a language mishap during a big meeting. I misunderstood a client’s request, and it took us a bit to untangle the mess. It was embarrassing, to say the least, but a big learning moment.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a hit to the confidence, for sure. Made me realise how much more I need to focus on the language nuances, especially in professional contexts where precision is critical.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I doubled down on my language studies, and also started using Duolingo more religiously. I reached out to colleagues who could help bridge the gap and learned from the error. Mistakes happen, but it’s how you handle them that counts.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a moment to breathe and get back to the ocean helps. A long, peaceful dive can clear the head. Besides that, small breaks and chatting with mates for some laughs really lighten the load.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I’d love to be fluent in Japanese, managing some major projects at Mikimoto, and maybe even lead an initiative that bridges Australian and Japanese pearl industries. Oh, and I’ll never be far from the sea.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d like to see my language skills at a level where I can navigate complex conversations with ease and really feel a part of the community here, both personally and professionally.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Mostly through classes and a tutor here in Japan. It was okay but slow-going, and I struggled with consistent practice due to diving schedules. I tried flashcards and apps like Rosetta Stone, but they didn’t quite stick.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: Finding the time to sit down for a full class was tough, and without consistent practice, I felt like I was treading water. The apps I used before didn’t engage me enough to keep coming back.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was one time I’d prepared for a meeting months in advance using these methods, and when it came down to it, I was still floundering with basic phrases. Highlighted how ineffective it was.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A mate from the dive team mentioned it. Said it was like a game and easy to fit into daily life, so I figured I’d give it a shot.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The gamified approach sounded interesting. I needed something I could do regularly that didn’t feel like a chore. Plus, it was free, so I didn’t see the harm in trying it out.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: Alright, so I pop it open on the train, heading to work. I start with a review session, which throws me a mix of vocabulary and phrase matching. There’s this leaderboard thing that pushes me a bit too—not that I’m competitive or anything. Then I dive into a new lesson about business phrases, practicing speaking and listening. The little owl gives me feedback, and I try to fix any mistakes. The streak counter keeps me coming back, so I make sure to finish the session on a high note.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: Definitely the repetition and instant feedback. Helps me correct mistakes on the spot. The app’s got varied exercises too, which breaks the monotony and covers all the language skills.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes the phrases are a bit unnatural or too formal. Not everything is relevant to daily life or professional settings. It's like being caught in an old diving net—just a bit of a snag that slows things down.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: The lack of cultural context. I find that knowing why a phrase is used in a certain way is just as important as the phrase itself. It's hard to capture that with an app. Feels a bit like diving in murky waters.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: There was a phrase I learned from Duolingo that I tried to use at a business lunch, and it didn’t quite land right. Someone explained later that it was too casual for the setting, which was a tad embarrassing.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, I mix it with real conversations and watch Japanese shows or listen to podcasts. It helps me pick up on the subtleties and the flow of natural conversations, which Duolingo can't provide on its own.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Cultural nuance and real-life application. Talking with people and consuming media gives me context and helps me sound more natural, like I’m part of the culture, not just spitting out textbook phrases.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: If I’m unable to effectively communicate during an important meeting or negotiation, it could impact both relationships and business. It’s crucial that I not just know the language but use it correctly in context.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I’m hoping it can sharpen my skills and keep my Japanese fresh and top of mind. Ideally, it should also introduce me to phrases and vocabulary relevant to my work with Mikimoto.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I can use what I’ve learned in actual conversations without a hitch—especially when the other person doesn’t switch to English. That’s a good sign it’s working.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d love to see more context-based lessons, especially for business language. Something that helps bridge the gap between common phrases and professional dialogue.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: More integration of cultural education. Language isn’t just about words; it’s about understanding customs and subtleties, which are critical in international business.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Just that language learning is a journey, like diving deeper into the ocean—you’ve got to enjoy the process as much as the destination. It's what keeps me going.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, why not? As long as it doesn't start diving without me!

Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey there! How's it going? I'm Zander, nice to chat with you today.

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: Oh wow, where do I begin? I grew up in South Africa, always running around, fascinated by wildlife. Learning Swahili felt like a natural step since I want to communicate better with the local guides and communities around the wildlife reserves. I’m really a visual learner, and photography helps me see the world differently, just like learning a new language does.

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in good ol' South Africa, in Johannesburg. Quite the bustling place, but my heart's always been with the bush.

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: It was vibrant, that's for sure. There's an energy in Joburg that's hard to match, but I spent a lot of time outside the city on safari trips. Those were the moments that really shaped me, you know? The bush was where I learned to find peace and where my love for wildlife photography began.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: A major turning point was definitely the first time I decided to leave South Africa for an extended trip to Kenya. It was supposed to be just a few months of work, capturing the annual wildebeest migration in the Maasai Mara. But, um, something about the place just rooted me there. It's like the land itself spoke to me, and I knew I had to stay longer.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Well, it opened my eyes to a whole new culture and way of living. The connection to nature here is different than back home, more raw and immediate. It made me realize that being closer to the wildlife and learning from local communities was what I really needed—it felt like I discovered a missing piece of myself here.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I sort of took it one step at a time. I extended my stay, rented a small place near the reserve, and started reaching out to local guides. I even joined some community projects. It was a mix of planning and going with the flow, really. I also began learning Swahili as part of integrating into the community.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, I'm really focused on building bridges between people and wildlife. It's important to me that people understand the beauty and importance of these creatures and their environments. Learning Swahili helps a lot because language is key to understanding and respecting local perspectives. Plus, it enhances my work by allowing me to connect better with the guides who are the real experts on the land.

Q: Why is that important?
A: It's vital because, without these connections, we risk losing the incredible biodiversity here. The guides have knowledge that can't be found in books or documentaries. I want to help tell these stories through my photography, and being able to communicate effectively is a big part of that mission.

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day, hmm, definitely starts early. I set off at dawn with my camera in hand, catch the first light as it hits the savannah. It’s magical. If I manage to photograph something unique or witness a special moment in wildlife behavior, that really makes my day. Later, I’d log onto Duolingo for a bit, maybe practice some Swahili with a guide, and end the day around a campfire, sharing stories.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: If I feel like I’ve captured something really special—like a lioness playing with her cubs or a breathtaking sunset—it gives me a sense of accomplishment. Plus, if I've had meaningful exchanges or learned something new in Swahili, it adds to the richness of the day.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: I tend to weigh the pros and cons, like a photo composition. I look at the elements and how they balance each other. But there's always an element of gut feeling. When a decision feels right, like the perfect moment to click the shutter, I just know. Sometimes I talk it through with colleagues or local friends who know the lay of the land better than I do.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: I'd say a bit of both, really. As a photographer, I need to plan my shoots down to the right lighting and positioning. But wildlife is unpredictable, so you have to be ready to adapt—that's where going with the flow comes in.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Sure, just the other week, I had planned to photograph elephants at a watering hole. I got everything set up, but then some wildebeests showed up first, and there was a whole scene with them crossing a stream. Instead of sticking rigidly to my plan, I switched focus and ended up with some amazing shots that I hadn't anticipated.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: Risk is part and parcel of my work. I mean, being close to wildlife always carries some risk, right? But it's calculated. I make sure to know the territory and the behaviors of the animals. It's a lot like adjusting your camera settings—you take into account the lighting and the movement before clicking that shutter.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Well, I usually start my day before sunrise, packing my gear and heading out to shoot as the day breaks. Mornings are the best for capturing wildlife in action, so I’m often out in the field until noon. Then I head back, review my shots, and have a quick lunch. In the afternoon, I might meet with local guides or community members to hear their stories, practicing my Swahili as I go. Evenings are for editing photos and winding down with some Duolingo practice or reading.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely the early mornings and the long hours out in the field. You have to be sharp, ready to react to unpredictable wildlife activity. And on top of that, understanding Swahili conversations with guides in real-time can be quite demanding, especially when it's technical or involves local idioms.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: I wish I had more energy to delve deeper into language learning. I'm quite aware that mastering Swahili would open up so many more doors, both personally and professionally. Also, I'd like to spend more time working on conservation projects. It’s all about balance, I guess.

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Honestly, it’s been the travel restrictions. They’ve made it tough to get to certain parts of Kenya or to come back to South Africa when needed. It’s limited the scope of my photography work a bit, and I've had to adjust my approach and find opportunities closer to home, which hasn't been all bad, but still frustrating.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I’ve adapted by focusing on projects within reachable areas. Virtual communication has become key, too. I’ve been working more with local guides and community members who can’t travel as well, collaborating remotely. And thankfully, tools like Duolingo keep me up with my language practice from anywhere.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: My family back in South Africa and a close-knit group of friends who are fellow photographers and conservationists. In Kenya, the local guides have become like family too—they’ve taught me so much about the land and its stories.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: They're built on shared experiences and mutual respect. My family has always supported my somewhat unconventional path, and with the friends and guides, there's a sense of camaraderie and shared passion for nature and wildlife.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: When I’m not out on the reserve, I’m usually in my little workspace at home, surrounded by my camera gear and, you know, photos of past expeditions on the walls, which keeps me inspired.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: It feels like home, like everything I need is within reach. It's a space filled with inspiration—sort of like a photo album of my life's adventures. There’s a sense of peace, and it allows me to focus and create without distraction.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: The environment I've created is as close to nature as possible, with plants and natural light. I think it reflects my personality and passions, which keeps me motivated and grounded.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I’d usually reach out to my fellow photographers or local guides. They have such a wealth of experience that it’s like consulting a living library. Sometimes a fresh perspective or a shared laugh in Swahili helps put things in perspective.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: Probably when I missed an important wildlife event because I was stuck in quarantine. I was supposed to document a significant wildlife migration, and being unable to be there felt like missing a once-in-a-lifetime shot. It was disheartening, to say the least.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: I felt quite restless and frustrated. It was more than just a lost opportunity for work; it was about being disconnected from my passion. I found myself questioning my choices and how I could adapt moving forward.

Q: How did you cope?
A: Ultimately, I focused on other projects that were within reach and tried to make the best of the situation. I dove deeper into editing past photos and created a new portfolio. Having a creative outlet helped me process it, and conversations with friends who were in similar situations really made a difference.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Honestly, a walk in nature is the best remedy. It puts things in perspective, reminds me of why I do what I do. I also find that going through my photos, reliving those captured moments, helps ground me when I’m feeling frazzled.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I envision a life where I'm even more integrated into the local communities here, perhaps leading photography workshops or conservation projects. I want to become fluent in Swahili, not just for daily communication but for deeper cultural understanding. Ideally, I'd live a life where every day feels as fulfilling as a successful day on safari.

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I’d love to have more stability. Maybe not in the traditional sense, but in having a consistent platform to share my work and stories about conservation. I also hope to reduce the logistical headaches that come with frequent traveling, so I can focus more on the creative aspects of my work.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, I was trying a mix of phrasebooks and language exchange with locals, but it was slow going. I would jot down phrases during conversations with guides and then look them up later. While practical, it was lacking structure and consistency, making it hard to track progress.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The biggest hassle was definitely the unpredictability of learning. Without a structured approach, I'd often find myself forgetting things I thought I'd learned, especially if I didn’t use them every day. It was like trying to capture a fast-moving animal without the right lens.

Q: Time it really failed?
A: There was a time when I was supposed to translate a phrase during a guided tour, and I completely fumbled with the words. It was embarrassing and also made me realize that my informal learning approach wasn't cutting it. That’s when I seriously considered more structured options.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: I actually heard about it from another photographer who's been using it to brush up on French. He mentioned how it felt like a game, which piqued my interest since learning can sometimes feel like a chore.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The game-like aspect was a big draw, but what really convinced me was its accessibility. I could practice anywhere, whether waiting in a line or just before heading out for a shoot. The promise of short, consistent lessons was appealing given my unpredictable schedule.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.

The lessons were mostly vocabulary exercises using images of common animals and landscape features. Q: Most helpful part?

Q: Most frustrating part?

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Honestly, I find the lack of depth challenging. I'd appreciate more cultural context and advanced conversations that reflect the kind of interactions I actually have. It's like when you're ready for a photo shoot but your gear can't capture the full grandeur of the scene.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: Just the other day, I was trying to follow a conversation about conservation strategies, and a lot of the terminology just wasn't covered in Duolingo’s basic lessons. It felt like I was using a wide-angle lens when I needed a telephoto to zoom in on the details.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, definitely. I complement Duolingo with real-life practice, chatting with locals and guides. Plus, I use a few Swahili language podcasts and YouTube channels, which help with picking up conversational nuances that you just can't get from an app alone.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: The workarounds give me a richer cultural experience and context. Listening to native speakers in their natural environments helps me understand not just the words, but the emotions and cultural significance behind them. It’s like capturing the full spectrum of light in a photo.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case, I suppose, would be hitting a plateau where I can no longer improve my Swahili to the level needed for deeper professional engagements. That’d feel like returning from a shoot with underexposed photos—knowing you missed capturing the full story.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it offers me a little puzzle to solve, something engaging and immediate that fits into my day. I want it to feel rewarding, like taking the perfect shot. Ideally, I’d like it to provide practice that’s relevant to my daily interactions out in the field.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I find myself using a phrase I learned without even thinking about it, like it’s second nature, that's when I know it's working. It's similar to snapping a photo at just the right moment—it feels effortless and natural.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: I’d love to see more context-based learning features, like scenarios specific to certain professions or environments. For example, modules focused on wildlife photography or conservation, where you can practice real-life applicable sentences and vocabulary.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: It’d be amazing if there were more community-driven language resources, where learners contribute to realism and relevance. A platform where local dialects and professional vernacular could be integrated would be game-changing. Like how photography evolves with shared techniques and insights.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: I think we touched on the essentials. Just to add, Duolingo's role in making language learning accessible is invaluable, but there's always room for growth, particularly in bridging cultural and contextual gaps.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, why not? As long as it helps improve the experience for folks like me, I'm all for it. Just don't have it stealing my photo credits, yeah?

A: The idea of bite-sized lessons that fit into my busy days was really appealing. Plus, it’s free, so I thought there was nothing to lose by giving it a try.

A: When I can use a phrase or word I learned in a real conversation, and it works seamlessly, that’s when I know it’s paid off. It feels like landing that perfect suplex – satisfying and effective.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I wish language learning was more integrated into daily life, easier to access and practice without having to carve out extra time. Like having mini-lessons pop up in unexpected places – a little surprise training session during my day.

A: Just that language is such a key part of who we are. For me, blending Mexican and Japanese cultures in my wrestling is amazing, and learning the language is crucial to make that blend really shine.

A: Sure, why not? As long as it’s ready to rumble and learn languages as fiercely as I do!
