Q: Intro greeting
A: Hey, I'm Boris. Nice to meet you. Ready to talk about language learning, let's get started, yeah?

Q: Short version of your life story?
A: I grew up in a small town in Serbia, you know, where basketball is practically religion. Played since I was a kid, made it to coaching, and now I'm here in Spain coaching for Liga ACB. It's been quite a journey, adapting to new cultures and languages. But hey, basketball is universal, right?

Q: Where did you grow up?
A: I grew up in a small town in Serbia. It's a place where everyone knows each other, and basketball is a big deal. Courts everywhere, kids playing all the time, you know?

Q: What was it like growing up there?
A: Growing up there was, I mean, simple but competitive. Everyone played basketball. We used to play on these outdoor courts, rain or shine, snow even. Had a lot of discipline instilled early, but also a lot of fun. It was rough, but it shaped me, like iron sharpening iron.

Q: One turning point in your life?
A: I guess a major turning point was moving to Spain for coaching. I had to learn Spanish fast, adjust to a new style of living—it's exciting but also a bit intimidating. Switching from just being comfortable in Serbian or English to needing to, like, coach in Spanish. Big shift.

Q: Why was that a turning point?
A: Because it was, like, starting from scratch in a way. New language, new team dynamics. Had to prove myself all over again. Couldn't just rely on my Serbian charm or English skills, had to really embrace the culture and language to succeed.

Q: How did you handle that situation?
A: I dove into learning Spanish right away. Used everything I could get—classes, books, apps like Duolingo. I also listened a lot, tried to pick up phrases from the players, coaches. Immersion is key, you know? Like jumping into the deep end of the pool.

Q: What do you care most about right now?
A: Right now, it's all about getting my team to the finals and of course, being fluent in Spanish. Those two things kinda go hand in hand. Communication is crucial in coaching, and I need to connect with my players, get my messages across without any language barrier.

Q: Why is that important?
A: Because to be an effective leader, a coach, you gotta communicate clearly and motivate your team. If they don't understand me, or if I can't relate to them in their language, I might as well be drawing plays in the sand, you know?

Q: What is a good day for you?
A: A good day? That's when my team executes plays perfectly, everyone gels together. Also, if I can get through a conversation in Spanish without stumbling too much, that's a win. Maybe finish the day with some good Serbian food, relax a bit.

Q: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
A: When I see the team work like a well-oiled machine, and I've managed to explain tactics in Spanish without needing to switch to English. It's about progress, little wins both on and off the court.

Q: How do you make big decisions?
A: Big decisions, I take time, analyze from all angles. Like reviewing game tapes. I gather input from assistant coaches, look at stats, players' moods. It's like a chess game, you know? Think ahead, anticipate moves.

Q: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
A: Definitely a planner. In basketball, you have to anticipate and strategize. But I'm flexible enough to adapt when things don't go as planned. You gotta move with the game.

Q: Example showing that?
A: Last season, we planned to play zone defense but the opposing team had incredible shooters. We had to switch to man-to-man on the fly. My initial plan didn't work, so I adapted. It's like having a playbook but knowing when to improvise.

Q: How do you handle risk?
A: I approach risk carefully, like assessing a three-point shot. High reward, but you gotta consider the odds. I weigh options, look at the worst-case scenarios, then make a call. Calculated risks, not reckless ones.

Q: Typical weekday?
A: Typical weekday starts early. I rise around 6, do a bit of exercise, then head to practice. We run drills, review game footage, have strategy meetings. I sneak in some Spanish learning during breaks. After practice, it's meetings with the staff, some more Spanish study at night, and prepping for the next day.

Q: Which parts take the most energy?
A: Definitely practice sessions and meetings. Keeping the team motivated, addressing issues, making sure everyone is on the same page. It requires a lot of mental energy. And learning Spanish, it can be draining trying to get all the nuances right.

Q: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
A: More time to just relax and immerse in Spanish culture. I feel like I'm always on the move, and while I do learn the language, I don't get to enjoy living here as much as I'd like, you know?

Q: Biggest constraint last year?
A: Biggest constraint was definitely time. Balancing the team, games, my personal life. Sometimes, it felt like I needed to be in two places at once, and learning Spanish was another layer. It's a lot to juggle.

Q: How do you deal with that constraint?
A: I had to prioritize, make a tighter schedule. Cut out some non-essential things, focus more on the essentials. Learned to manage my time better, find little pockets here and there to squeeze in some language practice.

Q: People you feel closest to?
A: I'm close to my family back in Serbia, of course. Here, it's mostly my assistant coaches and a few players that I bond with. We share a lot of moments on and off the court.

Q: Describe those relationships.
A: With family, it's like home is always there. With the team, it's trust and respect. We work hard together, celebrate wins, analyze losses. It's a bit like a second family.

Q: Where do you spend most of your time?
A: Most of my time is at the gym or on the court. It's where everything happens for me. Practice, games, strategy sessions—it all revolves around the court.

Q: How do you feel in those spaces?
A: I feel alive, in my element. It's where I thrive, where I bring out the best in myself and others. But there's also a sense of pressure, you know? Wanting to always do better, push the team further.

Q: What makes you feel that way?
A: It's the passion for the game, the desire to succeed and the responsibility to lead. These spaces are where I can impact lives, both professionally and personally. It's a mix of adrenaline and fulfillment.

Q: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
A: I usually turn to my assistant coaches first. We brainstorm solutions together. They understand the game and the dynamics, so it's easy to map out strategies together. For personal issues, I talk to family and a few close friends.

Q: One tough moment in the last year?
A: One tough moment was losing a critical game mid-season. It was a wake-up call about team dynamics and communication issues. We had to dig deep to figure out what went wrong and fix it before it was too late.

Q: How did it affect you?
A: It was a blow, honestly. It made me question my approach, whether I was doing enough to unite the team and communicate effectively in Spanish. But it also motivated me to push harder, reassess strategies, and get everyone on the same page.

Q: How did you cope?
A: I took it as a learning experience. Held team meetings, one-on-ones with players. Spent extra time on language practice to make sure I was clear. I focused on rebuilding morale and tweaking our strategy. Sometimes setbacks are the best teachers.

Q: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
A: Taking a step back, maybe watching some classic basketball games or listening to Serbian music. Also, exercise, like a good run or lifting weights, that helps me clear my mind.

Q: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
A: I hope to be more fluent in Spanish, maybe even coach at a higher level, like a EuroLeague team or even NBA someday. I want my kids to see me succeed here, and who knows, maybe they’ll pick up Spanish and basketball too. Keep evolving, you know?

Q: What do you want to be different?
A: I want to feel more comfortable culturally and linguistically in Spain. Less like the outsider, more like a local. It would be great to reach a point where I don't have to think twice before speaking Spanish.

Q: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
A: Before Duolingo, it was mostly books and tapes, you know, those old-school methods. I also tried watching Spanish TV shows. It helped but was really time-consuming and not very interactive. I often felt like I wasn't making enough progress.

Q: Most annoying part of old method?
A: The books were too formal and not practical for everyday conversations. Tapes weren't interactive, just repetitive. It felt like learning in a vacuum, without feedback or real-world application, you know?

Q: Time it really failed?
A: I remember trying to hold a conversation with a taxi driver, and I completely blanked. I knew the words but couldn't string them together naturally. It was frustrating and embarrassing, a clear sign I needed a different approach.

Q: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
A: A colleague recommended it. They said it was fun and easy to use, like a game. I was skeptical at first but gave it a shot. Turned out to be a pretty handy tool.

Q: What convinced you to try it?
A: The idea that it's like a game, leveling up, reminded me of practicing drills. If I could fit it into my commute or break time, why not? Plus, it was free, so there was nothing to lose.

Q: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
A: So, I open the app, get to the home screen. I usually choose a section I struggle with, like verb conjugations. I do a few exercises, fill in the blanks, repeat phrases out loud. There was this moment the other day—'el equipo está listo'—translates to 'the team is ready'. I paused and thought, 'Yes, that's what I need to be saying!' It feels rewarding when I unlock a new skill, kind of like achieving a milestone on the court.

Q: Most helpful part?
A: The repetition and immediate feedback are great. If I make a mistake, it corrects me on the spot. It's like having a mini-coach in my pocket. Helps reinforce the basics, which is essential in language like it is in basketball.

Q: Most frustrating part?
A: Sometimes the sentences are weird, not really useful in daily conversations. Like, when will I ever need to say, 'The penguin drinks milk'? It's a bit annoying when you're trying to learn practically useful language.

Q: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
A: Overall, it's the lack of context in the language. It's great for vocabulary, but you don't really learn how to use phrases naturally in a conversation. It's missing that real-world applicability sometimes.

Q: One time that frustration showed up?
A: I was in a restaurant, and I tried to order in Spanish using phrases I learned. The waiter looked confused, and I realized I was being too formal or using wrong verb conjugations. It was a disconnect between app learning and real-life application.

Q: Do you use workarounds?
A: Yeah, I supplement with conversations, watching local TV, and listening to Spanish podcasts. It helps bridge the gap Duolingo leaves. I need to hear the language in context, like how you'd watch old games to understand plays better.

Q: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
A: Context and real-life application. Hearing native speakers use idioms, slang, stuff Duolingo doesn't cover. It's like studying more advanced plays—you get nuance and a better feel for the flow.

Q: Worst-case scenario in this space?
A: Worst-case? Not being able to communicate with my team effectively, missing out on that connection. Language is key to coaching, and the thought of failing because of a language barrier, it's unsettling.

Q: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
A: I hope it helps me get one step closer to fluency. Each session, I want to feel like I've chipped away at the language barrier, getting ready to use what I learned in real conversations.

Q: How do you know Duolingo worked?
A: When I find myself using phrases naturally in conversation or picking up things in TV shows I didn't get before. It's like realizing all those practice drills have paid off when you hit that perfect shot.

Q: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
A: Maybe more emphasis on realistic dialogue, practical usage, and less fantasy sentences. It would make the transition from learning to using much smoother.

Q: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
A: I'd say, more integration with cultural learning. Language is tied to culture, and understanding both can make learning more immersive. It's like understanding a team's background; it informs how they play.

Q: Anything important we didn't cover?
A: Only that every tool has its limits. It's up to the learner to push beyond them. Like any athlete, you train but have to get into the game to really learn.

Q: Permission to build a digital twin?
A: Sure, why not? As long as it's not taking my place on the court, I'm fine with it.
